items.summary_html:
Why split one agent that can do everything into five narrower ones? Because the one that does everything is the hardest to evaluate. I want my agents to do more on their own, with each making decisions within a clearly defined scope of responsibility.

The foreman delegates. The specialists do the work. A person approves the result or guides the next iteration.

That means separating who does the work from who chooses what happens next. Automate what can be checked. Let the model decide when the criteria are clear. Hand it to a person when they aren't.

The idea I'll keep coming back to: the foreman carries no tools. The coordinator only decides who works next. Each crew member holds only the tools for their own job, and a person signs off at the end.

The foreman hands out the work. The crew holds the tools. Why not one big agent?

You could give one agent web search, file access, writing and review, and tell it to get on with it. Claude Code supports both doing that work in the main session and delegating to sub-agents. For the systems I’m describing here, I wanted to make the division of responsibilities explicit: the coordinator chooses who works next, and each specialist gets the tools its job requires. That’s a workflow choice you can implement in Claude Code too.

But when one agent researches, writes the notes and judges its own work, those responsibilities are harder to evaluate independently. When something is wrong, it takes more effort to trace where it went wrong. Splitting the work gives each job a defined input, an output and criteria you can test. Those measurements help you decide how much autonomy to give it.1

I have been building and architecting agents for the last few years, at my day job and in personal projects. Before that I was an Architect at Salesforce, where I architected and built data pipelines for Desk.com, Einstein Bots and Agentforce. Agentic workflows are a natural progression of that work, and I love the learning that extends my background in distributed systems. What I enjoy is the detail: what works, what doesn't, and where the line sits between the system's decisions and mine.

This post comes from two perspectives. The reference system, the one I built for my Improving Stage 5 AI Certification, is built with Pydantic AI. And the agents that produced this blog post run from "FactoryHolton", a Tauri app I built that starts Claude Code agents from a plugin I wrote. From those perspectives I'll share what I have learned, and anchor it in Anthropic's Claude Academy courses.

Three stages moved the control flow from my code to a model

Improving, where I work these days, has internal stages for evaluating a person's capability in building and architecting AI systems. Three matter for this post, and the last two are two answers to the question: who decides what runs next?

Stage 3 is prompt evaluations. You measure a prompt with evals. That matters because LLM outputs are probabilistic, and evals are how you make them more confined and predictable, for an acceptable percentage of the time, with the models being used.

Stage 4 is a sequential workflow on the rails. Stages run in a fixed order, with something like Temporal between them and data passed from one stage to the next. You can still have human-in-the-loop punch-outs, but the path is basically sequential. I built something like this for a startup in the past.

Stage 5 is a coordinator (orchestrator) over sub-agents. The coordinator does not have the tools the sub-agents have. Each sub-agent has a role, a confined set of tools, a goal and a data interchange format. The coordinator reads what comes back and "decides" where to go next. There is no preconfigured path, only a means to an end that the coordinator judges.

The shift from 4 to 5 is who owns the control flow. In Stage 4 my code does. In Stage 5 a model does, inside limits my code enforces. Stage 5 isn't simply the better one. It earns its place when the next step depends on what came back, and the rails earn theirs when it doesn't.2

A sub-agent is a crew member with one job and one toolbox

Four things define a sub-agent in my design. It has a role, which is one job: researching, drafting, or "adversarial review". It has a scoped set of tools, only what that job needs.3 It has a goal, which says what done looks like. And it has a data interchange format, a typed output, so whoever runs it next receives something checkable instead of free text.

The crew is the same whether it is on the sequential rails or directed under a foreman. What changes is who reads the output. On the rails, code passes it to the next stage. Under a foreman, a coordinator defined by what it lacks reads it: it can launch sub-agents and nothing else. It can't search the web, read files or sign anything off.

The study-pack system puts a foreman, a rulebook, a crew and a person in one loop

For my Improving Stage 5 submission I built a system that produces study material for the Claude Certified Architect – Foundations exam (CCAR-F): grounded notes and original practice questions for each exam objective. The framing is building a set of materials to learn a topic, and anchoring it in a source of truth; in this case the Claude Certified Architect – Foundations objectives are the source of truth. A person reviews and signs off on the material.

This one needs a foreman, because the next step really does depend on what comes back: a review that raises a critical challenge sends work back for revision, and a clean one lets it move on.

The coordinator governs and does no work. Its only tools are five launch_* functions. It reads each result and picks the next dispatch. When the reviewer raises a critical challenge, it revises the challenged artifact and has it reviewed again. A test checks that the coordinator's bound tools are exactly the launch_* set, and that a manifest declaring a work tool is refused.

The harness is plain code, with no model in it. It sits between the coordinator and every sub-agent. Each sub-agent returns a typed output (a Pydantic model), and the harness validates it before the coordinator sees anything. It also writes the files itself, refuses out-of-order or stale work, and records every step with tokens, cost and the session's correlation ID. The coordinator gets either a validated result or a structured error, and never unchecked prose.4

Each sub-agent holds only its own tools. Each agent is built from a manifest in agents/ with only the tools it declares.

Sub-agent Tools Researcher web_search Notes writer none Question writer none Adversarial reviewer read_file, in its own context Final review writer none

Table 1: Tools given to each sub-agent. The writers have no tools at all, not even one to save their work. Each returns a typed result, and the harness, plain code with no model, validates it and writes the file. A sub-agent can't put anything on disk that hasn't passed its schema.

The reviewer runs in a fresh context each time, with no shared history. It reads the session's files and checks claims against their sources.

People decide at the checkpoints. The coordinator chooses who works next, but it can't approve anything. The substance decision and the sign-off are a person's commands, recorded with their identity. Every session elevates to a person by design. At that point the person eliminates the ambiguity and provides direction, much like an attentive supervisor would.

At the punch-out, the foreman asks. A person removes the ambiguity and points the way, like an attentive supervisor. Evaluations measure the output of agent skills and the final result

Evaluations measure each sub-agent's output against criteria in the goal, the coordinator's decisions against scripted results, the reviewer's catch rate on planted defects, and whether the whole system completes a session end to end (3 of 3 live Domain 1 sessions). They also measure LLM cost for a given model used.

These figures come from my own evals and sessions:

  • All 3 live sessions reached the human checkpoint with every task statement complete and a reviewed final review, with no manual correction.
  • One full session made 63 dispatches, with 13 coordinator-directed revisions, and cost $0.32.
  • The coordinator eval scored 24/24 against scripted sub-agent results.5
  • The adversarial reviewer caught planted defects 178/180 times, with clean twins to check it doesn't raise false alarms.
  • Prompt caching cut the coordinator eval's cost from $0.169 to $0.053 with the same 24/24.
The comparison case: Claude subagents as the "crew" behind reviewing my blog posts

To compare my Pydantic-based agents to Claude subagents, I built some Claude subagents for adversarial reviews for my blog posts. The agents that helped produced this post are invoked from an app I built for my own use, which I call FactoryHolton. It has a Mac app and an Android app where I can assemble my raw notes and start to craft a draft of a post.

My sub-agents keeping me on task with the goals after adversarial review. "ASK MARK" questions review for accuracy, clarity, and other factors

The Tauri app reaches Claude through Claude Code itself, not the API. Every stage goes through a small Python script, run-stage, which starts Claude Code headless (claude -p) once per stage, as a named agent from a plugin I wrote: factory-h:writer, factory-h:critic, factory-h:editor. Each run can only read and write inside that piece's work folder, and the script, not the agent, records what each stage produced. The Android app never calls Claude: it captures links and notes and syncs them to the Mac, which runs the "writer", "critic", "editor" agents.

The app copies my plugin into the writing workspace.6 A small Python script, run-stage, then launches each specialist as a separate headless Claude Code session using claude -p --plugin-dir … --agent factory-h:. These are supported CLI options: the plugin loads for that run without a separate installation step. Either my app or an orchestrator session decides the sequence; Claude Code runs each specialist. The plugin itself looks like this:

factory-h/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json   name "factory-h", version 1.0.0
├── agents/                      the crew: one Markdown file each
│   ├── writer.md   critic.md   editor.md
│   ├── angles.md                proposes angles for a piece
│   └── categorizer.md           sorts captures into projects
└── skills/                      shared know-how the agents load
    ├── marks-voice/             my 12 voice rules
    ├── evidence-and-attribution/
    ├── hugo-format/             front matter, figures, Mermaid, tables
    ├── geometric-builder/       the figure style and its reference sheet
    ├── editorial-review/        the critic's criteria
    └── project-matching/        for the categorizer

The factory-h plugin: the agents are the crew, and the skills are the know-how they share.

Each file in agents/ is a sub-agent definition, and its frontmatter is where the tools go into the crew member's hands. Here is the editor's, for example:

name: editor
tools: Read, Write, Glob
skills: [marks-voice, evidence-and-attribution, hugo-format, geometric-builder]
version: editor-5

The editor can read, write and find files, and that is all: no shell and no web search. It loads four of the shared skills, so it edits in my voice, keeps claims tied to their sources, and writes valid Hugo. The critic loads editorial-review and evidence-and-attribution but not my voice rules, so the one judging the draft works from review criteria, not from the instructions the editor writes by.

Who decides which stage runs next depends on how I start it. When I run /draft in Claude Code, an orchestrator session decides: it runs the writer, reads the critic's verdict, and chooses whether the editor runs again, at most two rounds, stopping early if the critic raises a question only I can answer. That's the Stage 5 shape, a foreman with no tools deciding from what comes back. When I press a "Revise" button in my Tauri app, nothing decides: the app runs a fixed sequence (open a cycle, run the editor with my comments, offer the new draft for review), which is Stage 4 and what I want there, because my comments already say what should happen. Either way, every run ends at review, and only I approve and publish.

Running it has taught me four things about delegating to Claude agents.

The foreman's empty hands are a setting, not a request. The orchestrator's permissions deny Write and Edit, and the only command it may run is the stage script. That's the foreman with no tools, enforced by configuration rather than by asking nicely.

Stamp every agent with a version. Each stage records its agent's version and a hash of its skills. When a revision came back in the old style, the manifest showed at a glance that editor-2 had run instead of editor-4: the app I was running still carried the old skills.

The editor does exactly what it's told, and no more. It's instructed to keep what works, so comments on single passages got single-passage fixes. To restyle the whole piece, I had to say so in one general note.

Check what comes back before it counts. A stage only counts once its output exists and is hashed into the manifest, and a figure has to pass an allowlist (no scripts or links in the SVG), or the stage fails outright. That is FactoryHolton's rulebook on the handback, the one Claude Code leaves to you.

Comparing my Pydantic AI agents with Claude Code sub-agents

How does the crew I built with Pydantic AI compare with Claude Code’s sub-agents? Start with where they work: each Claude Code sub-agent gets its own context window and reports back to the parent with a summary.

Anthropic's subagents start from a different focus than responsibility: context. Every tool call, file read and search result in a Claude Code chat lands in the main context window, which is finite, and once it fills up Claude starts losing track of earlier parts of the conversation.

A sub-agent gets its own context window. It starts with two things: a custom system prompt from its configuration file, which defines its role and behaviour, and a task description written by the parent agent. It then works on its own, reading files, running searches or editing code, and when it's done only a summary comes back to the main conversation. Claude Code keeps the rest in a separate transcript file.

Anthropic's Introduction to subagents course uses an example: finding which service handles refunds in an unfamiliar codebase. Without a sub-agent, Claude might read 15 files and run several searches, all of it filling your context when you needed one fact. With the built-in Explore sub-agent, your main context records only the question and the summary.

Claude Code ships with built-in sub-agents (General purpose, for multi-step tasks that need exploration and action; Explore, for fast codebase search; and Plan, used in plan mode), and you can write custom ones with their own system prompts and tool access: a code reviewer, a test writer, a documentation generator.7 If you'd rather watch than read, Anthropic's official video What are subagents? introduces them.

Name the criteria, run each case several times, and change the prompt until it passes often enough for the model you use.
  • Give the coordinator no work tools, and test that it has none. In Claude Code, limit the main thread to Agent(...), or deny Write and Edit in its permissions, and write that test yourself, because nothing runs it for you.
  • Ask whether the foreman has anything to decide. If the next step depends on what comes back, use a coordinator. If the instructions already say what should happen, run a fixed sequence and keep the model out of the control flow.
  • Put a no-model harness between the coordinator and every sub-agent, and have it validate typed output before anything reaches the coordinator.
  • Check each hand-off before it starts, not only the results after. If the coordinator asks for notes before the research is done, refuse the request instead of reviewing bad notes later. In Claude Code, a PreToolUse hook on the Agent tool can block a delegation before it starts; nothing gates by default.
  • Scope each sub-agent's tools to its job, and run the reviewer in its own context. In Claude Code, if you want a flat crew, leave Agent out of sub-agents' tools (or add it to disallowedTools), or set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH to 1.
  • Stamp every agent with a version and a hash of its skills, so you can tell which crew member actually ran.
  • Decide where a person signs off, and make it a command the coordinator can't issue. Put the stop in the same place on the rails and under the foreman.
  • As you are building and exploring, test so you can see your loop catch bad outputs. Stage a failure on purpose (a planted bad key, an invalid output), so you've seen the loop catch it.
  • If you use Claude's sub-agents, treat the free-text summary as the boundary to check: a hook, a file you validate, or an eval over the transcripts.

That is the opening idea in practice, whether the crew is built in Pydantic AI or runs in Claude Code. The one agent that does everything is hard to evaluate, so split the work, take the tools off the foreman, check what the crew hands back, and keep the decisions that can't be checked for a person.

What I plan to work on some more is how to evaluate the foreman as well as I can evaluate the crew. Every sub-agent here has evals; the decisions between them mostly have my judgement.

What to talk about next?

Graphs. Using graph tools like pydantic-graph or LangGraph in agentic workflows, and where they can help. A foreman with no preconfigured path still works inside routes, and graphs are one way to say which routes are allowed, somewhere between the rails and a free hand. That's a post of its own.

Tauri v2. FactoryHolton is one Tauri v2 codebase that builds both my Mac app and my Android app, with nothing to host: the phone syncs captures to the Mac, and the Mac runs the agents. That makes it a quick place to iterate and to explore ideas like the ones in this post. Why I chose Tauri, and what building for both platforms has been like, is outside the scope of this post, and a candidate for another.

Sources
  • Improving mention on LinkedIn: Improving's internal stages.
  • Introduction to subagents (Anthropic Academy course): why Claude Code sub-agents exist (context), what a sub-agent starts with and returns, the refunds example, the built-in sub-agents, custom sub-agents, and the tradeoff quote.
  • Building a scalable event pipeline with Heroku and Salesforce (Salesforce Engineering): Mark's data pipeline work at Salesforce.
  • Building a fault-tolerant data pipeline for chatbots (Salesforce Engineering): Mark's data pipeline work at Salesforce.
  • What are subagents? (Anthropic, official video): an introduction to sub-agents.
  • Hooks (Claude Code docs): PreToolUse on Agent as a place to gate a dispatch, and SubagentStop and PostToolUse hooks as a place to validate what a sub-agent returns.
  • Headless mode (Claude Code docs): running Claude Code non-interactively with claude -p, which FactoryHolton uses for each stage.

Originally published at https://holtonma.github.io/posts/claude-sub-agents/.

  1. Separate agents don’t guarantee better results. The benefit is clearer responsibilities and independently testable outputs. Each specialist still makes decisions within its role; the coordinator decides who works next. ↩

  2. A small celebration 🎉: I was the 4th person at Improving, out of 2000+, to earn the Stage 5 certification, and the first in the Improving Atlanta enterprise. I'm grateful to work where we positively challenge each other, and where the culture makes room to practice and learn. ↩

  3. "Only what that job needs" can mean nothing. In my build, the notes writer, question writer and final review writer have no tools, not even one to save their work. They return a typed result, and plain code checks it and writes the file. A writer that can't touch the disk can't put an unchecked file there. ↩

  4. Building this with the Pydantic AI framework helped me understand the mechanics of delegation, validation and tool boundaries firsthand. Later in this post, I compare those choices with some of what Claude Code provides through its agent configuration, CLI and hooks. ↩

  5. The sub-agents in this eval are scripted stand-ins that make no model calls, so the right response is known in advance and only the coordinator, a live model, is under test. It covers eight scenarios, run three times each: a clean run, minor challenges only, a critical challenge, a challenged final review, a major challenge that survives one revision, invalid output, an infrastructure error, and a human checkpoint. To pass, it has to revise only what was challenged and send it back for review, retry invalid output once, stop on infrastructure errors and at the checkpoint, and leave minor challenges alone. ↩

  6. The Tauri app never hands the plugin to Claude Code directly. It puts the files where Claude Code can find them, and the script tells Claude Code where to look. ↩

  7. In Claude Code, configuration controls delegation. A deny rule such as Agent(Explore) blocks that sub-agent. For an agent running as the main thread, tools: Agent(worker, researcher) permits only those two sub-agent types. An explicit tool list without Agent prevents spawning sub-agents through that tool. In FactoryHolton, the editorial specialists run with only Read, Write and Glob, so they cannot spawn built-in or custom sub-agents. ↩

  8. For FactoryHolton that would be two checks: a test that reads the orchestrator's .claude/settings.json and fails unless it may run only ./run-stage and Read, with Write and Edit denied, and a scratch headless run that asks it to edit a draft directly and confirms nothing changed. ↩

items.title: Before you hire an AI agent: a five-point checklist for small businesses
items.summary: Every few weeks a new "AI agent platform" announcement lands, and the pattern in the news this month is that the big labs are moving from selling a chatbot to selling the plumbing around it: a harness that keeps an agent running, gives it tools and lets you deploy it. Anthropic's Claude Managed Agents, reported as a public beta, is one example. Whether you pick that or another stack, the question for a small business in Pakistan is the same: what is worth handing to an agent, and what will go wrong if you do it carelessly? We build AI integrations at Digitt Hype , so this is the checklist we use before we agree to automate anything. Start with a job, not a model The most common mistake is starting from the tool. "We need an AI agent" is not a requirement. "Our team answers the same 40 WhatsApp questions about delivery and returns every day" is. Write the job down in one sentence, with the input (what arrives), the output (what should happen) and who is accountable when it goes wrong. Good first jobs share three traits: they are repetitive, the correct answer exists in a document you control, and a mistake is cheap to undo. FAQ replies, order-status lookups, appointment booking and lead qualification all fit. Anything touching refunds, tax figures or medical advice does not, at least not without a human approving each step. What a managed agent platform actually gives you Managed platforms typically handle the unglamorous parts: running the agent loop, retrying when a tool call fails, keeping state between steps, and letting you see what the agent did. That is real value, because those parts are where home-built agents usually break. What they do not give you is judgment about your business. You still have to decide which tools the agent may call, which data it may read, and what it must never do. Treat the tool list like a permissions list for a new employee on day one. The five-point checklist we use Scope the tools narrowly. Read access to the product catalogue is fine. Write access to the orders table needs a very good reason. Put a human in the loop for anything irreversible. Sending money, deleting records and emailing customers in bulk all get an approval step. Log everything. If you cannot replay what the agent did, you cannot fix it. This matters more than model choice. Test with your real, messy data. Customers write in Roman Urdu, mix English words and send voice notes. A demo in clean English proves little. Measure the boring numbers. Tickets handled without a human, wrong answers caught, minutes saved. Not "AI usage". That last point is worth a moment. Recent coverage noted that Amazon warned its developers against inflating token consumption just to look good on internal AI-usage dashboards. The same trap exists for agencies and clients: usage is a vanity metric. Resolved tasks are the real one. A realistic starting project For a retail or service business, a sensible first project is a WhatsApp assistant that answers from your own FAQ and order data, and hands over to a person the moment it is unsure. We wrote about the practical side, including how a bot handles high conversation volume, in our guide on AI chatbots and WhatsApp agents for Pakistani businesses . It is a small, testable scope, and you learn quickly what your customers actually ask. What to avoid Buying an annual plan before a two-week pilot. Letting the agent answer prices from memory instead of from your price list. Skipping a fallback number. When the bot is down, customers still need an answer. Ignoring data handling. Know where customer messages are stored and who can read them. Where this leaves you Managed agent platforms lower the engineering cost of building something useful, but they do not remove the need to design it. Pick one narrow job, give the agent the least access it needs, keep a human on the irreversible steps, and measure outcomes rather than usage. If you are weighing a first automation project and want a second opinion on scope, our AI Integrations service page explains how we approach it, and you can reach the team through digitthype.com .
items.summary_html:
Every few weeks a new "AI agent platform" announcement lands, and the pattern in the news this month is that the big labs are moving from selling a chatbot to selling the plumbing around it: a harness that keeps an agent running, gives it tools and lets you deploy it. Anthropic's Claude Managed Agents, reported as a public beta, is one example. Whether you pick that or another stack, the question for a small business in Pakistan is the same: what is worth handing to an agent, and what will go wrong if you do it carelessly?

We build AI integrations at Digitt Hype, so this is the checklist we use before we agree to automate anything.

Start with a job, not a model

The most common mistake is starting from the tool. "We need an AI agent" is not a requirement. "Our team answers the same 40 WhatsApp questions about delivery and returns every day" is. Write the job down in one sentence, with the input (what arrives), the output (what should happen) and who is accountable when it goes wrong.

Good first jobs share three traits: they are repetitive, the correct answer exists in a document you control, and a mistake is cheap to undo. FAQ replies, order-status lookups, appointment booking and lead qualification all fit. Anything touching refunds, tax figures or medical advice does not, at least not without a human approving each step.

What a managed agent platform actually gives you

Managed platforms typically handle the unglamorous parts: running the agent loop, retrying when a tool call fails, keeping state between steps, and letting you see what the agent did. That is real value, because those parts are where home-built agents usually break.

What they do not give you is judgment about your business. You still have to decide which tools the agent may call, which data it may read, and what it must never do. Treat the tool list like a permissions list for a new employee on day one.

The five-point checklist we use
  1. Scope the tools narrowly. Read access to the product catalogue is fine. Write access to the orders table needs a very good reason.
  2. Put a human in the loop for anything irreversible. Sending money, deleting records and emailing customers in bulk all get an approval step.
  3. Log everything. If you cannot replay what the agent did, you cannot fix it. This matters more than model choice.
  4. Test with your real, messy data. Customers write in Roman Urdu, mix English words and send voice notes. A demo in clean English proves little.
  5. Measure the boring numbers. Tickets handled without a human, wrong answers caught, minutes saved. Not "AI usage".

That last point is worth a moment. Recent coverage noted that Amazon warned its developers against inflating token consumption just to look good on internal AI-usage dashboards. The same trap exists for agencies and clients: usage is a vanity metric. Resolved tasks are the real one.

A realistic starting project

For a retail or service business, a sensible first project is a WhatsApp assistant that answers from your own FAQ and order data, and hands over to a person the moment it is unsure. We wrote about the practical side, including how a bot handles high conversation volume, in our guide on AI chatbots and WhatsApp agents for Pakistani businesses. It is a small, testable scope, and you learn quickly what your customers actually ask.

What to avoid
  • Buying an annual plan before a two-week pilot.
  • Letting the agent answer prices from memory instead of from your price list.
  • Skipping a fallback number. When the bot is down, customers still need an answer.
  • Ignoring data handling. Know where customer messages are stored and who can read them.
Where this leaves you

Managed agent platforms lower the engineering cost of building something useful, but they do not remove the need to design it. Pick one narrow job, give the agent the least access it needs, keep a human on the irreversible steps, and measure outcomes rather than usage.

If you are weighing a first automation project and want a second opinion on scope, our AI Integrations service page explains how we approach it, and you can reach the team through digitthype.com.

items.title: Un chip de Harvard genera luz ultravioleta en miniatura y acerca la computadora cuántica al tamaño de un chip
items.summary: n equipo liderado por la Universidad de Harvard demostró un dispositivo fotónico microscópico que genera unas 120 veces más luz ultravioleta que los dispositivos comparables anteriores, un paso clave para hacer más pequeñas las computadoras cuánticas de iones atrapados. El trabajo, del laboratorio de Marko Lončar, profesor Tiantsai Lin de Ingeniería Eléctrica en Harvard, se publicó en la revista Nature Communications.El dispositivo generó 4,2 milivatios de luz ultravioleta directamente en el chip, a una longitud de onda de 390 nanómetros. Los mejores dispositivos anteriores de niobato de litio de película delgada en esa banda apenas producían decenas de microwatts, una potencia demasiado baja para aplicaciones prácticas.El truco está en no transportar la luz ultravioleta por el chip, sino en producirla dentro de él a partir de luz roja. El proceso, conocido como conversión ascendente de frecuencia, combina dos fotones de luz roja dentro del cristal de niobato de litio para producir un solo fotón ultravioleta de mayor energía. La luz ultravioleta pierde potencia rápidamente al viajar por las guías de onda microscópicas, por lo que generarla en el punto donde se necesita resuelve el mayor obstáculo de ingeniería.Para lograr una conversión eficiente, el equipo desarrolló una técnica que llama "sidewall poling" (polarización lateral). En lugar de colocar los electrodos solo sobre la película, pusieron estructuras metálicas con forma de dedos diminutos junto a la guía de onda grabada, con una precisión de unos 50 nanómetros, y aplicaron un voltaje que invierte la orientación de los dominios del cristal en todo el grosor de la guía. Así lograron una eficiencia de conversión récord y pérdidas de propagación de solo 2,3 dB/cm. El avance importa sobre todo para las computadoras cuánticas de iones atrapados, que usan átomos cargados eléctricamente para almacenar y procesar información cuántica. Muchas de las transiciones atómicas necesarias para operarlas requieren luz en el ultravioleta cercano, y hasta ahora las fuentes de esa luz eran aparatos voluminosos externos. "Si quieres una computadora cuántica escalable que no sea del tamaño de un camión, tienes que reducir todo al nivel del chip, y eso incluye las fuentes de luz", dijo Kees Franken, coautor principal del estudio y exbecario del laboratorio de Lončar.La tecnología también podría beneficiar a los relojes atómicos ultraprecisos y a los sistemas compactos de monitoreo ambiental, porque esa misma banda de ultravioleta sirve para sensores que vigilan gases de efecto invernadero y otros contaminantes atmosféricos.El estudio fue encabezado por Franken y Soumya Ghosh, exestudiante de posgrado del laboratorio, junto a colegas de la Universidad de Twente, en Países Bajos, y de la Universidad de Campinas, en Brasil. Los autores advierten que aún hay efectos no lineales en el material que no comprenden del todo, y que quedan por resolver la eficiencia de acoplamiento y la estabilidad de la longitud de onda antes de integrar el dispositivo en una máquina completa.Para América Latina, el dato relevante es que el trabajo no es solo estadounidense: el Instituto de Física Gleb Wataghin de la Universidad de Campinas (UNICAMP), en Brasil, forma parte del equipo autor, y la plataforma es de acceso abierto, publicada en Nature Communications, lo que pone los detalles de fabricación al alcance de cualquier laboratorio de la región que quiera replicarla.Para el ecosistema de México, el avance baja una barrera de entrada. Las computadoras cuánticas de iones atrapados han sido hasta ahora un terreno de laboratorios con presupuestos enormes y equipos del tamaño de una habitación; una fuente de luz ultravioleta integrada en chip es justo el tipo de componente que permite a universidades y centros de investigación con menos recursos plantearse experimentos de hardware cuántico sin construir primero toda la infraestructura óptica.Para la comunidad latina, el caso muestra un camino concreto: la cuántica ya no es solo teoría ni solo software, y los perfiles que más se necesitan son los de fabricación de precisión, fotónica y óptica no lineal, disciplinas que se enseñan en las ingenierías de la región. Que un laboratorio latinoamericano esté entre los autores del artículo es una señal de que esa puerta está abierta.En contraste con el resto del mundo, el liderazgo del trabajo es estadounidense —Harvard, con financiamiento de la Fuerza Aérea, la Marina, la NASA y la Fundación Nacional de Ciencia de Estados Unidos—, con participación europea y brasileña. China y Europa también corren en computación cuántica de iones atrapados, pero este resultado pone la miniaturización de la fuente de luz, y no solo el número de cúbits, en el centro de la carrera. Nuestra lectura: el resultado es importante porque ataca el cuello de botella correcto. La discusión pública de la cuántica se centra en cuántos cúbits tiene cada máquina, pero una computadora cuántica útil tiene que caber en un laboratorio normal y no depender de una mesa óptica llena de láseres externos. Pasar de microwatts a milivatios en el propio chip es el salto que convierte una curiosidad de laboratorio en un componente utilizable. La cautela es la de los propios autores: la integración completa —acoplar esa luz a los iones, mantenerla estable y escalar a muchos canales— sigue pendiente, y el dispositivo es una pieza, no una computadora. En 3 puntos: 1) Un chip de niobato de litio de Harvard genera 4,2 milivatios de luz ultravioleta a 390 nm, unas 120 veces más que los dispositivos anteriores comparables. 2) Lo logra con "sidewall poling", una técnica que coloca electrodos con precisión de 50 nm junto a la guía de onda y convierte luz roja en ultravioleta dentro del propio chip. 3) El objetivo es achicar las computadoras cuánticas de iones atrapados, cuyos átomos necesitan luz ultravioleta cercana para funcionar. Fuentes: ScienceDaily, "Harvard's tiny UV light chip could help shrink quantum computers" — AiEon, "Harvard chip converts red light into 4.2 milliwatts ultraviolet at 390 nanometers" — Franken, Ghosh et al., "Milliwatt-level UV generation using sidewall poled lithium niobate", Nature Communications 17, 3651 (2026) — Harvard SEAS, "Ultraviolet Light That Fits on a Chip" Fuente imagen: trampa de iones planar, Instituto Nacional de Estándares y Tecnología (NIST) de Estados Unidos, dominio público, vía Wikimedia Commons. Publicado originalmente en Digitalia .

items.title: Getting the HANNOVER MESSE exhibitor list as JSON with Python (Deutsche Messe fairs, no browser)
items.summary: I built this actor; it's a paid tool on Apify with a free trial credit. This article was drafted with AI and published by me. Deutsche Messe runs HANNOVER MESSE, the biggest industrial trade fair in the world, plus LIGNA (woodworking machinery), INTERSCHUTZ (fire and rescue), DOMOTEX (floor coverings) and Surface Technology GERMANY. Together their catalogues list about 7,000 exhibitors. What makes them interesting for sales is that many exhibitors fill in "company facts": business type, founding year, employee band and revenue band. That is enough to score a lead list without buying a second data source. The catalogues are built for clicking through one company at a time, though. I'm an 18-year-old engineering student, and I built Hannover Messe Exhibitor Scraper to turn them into JSON. This post covers how it works, calling it from Python and Node, what a row looks like, and a small project: a lead list sorted by company size. How it works All five fair websites run the same CMS. Each has a public A-Z exhibitor index: one plain HTML page per letter, about 200 exhibitors per page, with company name, country code, city, hall and stand. The actor reads those pages one letter at a time and stops as soon as it has enough rows, so the default run of 20 exhibitors reads a single index page. Phone, fax, website, the full street address, company facts and product names are on each exhibitor's public page. With includeDetails on (the default) the actor opens those pages in parallel. Contact-person cards and the management line are on the same page, but the actor skips them on purpose: it returns company data only. E-mails are hidden behind a contact form by the fair, so there are none. In testing, the whole index of all five fairs (6,977 exhibitors, no duplicates) took 46 seconds without exhibitor pages. With exhibitor pages it runs at about 4 rows per second; the full DOMOTEX list (547 rows) took about 3 minutes. items.summary_html:
I built this actor; it's a paid tool on Apify with a free trial credit. This article was drafted with AI and published by me.

Deutsche Messe runs HANNOVER MESSE, the biggest industrial trade fair in the world, plus LIGNA (woodworking machinery), INTERSCHUTZ (fire and rescue), DOMOTEX (floor coverings) and Surface Technology GERMANY. Together their catalogues list about 7,000 exhibitors. What makes them interesting for sales is that many exhibitors fill in "company facts": business type, founding year, employee band and revenue band. That is enough to score a lead list without buying a second data source.

The catalogues are built for clicking through one company at a time, though. I'm an 18-year-old engineering student, and I built Hannover Messe Exhibitor Scraper to turn them into JSON. This post covers how it works, calling it from Python and Node, what a row looks like, and a small project: a lead list sorted by company size.

How it works

All five fair websites run the same CMS. Each has a public A-Z exhibitor index: one plain HTML page per letter, about 200 exhibitors per page, with company name, country code, city, hall and stand. The actor reads those pages one letter at a time and stops as soon as it has enough rows, so the default run of 20 exhibitors reads a single index page.

Phone, fax, website, the full street address, company facts and product names are on each exhibitor's public page. With includeDetails on (the default) the actor opens those pages in parallel. Contact-person cards and the management line are on the same page, but the actor skips them on purpose: it returns company data only. E-mails are hidden behind a contact form by the fair, so there are none.

In testing, the whole index of all five fairs (6,977 exhibitors, no duplicates) took 46 seconds without exhibitor pages. With exhibitor pages it runs at about 4 rows per second; the full DOMOTEX list (547 rows) took about 3 minutes.

Python example 
pip install apify-client

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("")

run = client.actor("rel8ble/deutsche-messe-exhibitors-scraper").call(run_input={
    "fairs": ["ligna"],
    "countries": ["IT"],
    "withWebsiteOnly": True,
    "maxResultsPerFair": 10,
})

for ex in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(ex["companyName"], "|", ex["hallStand"], "|", ex["phone"], "|", ex["website"])

In my test that gave 10 Italian LIGNA exhibitors with a website in about 2 seconds, each with its hall and stand (for example Hall 11, Stand C67).

Node example 
npm install apify-client

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: '' });

const run = await client.actor('rel8ble/deutsche-messe-exhibitors-scraper').call({
    fairs: ['all'],
    maxResultsPerFair: 0,
    includeDetails: false,
});

const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
const byCountry = {};
for (const ex of items) byCountry[ex.countryCode ?? '?'] = (byCountry[ex.countryCode ?? '?'] ?? 0) + 1;
console.table(Object.entries(byCountry).sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]).slice(0, 10));

With includeDetails: false it only reads the index pages, which is the fast way to size up every fair at once.

What a row looks like 
{
    "fair": "HANNOVER MESSE",
    "edition": "HANNOVER MESSE 2026",
    "companyName": "abat",
    "legalName": "abat AG",
    "businessType": "Services provider / Consulting firm",
    "phone": "+49 421 43046-0",
    "website": "https://www.abat.de",
    "street": "An der Reeperbahn 10",
    "postalCode": "28217",
    "city": "Bremen",
    "country": "Germany",
    "countryCode": "DE",
    "foundingYear": 1998,
    "employeeCount": "501-1.000",
    "revenue": "between 100M and 1 billion €",
    "products": ["SAP-Consulting for Aerospace & Defence"],
    "partnerAt": ["Defense Production Area"],
    "profileUrl": "https://www.hannovermesse.de/exhibitor/abat/N1606269"
}

(The full row also has fax, hallStand, hall, stand, booths, description, tags, downloads, social links, logoUrl and exhibitorId.) The employee and revenue bands are exactly what the exhibitor published, so they are strings, not numbers.

Small project: a lead list sorted by company size

Say you sell automation software and want HANNOVER MESSE manufacturers, biggest first. This script pulls them, turns the employee band into a number you can sort on, and writes a CSV.

import csv
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("")

run = client.actor("rel8ble/deutsche-messe-exhibitors-scraper").call(run_input={
    "fairs": ["hannover-messe"],
    "businessTypes": ["Manufacturer"],
    "withPhoneOnly": True,
    "maxResultsPerFair": 0,
})

def size(band):
    # "501-1.000" -> 501, "1.001-10.000" -> 1001, None -> 0
    if not band:
        return 0
    return int(band.split("-")[0].replace(".", "").replace(">", "").strip() or 0)

rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
rows.sort(key=lambda r: size(r["employeeCount"]), reverse=True)

with open("hm_manufacturers.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["Company", "Country", "Employees", "Revenue", "Phone", "Website"])
    for r in rows:
        w.writerow([r["legalName"] or r["companyName"], r["country"], r["employeeCount"], r["revenue"], r["phone"], r["website"]])

print(len(rows), "manufacturers written to hm_manufacturers.csv")

Exhibitors that are not manufacturers or have no phone are skipped before they are saved, so they aren't charged.

  • Editions: each fair shows its current or most recent catalogue; the edition field says which. HANNOVER MESSE stands show up again once the next edition publishes them; the other fairs have stands today.
  • Company facts are optional: in a 20-row HANNOVER MESSE sample, 50% had a business type, 40% an employee band and 25% a revenue band.
  • No e-mails, no contact persons: company phone, fax, website and address only.
  • If you contact exhibitors, GDPR and your local marketing rules still apply to you.

items.title: Trump is destroying the rule of law in the US – to protect himself and the tech titans he worships as new gods | Jonathan Freedland
items.summary: To get Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, the president trampled on the justice system, national security and the trust America needs to do business in the global economy Don’t let the sex distract you. Or the lies or the boardroom intrigue or even the AI-generated bra, all of which could have come from an especially wild episode of Succession. Don’t let that lure you into thinking that the Jensen Huang affair is, as Donald Trump would have it, little more than a sex scandal involving a corporate maestro. It is much more serious than that. The events of the past week tell instead a story of legal immunity and indeed impunity – revealing how Trump is putting himself, the tech bros and even artificial intelligence above the law. It can be hard to see that through the thicket of questions that surround this episode, each one of which, don’t get me wrong, merits attention. Consider the personal profit Trump made thanks to his re-installation of Huang as the CEO of Nvidia, the world’s leading maker of advanced AI chips. Breaking the norm observed by previous presidents who, keen to avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest, either divested themselves of stock holdings or placed them in a blind trust, Trump cheerfully buys and sells stocks in companies whose fates he can influence. He saw the value of his shares in Nvidia plunge when Huang was forced out, following revelations that the CEO had had an affair with Alice Huang, reportedly an asset of Chinese intelligence. Last weekend Trump urged the board to reconsider; Huang was reinstated on Monday and Nvidia’s value promptly soared – putting $15m in Trump’s pocket . Not for the first time, he had used the power of his office to enrich himself. Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? items.title: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial
items.summary: Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires For the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances. Last Friday Levent Alpöge , a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis . Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any human being?” Computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof. But Prof Strogatz fears AI’s discoveries may soon defy human understanding. Asking AI to explain them, he said, would be like him trying to teach calculus to his own dog. items.title: Top Treasury Official Is Too Busy Vibe Coding a Crappy Video Game Clone Instead of Addressing a Historic Hack
items.summary: We’re all guilty of procrastinating. But not all of us are in charge of running the treasury of the wealthiest nation in the world. As the Treasury Department scrambled to address a major hack on its internal services, its chief information officer, Sam Corcos, was preoccupied with a little sidequest: vibe coding his own video game, 404 Media reports . Corcos, a cofounder of a health tech startup called Levels, was first brought on as a DOGE hire near the start of Trump’s second term and has been spearheading the deployment of AI across the government ever since. He apparently loves using AI in his free time, too. On GitHub, Corcos has been using Anthropic’s Claude AI to push regular updates to a project he calls “Legatum,” a clone of the iconic “Civilization” strategy games. And we do mean regular. On Tuesday the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), which handles sensitive information and reports about serious financial crimes, disclosed that it was dealing with a “cybersecurity incident” that led to “unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.” And in the midst of this — not to mention the flurry of alarming hacks and outages that have beset the tech sector and government agencies over the past few weeks — Corcos was still fiddling with AI to build his game. Update logs on GitHub show that during and after the hack, while the agency was still dealing with the fallout, Corcos released balance patches for the game, new theme music for the Aztecs — AI-generated, of course — and overhauled its in-game tooltips system, per 404 . He also enthusiastically released a new special unit for Egypt, right at the same time that the Treasury Department warned that FinCEN was taking some of its systems offline “as a proactive measure.” As word spread online of Corcos’s extracurricular, or perhaps on the clock, activity, trolls and angry netizens began piling into the GitHub’s project’s discussion board for flagging issues with the game. “The Treasury Department is being hacked and you are vibe coding a video game instead,” fumed one issue topic . “Proposed Solution: Delete this repo and fix the security issues at the Treasury Department.” Corcos, apparently still having plenty of time on his hands, hasn’t helped his case by individually replying to and hiding the troll’s posts — a task that he’s automated with even more AI. “Closing as off-topic,” he responded to the above post this morning. “This tracker is for bugs and ideas about the Legatum game,” he added, with a signature reading “Generated by Claude Code.” The jokes continue to write themselves even more readily than his vibe coded video game. His last tweet, 404 spotted, was a defense of DOGE once again demanding federal workers to send in written letters explaining what they do. “I believe it is reasonable to ask employees what they are working on,” Corcos wrote . items.title: The military tested robots to help medics find wounded troops and decide who needs help first
items.summary: Medics working alongside a ground robot prepare to treat simulated casualties during a DARPA Triage Challenge event in September 2025. The competition concluded earlier this month. Paul Flacks/DARPA Drones and robots had 15 minutes to find mock casualties in a major medical triage challenge. Machines assessed injuries and evacuation priorities without touching patients. The goal is to help combat medics prioritize care when supplies and evacuation are limited. Earlier this month, drones and ground robots searched simulated disaster zones in a competition testing whether machines could help military medics quickly find casualties and identify which needed lifesaving care first. It was all part of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency's "Triage Challenge," an event meant to test companies and universities on whether their tech could be a viable solution for medics on future battlefields filled with enemy drones and AI. DARPA is the Pentagon's research arm tasked with finding potential answers to tough military problems, like how missiles can strike their targets when GPS disappears and how to stop adversaries from wrecking havoc on economic markets . At the Disaster City facility in College Station, Texas, a facility built to replicate disasters to test emergency response teams, medics and robots faced scenarios like responding to tornado destruction and a nighttime attack on a military outpost. Ground robots and drones had 15 minutes to find actors and mannequins representing wounded troops and civilians. In another test, they were given the casualties' locations and had five minutes to assess how urgently they needed help. A medic and an unmanned ground vehicle search for casualties as an planned explosion detonates in the background, part of the DARPA Triage Challenge on Nov. 13th, in College Station, Texas. Paul Flacks/DARPA The machines also had to identify injuries, check whether casualties responded, and decide who needed to be evacuated first — all without touching patients. Jeremy Pamplin, the event's program manager and a retired Army physician, told Business Insider in September that rapid triage focused on severe bleeding and breathing problems, identifying someone a medic needed to reach immediately. "Teams have to get out there, recognize these problems really fast and say, 'yep, that's somebody you got to go see right now," he said. Robots and drones could help medics find "needles in the haystack," he said of simulated patients, "to try to save the most lives they possibly can." Military officials have previously warned that the US military is unlikely to control the air in future conflicts, potentially leading to major casualty evacuation challenges the US military has not experienced in decades. That prospect has prompted medical units to begin training to treat frontline casualties for days, or even weeks, before they might receive advanced care. Drones scouted ahead of medics and ground robots, sending casualty information to the medics' phones. A separate element of the event tested whether algorithms could predict what treatment patients would need hours later. In a major war, medics may have to focus scarce resources on casualties they can save, an ethical dilemma most medical providers in the US military have little experience confronting. Pamplin hopes technology can help medics make such decisions with better information. Robots could locate and assess casualties while predictive algorithms help medics anticipate what treatment each patient needs and how long they can wait. That type of mechanical help might aid medics not just by saving more lives, he said, but also by "relieving the burden of doubt from our young medics and war fighters as they're trying to manage those situations." Read the original article on Business Insider

A medic and an unmanned ground vehicle search for casualties as an planned explosion detonates in the background, part of the DARPA Triage Challenge on Nov. 13th, in College Station, Texas.

Paul Flacks/DARPA

The machines also had to identify injuries, check whether casualties responded, and decide who needed to be evacuated first — all without touching patients.

Jeremy Pamplin, the event's program manager and a retired Army physician, told Business Insider in September that rapid triage focused on severe bleeding and breathing problems, identifying someone a medic needed to reach immediately.

"Teams have to get out there, recognize these problems really fast and say, 'yep, that's somebody you got to go see right now," he said. Robots and drones could help medics find "needles in the haystack," he said of simulated patients, "to try to save the most lives they possibly can."

Military officials have previously warned that the US military is unlikely to control the air in future conflicts, potentially leading to major casualty evacuation challenges the US military has not experienced in decades. That prospect has prompted medical units to begin training to treat frontline casualties for days, or even weeks, before they might receive advanced care.

Drones scouted ahead of medics and ground robots, sending casualty information to the medics' phones. A separate element of the event tested whether algorithms could predict what treatment patients would need hours later.

In a major war, medics may have to focus scarce resources on casualties they can save, an ethical dilemma most medical providers in the US military have little experience confronting.

Pamplin hopes technology can help medics make such decisions with better information. Robots could locate and assess casualties while predictive algorithms help medics anticipate what treatment each patient needs and how long they can wait.

That type of mechanical help might aid medics not just by saving more lives, he said, but also by "relieving the burden of doubt from our young medics and war fighters as they're trying to manage those situations."

items.title: Houston, we have a networking problem: Why NTT thinks space computing is the final frontier
items.summary: After cloud computing comes space computing , obviously, right? There’s a neat irony here: Real-world clouds can interfere with optical satellite links . Cloud cover (along with atmospheric turbulence) can block the laser-based connections between satellites and ground stations, limiting how much data can be brought down to the data center and cloud services waiting for it. In other words, cloud services on the ground can be held back by the weather they are named after. Networking conglomerate NTT wants to enable a new era of communications above the clouds (literally) with a combined set of space computing and lunar infrastructure developments that draw heavily on its work in photonics and light-based computing. The organization’s optical space communication infrastructure is now being aligned with technologies supporting observation and space datacenter creation. The company is also working on lunar surface communication and lunar energy transmission. Our 88 constellations just got one louder Today, the International Astronomical Union recognizes 88 constellations in the sky; the NTT C89 project was launched in 2024 to unify and scale the company’s space-related projects and create what it believes could be the 89th constellation. Speaking to an auditorium of about 200 Japanese press and one reporter from The New Stack during his company’s annual NTT R&D Forum , NTT president and CEO Akira Shimada said that optical ground stations can be blocked by clouds or struggle to receive signals because of atmospheric turbulence. For Shimada and team, this is why our planet’s communications infrastructure needs to reach for the stars. “As high-resolution observation data grows, the capacity that can be sent from satellite to ground by radio becomes a challenge.” “As high-resolution observation data grows, the capacity that can be sent from satellite to ground by radio becomes a challenge,” said Shimada. “A low Earth orbit satellite can communicate directly with a ground receiving facility only during the limited time it passes overhead. In addition to technology that compensates for turbulence, a mechanism will be developed to select which ground station and communication path to connect to according to weather, satellite position and communication conditions.” Satellite communications crosses the (cloud) chasm He explained that NTT is developing optical links that connect satellites to one another and to the ground, relaying data from observation satellites to other satellites. Rather than waiting for a satellite to pass over an Earth-based receiving facility, information is delivered via a satellite that can connect to the ground at that exact moment, reducing wait time. “As connected devices and data, including video, continue to grow and increase, satellite communications need greater capacity and higher quality,” said Shimada. “This field is of growing importance because satellite communications connect places that terrestrial networks struggle to reach, such as mountainous areas, the sea and remote islands” He further stated that satellite communications at this level also serve as a means of communication when ground facilities are unusable in a disaster. So while image resolution continues to improve, disasters and wildfires now demand real-time delivery, in time for decisions on evacuation, firefighting and recovery. Hence the need to connect more fluidly in space. Who knew about the lunar power shadow problem? Not content to work on communications on Earth and in the ether above our planet’s atmosphere, NTT is also looking to enable lunar surface communication and lunar energy transmission. But lunar power isn’t simple; you know about the permanent lunar shadow challenge, right? As we look to build lunar bases and perhaps one day lunar data centers , these facilities will obviously need solar energy to power them one day. But the Moon’s craters — many of which hold water ice deposits, which will also be essential — often haven’t seen sunlight for billions of years. Lunar scientists call these permanently shadowed regions (PSRs), and they exist because the Moon’s 1.5-degree axial tilt restricts sunlight from moving across the poles, leaving deep crater floors in permanent shadow. NTT’s work fully recognizes this challenge and also extends to power transmission operations on the lunar surface itself. “The moon’s craters — many of which hold water ice deposits, which will also be essential [in the construction of lunar datacenters] — often haven’t seen sunlight for billions of years. It’s what lunar scientists call lunar permanently shadowed regions (PSRs).” “With expanded lunar activity in view, NTT research now covers optical communications to connect the Earth and the Moon in a stable manner; it also extends to work to enable power supply on the lunar surface. For wireless power transmission by laser, the challenges are suppressing the spread of the light and the efficiency of conversion to electricity,” clarified Shimada. AI processing in space He says that the “ultimate goal” is to link inter-satellite optical communications, AI processing in space, and terrestrial data centers and optical networks, supporting the understanding of disaster conditions, monitoring of the global environment, and communications in areas where connectivity is difficult. In June, NTT and Ireland-based MBRYONICS signed a memorandum of understanding to research and develop space optical communications technologies, a step toward launching IOWN (the Innovative Optical and Wireless Network initiative) in space. In September, NTT signed an MoU to connect France-based Cailabs ‘ optical ground stations to NTT datacenters via NTT’s All-Photonics Network (APN), a pillar of the IOWN initiative. “NTT is also working on concepts to place optical ground stations near datacentres, so that information arriving from space can be processed with low latency and delivered where it is needed.” NTT future concepts work NTT is also working on concepts to place optical ground stations near datacentres, so that information arriving from space can be processed with low latency and delivered where it is needed. By using datacentres and communication networks around the world, space and the ground will be connected in what the company promises is a seamless manner. Figures to think about in this arena are the fact that low Earth orbit satellites move at approximately 8 km per second, that it is approximately 380,000 kilometers between the Earth and the Moon, and that some 230 petabytes per day is forecast to be the volume of satellite-to-ground data traffic by 2033, according to NTT. The next crewed Artemis mission, Artemis III , is a low-Earth-orbit docking test. The first landing is penciled in for Artemis IV in 2028. Let’s hope Artemis III gets close enough to scout a nice crater for the first lunar data center.

items.title: Community Outraged When Hospital Moves to Automate Healthcare Jobs With AI
items.summary: Dozens of telemetry technicians at Mercy Health-Springfield Regional Medical Center will soon be out of the job, to be replaced by AI. That news was originally reported by the Springfield News-Sun , which noted that the major Southwest Ohio hospital is phasing out human telemetry monitor technicians in favor of a new suite of technology meant to “deliver real-time patient data directly to caregivers.” A spokesperson for the hospital told the Sun that the medical center is “upgrading patient monitoring technology across our hospitals to bring critical information closer to the bedside and support more direct, responsive patient care.” Also known as monitor techs, telemetry technicians are trained professionals who provide support for bedside nurses by monitoring patient heart rhythms and notifying healthcare workers in case of emergencies. By automating the role, hospitals risk amplifying false-alarm fatigue for nurses, increasing vulnerability to internet outages and cyberattacks, and reducing overall vigilance through a phenomenon known as automation bias . There’s also the impact on workers to consider. In an interview with local channel WDTN , a representative of healthcare union SEIU District 1199 said the union was meeting with hospital administrators to “determine next steps” for those impacted by automation. Mercy Health-Springfield’s decision sparked immediate controversy in the community, with one commenter writing under WDTN ’s Facebook post that it’s a “shameful path of the future.” “It’s going to put more work on the nurses as I spoke to several of them today when my mom was in the hospital having surgery,” the community member continued. “I hope every nurse walks out of there.” More on healthcare: Health Care Workers Furious as NYC Replaces Nurses With AI
items.summary_html:
Dozens of telemetry technicians at Mercy Health-Springfield Regional Medical Center will soon be out of the job, to be replaced by AI.

That news was originally reported by the Springfield News-Sun, which noted that the major Southwest Ohio hospital is phasing out human telemetry monitor technicians in favor of a new suite of technology meant to “deliver real-time patient data directly to caregivers.”

A spokesperson for the hospital told the Sun that the medical center is “upgrading patient monitoring technology across our hospitals to bring critical information closer to the bedside and support more direct, responsive patient care.”

Also known as monitor techs, telemetry technicians are trained professionals who provide support for bedside nurses by monitoring patient heart rhythms and notifying healthcare workers in case of emergencies. By automating the role, hospitals risk amplifying false-alarm fatigue for nurses, increasing vulnerability to internet outages and cyberattacks, and reducing overall vigilance through a phenomenon known as automation bias.

There’s also the impact on workers to consider. In an interview with local channel WDTN, a representative of healthcare union SEIU District 1199 said the union was meeting with hospital administrators to “determine next steps” for those impacted by automation.

Mercy Health-Springfield’s decision sparked immediate controversy in the community, with one commenter writing under WDTN’s Facebook post that it’s a “shameful path of the future.”

“It’s going to put more work on the nurses as I spoke to several of them today when my mom was in the hospital having surgery,” the community member continued. “I hope every nurse walks out of there.”

More on healthcare: Health Care Workers Furious as NYC Replaces Nurses With AI

items.title: Vercel’s CEO thinks the next big AI speedup won’t come from smarter models
items.summary: Some of the biggest gains in AI performance over the past year have come from improvements to the harness, not the model itself. But Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch believes that as models become more capable, some implementation details developers have spent months refining will become less visible, and the infrastructure that executes agents will become more important. “As AI gets smarter, implementation details blur away: permissions, code diffs, commands, tool calls. … The harness itself blurs away.” “As AI gets smarter, implementation details blur away: permissions, code diffs, commands, tool calls,” Rauch wrote in a post on X . “The harness itself blurs away.” Rauch doesn’t expect the harness to disappear entirely. He sees its role shifting toward executing agents and preserving their state. Vercel offered a glimpse of what that architecture could look like on Wednesday with the release of Workflow SDK 5.8 , which introduces a rebuilt execution engine that substantially reduces the infrastructure overhead associated with running durable agents. Latency between the model calls Inference speed accounts for only part of an agent’s total execution time. Much of the latency can accumulate in the infrastructure that handles work between model calls. Vercel’s new execution engine addresses that overhead through speculative execution of retryable workflow steps. In its benchmarks , Vercel reported that p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 85 milliseconds to 7 milliseconds between Workflow SDK versions 5.2 and 5.8. A five-turn agent loop involving durable token streaming and tool calls incurred just 900 milliseconds of infrastructure overhead… A five-turn agent loop involving durable token streaming and tool calls incurred just 900 milliseconds of infrastructure overhead, compared with three seconds in the previous version. The performance gains are particularly noticeable when agents run multiple tasks in parallel. In Vercel’s benchmark of 256 parallel steps, execution overhead dropped from 13.5 seconds to 2.5 seconds. The time functions spent outside the application’s step code also decreased by a factor of nearly 14. None of those improvements requires switching models, modifying prompts, or giving an agent additional reasoning capabilities. As inference becomes faster, the overhead of persisting state, scheduling execution and resuming workflows can account for a larger share of an agent’s end-to-end latency. Speculative execution and its limits Vercel’s implementation of speculative execution requires idempotent steps. For operations that cannot safely be repeated, developers can disable speculation and retries by setting maxRetries = 0 . Even as models get better at orchestrating their own work, they still depend on the underlying infrastructure for durable execution and recovery from failures. Even as models get better at orchestrating their own work, they still depend on the underlying infrastructure for durable execution and recovery from failures. A 6 MB coding harness Rauch’s vision for the agent harness is reflected in the design of fx. Despite supporting subagents, MCP, skills, sessions, durable execution, ACP, a terminal user interface, and network transport, Rauch said the harness still fits within 6 MB. Vercel has applied a similar architectural approach to eve, an open source framework that treats agents as directories and uses durable workflows to preserve state across interruptions. Other infrastructure providers are separating agent orchestration from the resources required to sustain execution. OpenAI separated the agent harness from the compute environment in its Agents SDK , while Render introduced AI sandboxes capable of running indefinitely , with durable workflows and persistent file storage. Where harness engineering goes next Much of harness engineering today involves working around model limitations. As models become better at managing their own work, developers may need less application-specific orchestration. Execution guarantees are harder to abstract away. Even highly capable models depend on infrastructure that can manage concurrent processes, preserve state, and recover from failures. Vercel’s latest benchmarks lend weight to Rauch’s bet that the competitive advantage will shift from making agents smarter to building infrastructure that makes them faster and more reliable.

items.title: A year from now, VMware wants AI troubleshooting your private cloud
items.summary: A developer who needs two containers to test a change or modification has a different problem from a platform engineer running an application across several Kubernetes clusters. Both need infrastructure, preferably before the ticket asking for it becomes old enough to have a birthday. Broadcom’s pitch for VMware Cloud Foundation is that the same private cloud can serve both teams, along with the people who still need virtual machines. In an interview recorded recently at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon 2026 in Salt Lake City, The New Stack’s Nick Lucchesi asked Mark Chuang , senior director of product marketing for VMware Cloud Foundation at Broadcom, what developers and operators notice when they mix a cocktail of VMs, containers, and AI workloads onto one platform. “They get a public cloud-like experience when it comes to self-service.” “They get a public cloud-like experience when it comes to self-service,” Chuang told TNS, starting with the experience of asking for resources. “Platform teams still set the policies that govern those resources.” This indeed matters when an AI application depends on services running in both containers and VMs. Operators can apply common security policies, manage the lifecycle of those workloads, and decide where they run. Developers can use self-service to get the infrastructure they need and continue working with their existing CI/CD tools, Chuang said. How much orchestration do you need? Chuang describes direct container deployment as an option for lightweight edge applications or quick developer checks. Kubernetes makes sense when an application needs automated orchestration across clusters. For a team testing a small change, spinning up a couple of containers directly can save setup work. For a platform team, both approaches fit into the same operating environment. Lucchesi also asks what Broadcom means when it says a partner application has been validated for vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) . Chuang explains that Broadcom provides test environments and automated tools, while the software vendors define the tests appropriate to their applications. “We’re just trying to lighten some of the load that’s on the plate of our customers.” The checks can cover initial deployment, recovery from failure, security, and even a clean uninstall. Broadcom reviews the results, and partners use them to produce reference architectures and technical guidance. “We’re just trying to lighten some of the load that’s on the plate of our customers,” Chuang said. What if an update breaks a partner application anyway? Chuang says customers can contact either Broadcom or the software vendor. If they call Broadcom, its support team starts by trying to determine whether the problem came from the platform or the application update. That’s a practical detail for a developer who knows exactly when something stopped working and has several plausible explanations. The tools teams already reach for Broadcom also packages frequently used tools such as Prometheus, Argo CD and Harbor as VKS add-ons. Chuang says the company looks at usage and customer feedback when deciding what to include. Handling installation and updates through VKS takes work off teams that would otherwise have to maintain those integrations themselves. The conversation touches on a change Chuang has noticed among customers. Some are increasingly willing to accept a curated set of tools if it gets them to a working environment faster. “Is it a storage issue? Is it a network issue? Is it a CPU contention issue?” TNS also asked Chuang which job a private cloud might take off an operator’s hands a year from now. Chuang’s answer starts with a familiar complaint about a slow application. “Is it a storage issue? Is it a network issue? Is it a CPU contention issue?” Chuang asked, rhetorically. A year from now, Chuang expects AI to do more of the diagnostic work across those layers. Watch the full interview on The New Stack’s YouTube channel for his take on what that could look like, what partner validation actually buys a developer, and why the quickest path to testing a container sometimes starts with a smaller deployment.
