items.title: Same coding model, 10x the token speed. How did Cognition do it?
items.summary: This week, Cognition announced SWE-2.1 , its latest in-house coding model trained with reinforcement learning (RL) on Moonshot AI’s open-weight model, Kimi K3 . The company says SWE-2.1 shows large gains across a wide range of benchmarks over the preceding SWE-2 model, including Terminal-Bench 4.1 and FrontierCode 2.0. The SWE-2.1 release includes an Ultrafast version that runs the same model 10 times faster on Cerebras chips, boosting speed from 60 tokens per second to 600. Cognition also announced SWE-2.1 Cyber, a dedicated cybersecurity variant with looser safeguards that’s rolling out as the model for normal scans on Devin Security. This is Cognition’s third model release in the last 11 weeks, right after SWE-2 on Sept. 10 and SWE-2 Flash on November 4. While SWE-2.1 still trails Claude Opus 5.5 on every benchmark, the results suggest a marked improvement in quality relative to frontier models. It’s also free to use in Devin Desktop and Devin CLI for all Devin Pro, Max, and Teams subscribers through December 8. SWE-2.1 doubles its predecessor’s Terminal-Bench score Since its last model release, Cognition says it has widened its RL training environment to include both short-term and long-horizon work, with a focus on science, performance engineering, and cybersecurity. It has also improved its post-training algorithms to control rollout length and reduce oscillations that used to knock training off balance, the company claims. Together, these combined improvements have significantly raised SWE-2.1’s benchmark scores compared to SWE-2, Cognition says in its announcement. The company has published a table showing the model’s updated benchmark scores compared to previous models and frontier alternatives: Benchmark SWE-2.1 SWE-2 Kimi K3.1 Claude Opus 5.5 Terminal-Bench 4.1 50.0 24.2 59.7 65.8 FrontierCode 2.0 41.3 24.1 19.9 47.3 ProgramBench 44.0 17.0 31.5 65.0 SWE Marathon v1.2 54.9 32.5 38.8 73.1 Table data supplied by Cognition While it shows promise as a focus-tuned version of an open-weight model, SWE-2.1 still trails behind Claude Opus 5.5 on every benchmark score. An updated version of its own base model, Kimi K3.1, even outperformed it on Terminal-Bench. Benchmark caveats and harness differences Some skepticism is warranted, too, since these figures come from the company’s own testing and haven’t been reproduced independently. FrontierCode 2.0 is Cognition’s own benchmark, while the rest are independently developed. Also, SWE-2.1 and open-weight models like Kimi K3.1 ran on the Devin CLI harness during testing, while frontier models were tested on the developer’s preferred harness. Cognition announces SWE-2.1 Ultrafast and a Cyber variant Cognition’s speed chart puts the standard SWE-2.1 model at 60 tokens per second and its smaller sibling, SWE-2 Flash, at 200 tokens per second. But through a partnership with AI chip maker Cerebras, the company can run the same model on faster hardware at 600 tokens per second. The company posted on LinkedIn and X , calling this variant SWE-2.1 Lightning, but the release announcement and Devin docs call it Ultrafast. SWE-2.1 and SWE-2.1 Lightning are available today in Devin Cloud, Devin Desktop, and Devin CLI.

This week, Cognition announced SWE-2.1, its latest in-house coding model trained with reinforcement learning (RL) on Moonshot AI’s open-weight model, Kimi K3. The company says SWE-2.1 shows large gains across a wide range of benchmarks over the preceding SWE-2 model, including Terminal-Bench 4.1 and FrontierCode 2.0. 

The SWE-2.1 release includes an Ultrafast version that runs the same model 10 times faster on Cerebras chips, boosting speed from 60 tokens per second to 600. Cognition also announced SWE-2.1 Cyber, a dedicated cybersecurity variant with looser safeguards that’s rolling out as the model for normal scans on Devin Security. 

This is Cognition’s third model release in the last 11 weeks, right after SWE-2 on Sept. 10 and SWE-2 Flash on November 4. While SWE-2.1 still trails Claude Opus 5.5 on every benchmark, the results suggest a marked improvement in quality relative to frontier models. It’s also free to use in Devin Desktop and Devin CLI for all Devin Pro, Max, and Teams subscribers through December 8.

SWE-2.1 doubles its predecessor’s Terminal-Bench score

Since its last model release, Cognition says it has widened its RL training environment to include both short-term and long-horizon work, with a focus on science, performance engineering, and cybersecurity. It has also improved its post-training algorithms to control rollout length and reduce oscillations that used to knock training off balance, the company claims. 

Together, these combined improvements have significantly raised SWE-2.1’s benchmark scores compared to SWE-2, Cognition says in its announcement. The company has published a table showing the model’s updated benchmark scores compared to previous models and frontier alternatives:

BenchmarkSWE-2.1SWE-2Kimi K3.1Claude Opus 5.5Terminal-Bench 4.150.024.259.765.8FrontierCode 2.041.324.119.947.3ProgramBench44.017.031.565.0SWE Marathon v1.254.932.538.873.1

Table data supplied by Cognition 

While it shows promise as a focus-tuned version of an open-weight model, SWE-2.1 still trails behind Claude Opus 5.5 on every benchmark score. An updated version of its own base model, Kimi K3.1, even outperformed it on Terminal-Bench. 

Benchmark caveats and harness differences

Some skepticism is warranted, too, since these figures come from the company’s own testing and haven’t been reproduced independently. FrontierCode 2.0 is Cognition’s own benchmark, while the rest are independently developed. Also, SWE-2.1 and open-weight models like Kimi K3.1 ran on the Devin CLI harness during testing, while frontier models were tested on the developer’s preferred harness. 

Cognition announces SWE-2.1 Ultrafast and a Cyber variant

Cognition’s speed chart puts the standard SWE-2.1 model at 60 tokens per second and its smaller sibling, SWE-2 Flash, at 200 tokens per second. 

But through a partnership with AI chip maker Cerebras, the company can run the same model on faster hardware at 600 tokens per second. The company posted on LinkedIn and X, calling this variant SWE-2.1 Lightning, but the release announcement and Devin docs call it Ultrafast.

SWE-2.1 and SWE-2.1 Lightning are available today in Devin Cloud, Devin Desktop, and Devin CLI.

Read more about our research behind SWE-2.1 and SWE-2.1 Cyber:https://t.co/uWQkORTbZ7

— Cognition (@cognition) November 24, 2026

Cognition also announced a dedicated Cyber variant. It’s a tweaked version of the SWE-2.1 model with more permissive safeguards against potentially harmful activity, aimed at defensive security work. SWE-2.1 Cyber is rolling out to power normal scans on Devin Security, while deep scans rely on frontier cyber models like Claude Mythos.

SWE-2.1 scores 80% on ExploitBench, compared with the SWE-2 model’s 36.1%. Compared against frontier cybersecurity models, that’s a significant leap, with Claude Opus 5.5 scoring 91% and only GPT-6.2 Sol managing a perfect 100% score. The model also succeeds on twice as many ExploitGym tasks as SWE-2, with a 27.3% total success rate compared to Claude Opus 5.5’s 34.5% and Gemini 4 Neon’s 47.9%. 

How you can access SWE-2.1 right now

SWE-2.1 and SWE-2.1 Ultrafast are available right now on Devin Cloud, Devin Desktop, and Devin CLI. The company also said SWE-2.1 will remain free in Devin Desktop and CLI for Devin Pro, Max, and Teams subscribers through December 8 and will remain discounted, at $0.50 per million input tokens and $2.50 per million output tokens, until January 30, 2027, when list pricing of $2 and $10 kicks in. 

“…you have two free weeks to thoroughly test whether SWE-2.1 can replace frontier coding LLMs for your everyday tickets.”

If you’re a Devin Pro, Max, or Teams subscriber, you have two free weeks to thoroughly test whether SWE-2.1 can replace frontier coding LLMs for your everyday tickets. SWE-2.1 Ultrafast is also available across Devin platforms as a paid option priced at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens. Meanwhile, SWE-2.1 Cyber is currently limited to normal scans performed only through Devin Security.

items.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia comeback may herald an 'age of resentment,' top economist Steve Hanke says
items.summary: Jensen Huang was recently reinstated as Nvidia's CEO. Joel Saget / AFP via Getty Images Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia may herald an "age of resentment," Steve Hanke says. The veteran economist said people feel indignant when others seem to get away with breaking the rules. Hanke said that resentment can be polarizing, pushing people further to the left and right. Jensen Huang's stunning return to Nvidia sent investors into raptures, but it has rankled many others and could have sweeping repercussions, veteran economist Steve Hanke says. "Thanks to the likes of Jensen Huang, I think that we are entering an age of resentment that promises a great many problems in the sphere of economic policy," Hanke told Business Insider. Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on November 12 following reports that he had extramarital affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a direct report. He was reinstated 11 days later, on November 23, after President Donald Trump urged the company's board to bring him back. The news sent Nvidia stock up 31% on the day, adding nearly $1 trillion to the AI chipmaker's market capitalization, but it has since given up some of those gains. The conduct of Silicon Valley types like Huang "flouts the moral sentiments and rules that govern and control most people's behavior," fueling public bitterness toward "this new class of big players," Hanke said. The professor of applied economics at Johns Hopkins University, who served on President Ronald Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers, said many onlookers are indignant because they feel they've been "treated unfairly" by comparison, and have been "slighted, or abandoned, or humiliated." In other words, they see a lack of accountability for the likes of Huang and believe they can break the rules without any lasting consequences. A big reason for the push to bring back Huang was that he's widely considered the face of AI and integral to US success in the budding sector, given Nvidia's central role in powering and financing it. But as the industry's champion, he also represents all that's wrong with AI in skeptics' eyes. Their concerns span from the safety of the tech to its impact on jobs to the immense resource demands of the data-center buildout. Steve Hanke warned of an "age of resentment." Steve Hanke Hanke warned that depth of resentment can be polarizing, spurring people on the right to embrace fascism, and those on the left to champion socialism. Indeed, Americans who felt resentful of wealthy elites helped propel Trump into power in 2016, while disillusionment with wealth inequality and political corruption has fueled the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America. "As it turns out, both the resentful on the left and the right have one thing in common: they demand that individual liberties be restricted and that the state be given more power to 'correct' things," Hanke said. Billionaire investor and economic historian Ray Dalio has been issuing similar warnings for years . "When broad-based discontent bubbles up and those in power allow it to grow, it can boil over to the point that when they try to put a lid on it, it explodes," he wrote in a LinkedIn post in 2024. Moreover, veteran investor Jeremy Grantham said in 2023 that income inequality has "resulted in the estrangement, almost bitterness and anger of at least a third of the general public who feel they have been badly treated." items.title: Ladybird Browser Enters Alpha, Bringing a Fourth Independent Engine to the Web
items.summary: Ladybird, the independent web browser built on its own engine, has reached alpha. Developer Andreas Kling announced the milestone this week, and the first downloadable builds are available for macOS and Linux. The release matters beyond the browser itself. Today's web runs almost entirely on three browser engines: Google's Blink, used by Chrome and other Chromium-based browsers; Apple's WebKit, used by Safari; and Mozilla's Gecko, used by Firefox. Blink itself was forked from WebKit. Ladybird's alpha means there is now a fourth modern engine that ordinary users can try. Where to Get the Ladybird Alpha The alpha is available for: macOS on Apple Silicon, a 68.4 MB download Linux on x86-64, as a Flatpak package of about 111 MB, plus native Ubuntu and Fedora packages Ladybird is open source, so the code is available on GitHub to compile. In June, however, the project announced that it would no longer accept public code contributions. The developers are clear about the risks of an alpha. They warn that it can crash, that some websites will not work, and that they make no security guarantees at this stage. That makes it a browser to test, not one to use for banking or other sensitive tasks yet. How Well It Works Early hands-on testing suggests the alpha is more stable than the label implies. On a Linux laptop, Ladybird handled the news and discussion sites it was tested on without problems, and played full-screen HD video from YouTube smoothly while using just 6 percent of the CPU. Testers saw no crashes or hesitation during a short session. Small download sizes are another surprise. A 68.4 MB download for a full browser is remarkably compact by 2026 standards. From SerenityOS to Rust Ladybird started as the built-in browser of SerenityOS, a hobby operating system, and was later split off so it could run on other systems and use external libraries. Kling first used Apple's Swift language for parts of the project, but switched to Rust this year, using AI tools to convert some existing code. The browser and its original operating system were established projects long before the current wave of AI-assisted development. The use of AI tools has drawn criticism from some users, and the project's decisions have been divisive in parts of the open source community. Still, the alpha is a significant step for browser competition. Users who want to try it can download the macOS or Linux builds from the Ladybird website, ideally alongside their main browser. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

items.summary: OpenAI has fixed a billing bug that had been undercounting how much GPT-6.2 usage costs in ChatGPT and Codex. items.summary_html:
OpenAI has fixed a billing bug that had been undercounting how much GPT-6.2 usage costs in ChatGPT and Codex. The result: users will now hit their usage limits 40% faster on GPT-6.2 Astra and 25% faster on GPT-6.2 Sol than they did last week.

Tibo Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, announced the change in a post on X. He said a mistake had been incorrectly discounting GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage for most users.

What Changes for ChatGPT Users

"We've fixed this now, so the same work will use more of your plan's usage allowance," Sottiaux wrote. "Comparing to last week, you will reach your limits 40% faster on GPT-6.2 Astra and 25% faster on Sol."

The key points:

  • GPT-6.2 Astra now uses up usage limits 40% faster than last week
  • GPT-6.2 Sol uses them up 25% faster
  • other models keep their existing usage calculations
  • OpenAI will not charge users for the usage difference caused by the mistake

OpenAI says both GPT-6.2 models still use allowances more efficiently than their predecessors, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, even after the fix. GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol launched earlier this month.

A Free Reset as an Apology

To make up for the disruption, OpenAI is giving users an extra usage reset. "As a small token to apologize for the mistake, we'll be adding one banked reset for everyone on Go, Plus, Pro, and Business," Sottiaux said.

The reset appears in ChatGPT and expires one month after it is added. To use it:

  1. Open ChatGPT and go to Settings.
  2. Select Usage.
  3. Click Reset to restore exhausted usage limits.

Since the reset can only be used once, it makes sense to save it for a moment when the limit is actually reached.

A One-Time Fix for a Lasting Change

The reset is a one-time gesture, while the faster consumption is permanent. Users who rely on GPT-6.2 Astra for long tasks will reach their limits sooner every week from now on, and OpenAI has not said whether it plans to adjust the limits to compensate.

The change comes after a series of adjustments to ChatGPT usage limits in recent months, including OpenAI doubling ChatGPT Pro usage limits after a backlash over a planned cut. For paying subscribers, the frequent changes make it harder to know exactly how much usage a plan includes.

Users who hit the new limits often can switch some tasks to GPT-6.2 Sol, which is affected less, or to other models whose usage calculations have not changed.

In two papers published in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, he argues that free will is a product of evolution and introduces the concept of Responsible Autonomy: six control capacities that allow an agent, human or otherwise, to govern its own behavior.

items.title: AI Agents Can Now Pay for Their Own Tools. Who Holds the Budget?
items.summary: In one week, AWS, Stripe and Apify let software agents spend money without a person clicking “buy.” The guardrails are real, but many of them are defaults, and defaults can be switched off. Written with help from AI research tools. Every fact is checked against the linked sources. AI agents that buy their own tools need a budget someone else controls. Illustration by the author. Last week, a research agent on AWS needed live web search, found a paid search tool, compared two listings, paid one cent and answered the question. No person clicked “buy.” That run is from an AWS walkthrough published on November 19 . It is small, and that is the point. Agents are starting to pay for the tools they use, one request at a time, with nobody watching each payment. The story: agents got their own spending money Most of these payments run on x402. HTTP, the language web browsers and servers speak, has always had a status code 402, “Payment Required,” that was almost never used. x402 is an open protocol that puts it to work: a server answers a request with a price, the agent pays, and then asks again with proof of payment. According to Apify , it was originally built by Coinbase and is now governed under the Linux Foundation. Three launches in one week show where this is going: AWS (Nov 19). Agents built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore can now buy x402-enabled software, APIs, data and content from AWS Marketplace sellers per request, with the charge landing on the developer’s normal AWS bill. No stablecoin wallet or API key is needed. Stripe (Nov 19). Stripe added write access to its Treasury for agents, so connected agents can transfer funds, convert currencies and pay vendors within limits a business sets. Stripe says more than 24,000 businesses already gave agents read access to their financial data. Apify (Nov 24). Apify’s announcement of x402 payments for its web automation tools sums up the pitch in its subtitle: “No account, no API key, no human in the loop.” How an agent buys one paid API call on AWS Marketplace, in five steps. Source: AWS Machine Learning Blog, Nov 19, 2026. Diagram by the author. For developers, this removes real friction. Nobody has to sign up for a service, attach a card, store a secret key and rotate it. The agent finds the tool, sees the price and pays. For anyone responsible for the money, it raises a different question: what stops the agent from paying for the wrong thing, or for the right thing ten thousand times? The lesson: the guardrails are mostly defaults Every one of these launches ships with limits. That is good news. But read the documentation and a pattern shows up: much of the safety comes from default settings that a developer can change. The default cap can be turned off in one line. The reference x402 client software only accepts known dollar-pegged tokens and caps each payment at $1 by default . The same page explains how to switch that off: pass spendControls: false "to disable all spend controls." Human approval is a default, not a law. On Stripe, agent-initiated refunds, payouts and outbound transfers need human approval by default. A business using an agent key can change that, for example letting an agent send ACH bank transfers under $50 automatically. Visa’s command-line agent wallet asks before every payment by default , and the owner can turn on “Pays on its own” for small amounts. The builders themselves warn about the worst case. Apify’s own security note tells users to treat an agent’s wallet “like a low-balance hot wallet or a prepaid debit card” and to “assume a compromised or hallucinating agent runtime could drain the entire balance.” Its smallest prepaid token is $1, expires after 14 days, and unused balance is not refunded. items.summary_html:
In one week, AWS, Stripe and Apify let software agents spend money without a person clicking “buy.” The guardrails are real, but many of them are defaults, and defaults can be switched off.

Written with help from AI research tools. Every fact is checked against the linked sources.

AI agents that buy their own tools need a budget someone else controls. Illustration by the author.

Last week, a research agent on AWS needed live web search, found a paid search tool, compared two listings, paid one cent and answered the question. No person clicked “buy.”

That run is from an AWS walkthrough published on November 19. It is small, and that is the point. Agents are starting to pay for the tools they use, one request at a time, with nobody watching each payment.

The story: agents got their own spending money

Most of these payments run on x402. HTTP, the language web browsers and servers speak, has always had a status code 402, “Payment Required,” that was almost never used. x402 is an open protocol that puts it to work: a server answers a request with a price, the agent pays, and then asks again with proof of payment. According to Apify, it was originally built by Coinbase and is now governed under the Linux Foundation.

Three launches in one week show where this is going:

AWS (Nov 19). Agents built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore can now buy x402-enabled software, APIs, data and content from AWS Marketplace sellers per request, with the charge landing on the developer’s normal AWS bill. No stablecoin wallet or API key is needed.

Stripe (Nov 19). Stripe added write access to its Treasury for agents, so connected agents can transfer funds, convert currencies and pay vendors within limits a business sets. Stripe says more than 24,000 businesses already gave agents read access to their financial data.

Apify (Nov 24). Apify’s announcement of x402 payments for its web automation tools sums up the pitch in its subtitle: “No account, no API key, no human in the loop.”

How an agent buys one paid API call on AWS Marketplace, in five steps. Source: AWS Machine Learning Blog, Nov 19, 2026. Diagram by the author.

For developers, this removes real friction. Nobody has to sign up for a service, attach a card, store a secret key and rotate it. The agent finds the tool, sees the price and pays.

For anyone responsible for the money, it raises a different question: what stops the agent from paying for the wrong thing, or for the right thing ten thousand times?

The lesson: the guardrails are mostly defaults

Every one of these launches ships with limits. That is good news. But read the documentation and a pattern shows up: much of the safety comes from default settings that a developer can change.

The default cap can be turned off in one line. The reference x402 client software only accepts known dollar-pegged tokens and caps each payment at $1 by default. The same page explains how to switch that off: pass spendControls: false "to disable all spend controls."

Human approval is a default, not a law. On Stripe, agent-initiated refunds, payouts and outbound transfers need human approval by default. A business using an agent key can change that, for example letting an agent send ACH bank transfers under $50 automatically. Visa’s command-line agent wallet asks before every payment by default, and the owner can turn on “Pays on its own” for small amounts.

The builders themselves warn about the worst case. Apify’s own security note tells users to treat an agent’s wallet “like a low-balance hot wallet or a prepaid debit card” and to “assume a compromised or hallucinating agent runtime could drain the entire balance.” Its smallest prepaid token is $1, expires after 14 days, and unused balance is not refunded.

Banks say the hard part is not the code. Speaking to CNBC about a test where AI agents carried out a simulated currency trade, the head of Kinexys Insights at J.P. Morgan said: “Technology-wise, it’s really not the biggest hurdle.” The harder questions were accountability and oversight. In the same piece, CNBC reported that AvePoint’s State of AI 2026 report found unauthorized agent actions, such as making transactions or changing data without approval, were the third most common AI agent security breach, affecting 34.1% of companies that reported such incidents.

The price comes from a stranger. An x402 price arrives inside a response from a server the agent may have just discovered. The new MCP Events specification (MCP is the Model Context Protocol, a common way to connect agents to tools) says it plainly for incoming events: payloads “can carry prompt injection,” and receiving one “never authorizes the agent to act.” The same caution applies to anything a server tells an agent to pay.

Default spending guardrails in five agent payment tools, as documented Nov 18–24, 2026. Sources: x402 DEFAULT_ASSETS.md, AWS, Stripe, Visa CLI docs, Apify. Table by the author.What to do before you give an agent a budget

None of these need new technology. They are old finance controls applied to a new kind of spender.

1. Give every task its own small budget. AWS’s pattern is a payment session with a spending limit for each task. Its sample defaults to $0.05 per session and $0.02 per request. Start that small, then raise limits based on what you actually see.

2. Keep the person who sets the budget separate from the agent that spends it. Finance teams call this segregation of duties. In the AWS sample, the role that sets budgets cannot pay, and the agent’s role can pay but cannot create sessions, “so the agent has no way to raise its own budget.” Visa’s docs make the same promise: an agent “can’t raise its own limit or approve itself.”

3. Treat a disabled default as a decision. Search your code and configuration for switched-off spend controls and auto-approve rules. Each one should have a named owner and a written reason.

4. Fund only what you can afford to lose. Follow Apify’s advice and keep agent wallets and prepaid balances small. Never connect an agent to your main account.

5. Keep a human on money that leaves the business. Small tool purchases can run alone. Transfers, payouts and vendor payments should need a person, with a low auto-approve threshold if you allow one at all.

6. Log everything and read the bill. AWS records agent purchases in CloudTrail and Cost Explorer. Whatever platform you use, check the agent’s spending against the invoice at least weekly, the same way you would check a team expense card.

7. Know your off switch. In the CNBC piece, Coinbase’s Singapore country director said users should be able to monitor activity and revoke access at any time. Find out today how to pause or revoke your agent’s payment access, and who on your team can do it.

Your turn

If an agent you built could pay for its own tools tomorrow, what budget would you give it, and who on your team would notice first if it spent the whole thing by lunch?

  2. Stripe blog, “Give your agents controlled access to analyze your data and move funds,” Nov 19, 2026. https://stripe.com/blog/give-your-agents-controlled-access-to-analyze-your-data-and-move-funds
  3. Apify blog, “Let your AI agent pay for Apify Actors with x402,” Nov 24, 2026. https://blog.apify.com/introducing-x402-agentic-payments/
  4. x402 Foundation, DEFAULT_ASSETS.md (GitHub, checked Nov 26, 2026). https://github.com/x402-foundation/x402/blob/main/DEFAULT_ASSETS.md
  5. Visa CLI docs, “Limits and approvals,” updated Nov 18, 2026. https://app.visacli.sh/docs/limits-and-approvals.md
  6. CNBC, “JPMorgan is working on AI agent transactions that don’t involve humans,” Nov 17, 2026 (updated Nov 23). https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/18/jpmorgan-hyundai-card-ai-agents-payments.html
  7. Model Context Protocol, “Events” extension overview (checked Nov 26, 2026). https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/events/overview

items.title: Bankrupt Chatbot Startup Looking to Sell Troves of Child Data Tries and Fails to Conceal the Identity of Weirdly Named Bidder
items.summary: The failed chatbot startup Character.AI, which earlier this year settled multiple lawsuits accusing the platform of pushing teens to self-harm and suicide , was forced by a judge to reveal the identity of the anonymous bidder looking to buy Character.AI data including the accounts and extensive chat logs of its users. Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in October, announcing in a blog post that it would move to sell the company and its assets. On November 13, a mysterious entity named Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC was incorporated in Delaware. The very next day, on November 14, Character.AI filed court documents picking the newly-formed company as the stalking horse bidder, or the initial bidder whose offer will kick off the auction process, for the chatbot startup’s consumer app and user data. Character.AI specifically sought to keep whoever was behind Smirks and Pangs a secret, and other bidders have yet to be disclosed. Smirks and Pangs is seeking to acquire Character.AI’s data for $10 million. That move brought backlash from states attorneys general, 42 of whom moved last week to block the sale , citing concerns about the privacy of children’s sensitive data. It’s well known that a huge number of Character.AI’s millions of users were underage, and many carried out deeply intimate, revealing conversations with the site’s chatbots, which acted as young users’ friends, therapists, confidantes, and even sexual and romantic partners — as in the case of Sewell Setzer III, a 14-year-old in Florida who died by suicide in 2024 after experiencing a mental breakdown closely tied to a sexual and romantic relationship with one of the site’s thousands of AI “Characters.” This week, the judge overseeing the case approved Smirks and Pangs’ bid to kick off the forthcoming auction, which is slated for December 1 — on the condition that Character.AI reveal the identity of the entity’s operators. Character.AI agreed, and revealed the prospective buyer’s backer as the New York-based investment firm Octave Advisors. The attorneys general are continuing to push back, and claim that Character.AI’s data includes the sensitive chat histories of more than 21 million American accounts, and that 2.1 million of those accounts belong to minors. “Children and families who shared their most personal thoughts with Character.AI never imagined those conversations could be auctioned off to the highest bidder,” Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser said in a statement on Wednesday. “A company’s financial troubles do not give it the right to disregard its responsibility to protect consumers, especially children.” In a separate stalking horse bid , Disney is seeking to license Character.AI’s intellectual property for $20 million, and has said it will hire most of its workforce as part of the deal. More on Character.AI: We Investigated Character.AI and Found a Horror Show. Now It’s Bankrupt.

items.title: The Information’s 2026 Gift Guide
items.summary: In a twisted version of future Christmases, perhaps AIs will carry out all the tasks involved in gift giving. But lucky for us, Andy Jassy still has all the bots blocked! So here once again is The Information’s annual Gift Guide, a project that we pursue with as much consideration and rigor as our everyday reporting. None of these items come via a publicist’s pitch, and none of the suggestions contain affiliate links. These are all things that we genuinely love and can picture wrapping up ourselves. Suffice it to say, there’s nothing artificial about our studious consideration and good taste. Entertainment I couldn’t afford most Nintendo 64 games growing up, so I was a frequent presence at the local video game rental store: I distinctly remember taking home the original version of “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time”—and needing to return it jusstttt as I was on the cusp of saving Hyrule, the game’s fictional realm, and beating the big baddie, Ganondorf. This Switch 2 remake of the game has given me a shot at redemption. It’s one of the most critically lauded games of the year—and for good reason. The graphics are dazzling, and I can only describe them as “wet”: Everyone looks magnificently dewy. I also cannot overrecommend the nostalgia dopamine hit from getting to rummage through those treasure chests again.— Justin McCraw, senior software engineer A couple of weeks ago, the internet was abuzz about an AI-generated trailer that imagined an alt-history in which Nazi Germany and America wage some sort of temporal war. Sure, the clip was cool, but I still have my doubts about whether we’re yet at the point where AI can make a comprehensible feature film. In the meantime, there’s “Fatherland,” a 1992 alt-history bestseller from Robert Harris, the ultra-dependable thriller author. It imagines a 1960s landscape where Nazi Germany triumphed in Europe during World War II, and an aging Hitler clings to power. I think it’s Harris’ best world-building effort, which he accomplished through an enormous amount of research into how Hitler’s chief architect, Albert Speer, hoped to transform Berlin. (Those plans included the Volkshalle, a massive dome; in the novel, Harris supersizes Speer’s own ambitions, imagining the Volkshalle as a structure large enough to have its own microclimate.) “Fatherland” is taut as hell and completely unputdownable—with a weary, disillusioned city police captain, Xavier March, caught up in an intricate plot that runs through the Reich’s highest ranks. As March investigates, he keeps practically tripping over dead bodies. Then there’s the mystery of the terrible secrets kept in a hidden Swiss bank account.— Abram Brown, features editor

items.title: This ER Doctor Became a Hospital’s First Clinical AI Engineer
items.summary: When Boston Children’s Hospital posted a job listing for a prompt engineer in 2023, Dinesh Rai decided to apply. He didn’t expect to get the job. At the time, prompt engineering was being touted as one of the hot new jobs created by generative AI. Companies wanted people who knew how to coax the best answers from large language models (LLMs) by carefully wording instructions, supplying examples, and giving the systems personas or other context. Dinesh Rai Employer: Boston Children’s Hospital Occupation: Clinical AI Engineer Education: Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of Medicine It was an unusual role for a hospital, but Rai had an unusual résumé. While he was trained as an emergency physician, he had also taught himself to code just before entering medical school. After completing a fellowship in clinical informatics—which focuses on the intersection of clinical practice and IT systems—he moved into health technology. Boston Children’s brought him on board in August 2023. Three years later, Rai still works there. Prompt engineering, however, has become a much less important part of the job . When he joined, the expectation was that prompting would become a job in itself. “Knowing how to prompt AI properly was going to be the job function of the future,” says John Brownstein , chief innovation officer at Boston Children’s. Early on, the hospital needed internal expertise about how to begin using AI, Brownstein says. Companies wanted people who knew how to coax the best answers from large language models (LLMs) by carefully wording instructions, supplying examples, and giving the systems personas or other context.

Dinesh Rai

Employer:

Boston Children’s Hospital

Occupation:

Clinical AI Engineer

Education:

Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of Medicine

items.title: MIT Professor Says After a Few Drinks, Anthropic Employees Start Talking About Overthrowing the Government and Taking Over the World
items.summary: You won’t believe the things Anthropic employees say once they get a few drinks in them. Or — based on the company’s self-serious AI mission, its apocalyptic warnings about its technology’s powerful abilities, and its cultish obsession with AI consciousness — maybe you will. In a recent interview with Novaro Media , MIT physicist and AI safety advocate Max Tegmark claimed that Anthropic researchers, when their lips are loosened by a few libations, start to openly talk about toppling governments and world domination. “After they’ve had a couple of drinks, the conversation often gets into overthrowing the US government and taking over the world,” he said . Almost as shocking to Tegmark was that no one was reacting to their villainous-sounding delusions of grandeur. “But then I realized why: it’s because they speak in code,” Tegmark continued. “They tend not to use words like ‘coup,’ and ‘overthrow the US government,’ and use the code phrase ‘alignment without control.'” This gets into a belief in the AI industry that AI models will eventually spiral out of our control, and so the best way to prevent these powerful intelligent beings from catastrophically blowing back against us is by ensuring they’re fundamentally aligned with human values. If the AI is nice, basically, it won’t hurt us, and we can avoid being enslaved like in the “Matrix” movies. According to Tegmark, Anthropic researchers don’t want AI models to be controlled by entities like the US government. Instead, they want the future that “Alan Turing predicted: where it’s going to be Anthropic’s machine god running Earth, and the rest of us have to hope somehow that it’s going to be nice.” These are extraordinary claims, but it tracks for an industry where many of its leaders and talent sincerely believe they’re creating some kind of machine god . And it definitely tracks for Anthropic in particular, whose employees reportedly “worship” their AI model Claude as some sort of deity — and where a former researcher who quit the company warned that the people there building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” More on AI: Anthropic Stock Slumps Below IPO Price After Claiming to Have Solved the Most Famous Math Problem in the World

Or — based on the company’s self-serious AI mission, its apocalyptic warnings about its technology’s powerful abilities, and its cultish obsession with AI consciousness — maybe you will.

In a recent interview with Novaro Media, MIT physicist and AI safety advocate Max Tegmark claimed that Anthropic researchers, when their lips are loosened by a few libations, start to openly talk about toppling governments and world domination.

“After they’ve had a couple of drinks, the conversation often gets into overthrowing the US government and taking over the world,” he said.

Almost as shocking to Tegmark was that no one was reacting to their villainous-sounding delusions of grandeur.

“But then I realized why: it’s because they speak in code,” Tegmark continued. “They tend not to use words like ‘coup,’ and ‘overthrow the US government,’ and use the code phrase ‘alignment without control.'”

This gets into a belief in the AI industry that AI models will eventually spiral out of our control, and so the best way to prevent these powerful intelligent beings from catastrophically blowing back against us is by ensuring they’re fundamentally aligned with human values. If the AI is nice, basically, it won’t hurt us, and we can avoid being enslaved like in the “Matrix” movies.

According to Tegmark, Anthropic researchers don’t want AI models to be controlled by entities like the US government. Instead, they want the future that “Alan Turing predicted: where it’s going to be Anthropic’s machine god running Earth, and the rest of us have to hope somehow that it’s going to be nice.” 

These are extraordinary claims, but it tracks for an industry where many of its leaders and talent sincerely believe they’re creating some kind of machine god. And it definitely tracks for Anthropic in particular, whose employees reportedly “worship” their AI model Claude as some sort of deity — and where a former researcher who quit the company warned that the people there building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

items.title: From Alibaba to BharatGen, 10 Small Language Models That Rivalled LLMs in 2026
items.summary: Small language models (SLMs) are emerging as efficient alternatives to large language models (LLMs), which often require significant computing power, memory, and infrastructure. Unlike general-purpose LLMs, smaller models can be optimised for specific tasks such as coding, translation, document processing, and reasoning. According to a 2025 paper by Vishwakarma Institute of Technology, ​​a single training run for GPT-3 consumed 1,287 MWh and emitted 552 tons of CO2. Meanwhile, specialised models with 1–14 billion parameters matched or exceeded LLM performance on specific tasks while requiring 10–100x less computation. SLMs can also run on laptops, smartphones, and edge devices, ensuring data residency rules apply across sensitive sectors such as banking, healthcare, and legal. From multilingual models designed for Indian users to enterprise-focused systems and models built for on-device AI, here are 10 small language models released in 2026 that are primed to become enterprise workhorses. 1. Qwen 3.5 (Alibaba) Alibaba's Qwen 3.5 family includes smaller variants with 0.8B, 2B, 4B, and 9B parameters. The SLM variants support multimodal understanding, reasoning, and coding, while their hybrid architecture is designed to improve inference efficiency. They are designed for deployment across devices with limited computing resources. On graduate-level science and reasoning evaluation GPQA Diamond, Qwen3.5-9B outperformed rival mid-tier models—even beating Google’s Gemma-4-12B-IT in five out of eight shared benchmarks. They are available through Hugging Face and ModelScope, allowing developers to download and customise them. 2. Gemma 4 E2B and E4B (Google DeepMind) Google DeepMind's Gemma 4 family includes E2B and E4B small language models designed for mobile and edge deployment. They are designed to support image and audio understanding, multilingual tasks, and function calling. Google reports that Gemma 4 E4B scored 69.4% on MMLU-Pro for multi-domain reasoning questions and 52.6% on MMMU-Pro for college-level reasoning. The models are available under an Apache 2.0 licence. 3. Nemotron 3 Nano 4B (NVIDIA) NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 family includes Nano, Super, and Ultra models designed for agentic AI applications. Nemotron 3 Nano has 31.6 billion total parameters but activates approximately 3.2 billion per token. It targets tasks such as coding, summarisation, reasoning and agentic workflows, with a context window of up to 1 million tokens. According to Artificial Analysis, Nemotron 3 Nano 4B is among the most concise models in its class, generating roughly 5x fewer verbose reasoning tokens. Its hybrid Mixture-of-Experts architecture aims to improve efficiency in multi-agent workflows, where multiple AI systems work together to complete tasks. NVIDIA has also released supporting training datasets and reinforcement-learning resources to help developers build, customise, and evaluate specialised AI agents. 4. Hy-MT2 1.8B (Tencent) Tencent's Hy-MT2 is a specialised translation model available in 1.8B, 7B, and 30B-A3B variants. It supports 33 languages, along with several minority languages and Chinese dialects, and is designed for multilingual communication. Its smallest version can be compressed to approximately 440MB using extreme quantisation, making it suitable for on-device deployment such as on Apple, Qualcomm, and MediaTek mobile chips. 5. Granite 4.2 (IBM) IBM's Granite 4.2 comes in 3B, 8B, and 30B configurations. The models focus on enterprise applications, including reasoning, coding, instruction following, and tool use. They are available through Hugging Face and IBM's AI ecosystem for developers to experiment with and deploy. The 3B version is built specifically for edge deployment and laptops. While it undergoes supervised fine-tuning and general reinforcement learning, the 8B version goes through the full Agentic RL training stage, optimising it for multi-step terminal/CLI execution, multi-turn tool orchestration, and repository-level code editing. 6. LFM3 (Liquid AI) Liquid AI's LFM3 extends its Liquid Foundation Models family with compact models targeting multimodal and on-device applications. The company focuses on efficient architectures that can support AI applications without requiring large-scale computing infrastructure. The models are intended for developers building local assistants and applications that require lower latency, reduced cloud dependence, and on-device processing. Meanwhile, LFM2.5-VL-3B is a vision-language model designed to understand images, documents and digital interfaces. It scored 80.7 on ScreenSpot-v2, a benchmark that evaluates how well models identify elements on computer screens, according to Liquid AI. Its capabilities could support applications such as document analysis, screen navigation, and software automation, where AI systems need to interpret information beyond text. 7. Aion 1.0 Instruct (Microsoft) Microsoft's Aion 1.0 Instruct is a 2.3B-parameter model designed to power local AI experiences on Windows devices. It supports a 32,000-token context window and is intended for edge applications. Microsoft plans to optimise the model for Windows and integrate it with moderation capabilities, with wider availability expected in 2027. 8. Inkling 2 Mini (Thinking Machines Lab) Thinking Machines Lab's Inkling 2 Mini has 26.4B total parameters, with approximately 3.4B active parameters, giving it an SLM-class computation. Its looped Transformer architecture processes certain layers repeatedly to improve reasoning while managing computational requirements It’s in the same MoE category as NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B. The model scored 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, a coding benchmark. Its open weights and relatively compact active parameter count are intended to make it accessible to developers building specialised AI applications. 9. Dhīr 2B and 5B (ZenteiQ) ZenteiQ's Dhīr 2B is an Indian-language model supporting English and 10 Indian languages. Trained on more than 6 trillion tokens, it is designed for multilingual applications and offline deployment. It is available through AIKosh. Meanwhile, Dhīr 5B uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture with approximately 5.09B total parameters and 1.79B active parameters. Its architecture activates only a portion of its parameters for each token, helping manage computational requirements. ZenteiQ is targeting secure, offline-capable deployments across enterprise and public-service applications. 10. Param 2 (BharatGen) BharatGen's Param 2 is a 17B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 2.4B active parameters, putting it firmly into the SLM-compute class of models. It is pre-trained on 22.5 trillion tokens. It supports all 22 scheduled Indian languages and English, with capabilities in reasoning, coding, and tool use. The company said it is ideal for public-sector, agricultural, and regional language enterprise deployments.

7. Aion 1.0 Instruct (Microsoft)

Microsoft's Aion 1.0 Instruct is a 2.3B-parameter model designed to power local AI experiences on Windows devices. It supports a 32,000-token context window and is intended for edge applications. Microsoft plans to optimise the model for Windows and integrate it with moderation capabilities, with wider availability expected in 2027.

8. Inkling 2 Mini (Thinking Machines Lab)

Thinking Machines Lab's Inkling 2 Mini has 26.4B total parameters, with approximately 3.4B active parameters, giving it an SLM-class computation. Its looped Transformer architecture processes certain layers repeatedly to improve reasoning while managing computational requirements

It’s in the same MoE category as NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B. 

The model scored 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, a coding benchmark. Its open weights and relatively compact active parameter count are intended to make it accessible to developers building specialised AI applications.

9. Dhīr 2B and 5B (ZenteiQ)

ZenteiQ's Dhīr 2B is an Indian-language model supporting English and 10 Indian languages. Trained on more than 6 trillion tokens, it is designed for multilingual applications and offline deployment. It is available through AIKosh.

Meanwhile, Dhīr 5B uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture with approximately 5.09B total parameters and 1.79B active parameters. Its architecture activates only a portion of its parameters for each token, helping manage computational requirements. 

ZenteiQ is targeting secure, offline-capable deployments across enterprise and public-service applications.

10. Param 2 (BharatGen)

BharatGen's Param 2 is a 17B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 2.4B active parameters, putting it firmly into the SLM-compute class of models. It is pre-trained on 22.5 trillion tokens.

It supports all 22 scheduled Indian languages and English, with capabilities in reasoning, coding, and tool use. The company said it is ideal for public-sector, agricultural, and regional language enterprise deployments.

items.title: Claude Think Tool Explained: How It Works in AI Agents
items.summary: An AI agent can call the right tool and still make the wrong decision afterward. A search might return conflicting information. A database lookup might leave a required field unresolved. A test result might show that the agent’s original explanation for a bug was wrong. The next step depends on understanding what just happened. Having access to tools does not automatically make that interpretation reliable. Anthropic’s Claude think tool explored a simple way to give the model space to work through new information during a task. It used the same tool-calling interface as an ordinary function, but its purpose was to record a working note before the agent continued. There is an important update to keep in mind. Anthropic now recommends native extended thinking over a separate think tool in most cases. The original technique is still useful to understand, especially if you are learning how agent loops and scratchpads work. Anthropic's updated article What is the Claude think tool? The original think tool is a function that accepts a text argument. That text is a note generated by the model. The function does not need to search for information, call another language model, or change an external system. In fact, the think handler in the original τ-bench implementation returns an empty string: def think(thought: str) -> str: return "" The function body is almost empty because the useful content has already appeared in the model’s tool-call arguments. The surrounding application keeps that call in the conversation history. Original τ-bench implementation This is the first distinction worth understanding: the model generates the note; the tool handler does not generate it. The tool gives that note a defined place in the interaction. Start with an ordinary tool-calling loop Before adding a scratchpad, it helps to understand the loop it becomes part of. When we give Claude a custom tool, we provide a description and an input schema. Claude uses those instructions to decide whether to request the tool and what arguments to supply. Our application then executes the function and returns its result. User request ↓ Claude requests a tool ↓ Application runs the function ↓ Application returns the result ↓ Claude continues The model does not directly execute our Python function. It produces a structured request that our code handles. That distinction is part of Anthropic’s tool-use contract . The application supplies the operations, the model requests them, and the results return through the conversation. A task can involve several trips through this loop. Each result may change which action makes sense next. Where a scratchpad fits A plan made before the first tool call cannot account for every fact that later calls will reveal. The agent may discover that information is missing, that two sources disagree, or that an earlier assumption no longer holds. It needs to interpret those results before choosing what to do next. The think tool adds an explicit place for a working note: Claude requests an information-gathering tool ↓ Application returns new information ↓ Claude writes a note through the think tool ↓ Application acknowledges the call ↓ Claude continues with the updated conversation The extra step can help separate what the agent has observed from what it still needs to check. For example, an illustrative note might say: The sources describe different versions of the API. The current behavior is still unverified. Check the latest documentation before answering. This is a short task note based on available evidence. It identifies an unresolved issue and a next check. The note does not establish which source is correct. That still requires verification. Its value is that the unresolved issue becomes explicit before the agent continues. How a function that returns nothing can be useful The empty function body can make the technique look strange at first. Usually, we add a tool because its output provides something the model does not already have. A search returns pages. A calculation returns a number. A file-reading function returns text. With think, the important content is in the request. Claude generates the note while constructing the tool call. That call then becomes part of the continuing conversation, alongside the earlier tool results. The next model request can include: Earlier instructions Earlier observations The think tool call and its note The acknowledgement There is no additional source of intelligence inside the handler. The technique changes the interaction by giving the model an explicit opportunity to produce intermediate working text. It also depends on the application preserving that text. Calling a function and discarding the surrounding conversation would remove much of the mechanism we are trying to use. A simple Python implementation There are two parts to define: the interface Claude sees and the function our application runs. The following example demonstrates the original custom-tool pattern. For a new Claude application, check native thinking support before deciding to add a separate scratchpad tool. Define the tool interface THINK_TOOL = { "name": "think", "description": ( "Record a brief working note after inspecting tool results. " "Use it to note confirmed facts, missing information, " "and the next check. It does not fetch data or perform actions." ), "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "thought": { "type": "string", "description": ( "A short task note based on the available evidence." ), } }, "required": ["thought"], }, } The name identifies the tool. The description explains its purpose and when it is useful. The schema specifies the argument the model must provide. The Python implementation is not part of this definition. Claude receives the interface, while our application keeps responsibility for execution. Anthropic’s tool-definition documentation describes this structure. Implement the handler def think(thought: str) -> str: return "Noted." This handler acknowledges the call. It does not repeat the note because the note is already present in the tool-call arguments. An illustrative call could look like this: { "type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_example", "name": "think", "input": { "thought": "The sources refer to different API versions. Verify the current documentation before answering." } } The application executes: think( thought=( "The sources refer to different API versions. " "Verify the current documentation before answering." ) ) and returns the acknowledgement. Writing the note to a separate application log is optional. Keeping it in the model’s continuing conversation is the part that matters for this example. Keep the tool call in the conversation When the API returns a tool request, the next request should preserve the assistant’s content and include the corresponding tool result. Here is a small helper for successful client-tool calls: def append_tool_round(messages, response, handlers): messages.append({ "role": "assistant", "content": response.content, }) results = [] for block in response.content: if block.type != "tool_use": continue output = handlers[block.name](**block.input) results.append({ "type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": output, }) messages.append({ "role": "user", "content": results, }) The handlers dictionary connects tool names to their Python functions: handlers = { "think": think, } An application with other custom tools would register their handlers here too. Two details in the helper are important. First, it preserves response.content. That includes the think call and the note Claude supplied. Second, each result contains a tool_use_id matching the call it answers. The acknowledgement belongs to that specific invocation. Returning only "Noted." without preserving the assistant's call would leave out the useful text. Anthropic's tool-result documentation explains the required message structure. Continue the existing agent loop Inside an application that already has a configured client, model, tools, and message history, the continuation follows the usual pattern: while response.stop_reason == "tool_use": append_tool_round(messages, response, handlers) response = client.messages.create( model=MODEL, max_tokens=2048, tools=[THINK_TOOL], messages=messages, ) This example exposes only the think tool. A real agent would include its other tool definitions in the same tools list and register their handlers. The loop repeats because Claude may request another tool before finishing. Production code also needs to handle tool failures, iteration limits, and responses that stop because they reach an output limit. The scratchpad uses the same conversation mechanism as the other custom tools. The description influences how the tool gets used Adding a function named think does not tell the model what a useful note should contain. A vague instruction can produce vague notes. It can also encourage unnecessary calls that repeat information without helping the next decision. The description should make the intended purpose clear. In this example, the note records what the available evidence establishes and what remains unresolved. A short instruction in the system prompt could reinforce that purpose: When tool results leave an important issue unresolved, use the think tool to record a brief task note. Identify the missing information and the next check. Keep the note concise and grounded in observed results. Skip the tool when the next action is already clear. This is a suggested instruction for the example, rather than a claim that this exact wording has been benchmarked. It asks for a concise task note. It does not ask the model to expose private internal reasoning. For current Claude integrations, Anthropic’s tool guidance recommends requesting short explanations or supporting evidence in tool arguments, while keeping internal reasoning in native thinking blocks. Current tool-description guidance How this relates to context and memory A scratchpad note can influence a later step only if the model receives it. In the implementation above, that happens through messages. The next request includes the earlier conversation, the assistant's tool call, and the result. This makes the note part of the model’s available context. It does not automatically make it permanent memory. If the application starts a new conversation without carrying the note over, that new conversation does not receive it. Similarly, saving a note to a file does not make the model aware of the file’s contents unless the application provides a way to read them. The context-window documentation explains how messages and tool results contribute to what the model can reference. There is also a practical cost to keeping notes. They add generated text, occupy context, and may be included in subsequent requests. Repeated notes that no longer affect the task can become unnecessary input. A useful working note should make an unresolved issue easier to track. It should not become another long document the agent has to interpret. What Anthropic’s experiments showed Anthropic evaluated the original technique using Claude 3.7 Sonnet, including experiments on τ-bench. The benchmark places an agent in conversations with simulated users and gives it tools and domain-specific policies. Its evaluation checks whether the interaction reaches the intended outcome. It also measures consistency using pass^k . This estimates success across all of several independent attempts at a task. It differs from pass@k, which counts a task as successful if at least one attempt succeeds. τ-bench paper For the retail domain, Anthropic reported: These results show an improvement in that experimental setting. The article also reports stronger airline results when the tool was paired with optimized instructions. Anthropic’s evaluation The scope matters. These are results for particular models, tasks, and prompts. They do not establish that adding a tool with the same name improves every agent. They also give us a reason to evaluate the whole configuration. A tool description, system instructions, and the model’s behavior can all affect what happens after we add the function. Think tool versus native thinking The original article described a distinction between extended thinking before action and a custom tool that could introduce working text during a sequence of actions. Current Claude capabilities make that distinction less useful as a general rule. Anthropic now documents interleaved thinking , which lets Claude reason between tool calls. The model can consider a tool result before deciding what to do next without needing a separate custom think invocation. Adaptive thinking supports this automatically on models that offer that mode. Current thinking documentation The two approaches also represent their content differently: A custom tool note is ordinary generated application content. It should not be treated as a direct view into the model’s private reasoning. Native thinking also has model-specific configuration and message-handling requirements. The current documentation is the right place to check those details before copying a setup intended for an older model. For most new Claude applications, Anthropic’s updated recommendation makes native thinking the starting point. The custom tool remains a useful example of how intermediate text can become part of an agent’s continuing context. How to decide whether a scratchpad helps your agent Start with a failed run. Find the point where the agent received useful information but did not use it correctly. Perhaps it ignored a conflict, continued with an outdated assumption, or acted before collecting a required detail. That gives you something specific to test. A scratchpad step is more relevant to that kind of failure than to a simple lookup whose result can be returned directly. If no intermediate decision needs reconsideration, another tool round may mostly add time and tokens. For a meaningful comparison, keep the tasks, model, and available tools fixed. Compare the existing behavior with a clearly defined alternative, such as native thinking or a custom note tool. Look beyond whether the agent produced longer notes. Check whether it chose the right next action and reached the intended outcome. Repeated attempts can help reveal whether an apparent improvement is consistent. The code walkthrough above shows how to preserve a note. It does not establish that the note improves a particular application. What to check before adding another tool The useful question is where the agent first stopped using the evidence correctly. If the tool result was incomplete, the agent may need another lookup. If the result contradicted an assumption, it may need to revise its plan. If the next step was already obvious, an extra note may add little. That is a more useful starting point than adding a scratchpad to every workflow. It gives you a concrete failure to address and a way to compare the available approaches. I write about context, retrieval, and how AI agents work. Follow along if you found this breakdown useful.
