items.summary_html:
An AI agent can call the right tool and still make the wrong decision afterward. A search might return conflicting information. A database lookup might leave a required field unresolved. A test result might show that the agent’s original explanation for a bug was wrong.

The next step depends on understanding what just happened. Having access to tools does not automatically make that interpretation reliable.

Anthropic’s Claude think tool explored a simple way to give the model space to work through new information during a task. It used the same tool-calling interface as an ordinary function, but its purpose was to record a working note before the agent continued.

There is an important update to keep in mind. Anthropic now recommends native extended thinking over a separate think tool in most cases. The original technique is still useful to understand, especially if you are learning how agent loops and scratchpads work. Anthropic's updated article

What is the Claude think tool?

The original think tool is a function that accepts a text argument. That text is a note generated by the model. The function does not need to search for information, call another language model, or change an external system.

In fact, the think handler in the original τ-bench implementation returns an empty string:

def think(thought: str) -> str:
    return ""

The function body is almost empty because the useful content has already appeared in the model’s tool-call arguments. The surrounding application keeps that call in the conversation history. Original τ-bench implementation

This is the first distinction worth understanding: the model generates the note; the tool handler does not generate it. The tool gives that note a defined place in the interaction.

Start with an ordinary tool-calling loop

Before adding a scratchpad, it helps to understand the loop it becomes part of. When we give Claude a custom tool, we provide a description and an input schema. Claude uses those instructions to decide whether to request the tool and what arguments to supply. Our application then executes the function and returns its result.

User request
     ↓
Claude requests a tool
     ↓
Application runs the function
     ↓
Application returns the result
     ↓
Claude continues

The model does not directly execute our Python function. It produces a structured request that our code handles. That distinction is part of Anthropic’s tool-use contract. The application supplies the operations, the model requests them, and the results return through the conversation.

A task can involve several trips through this loop. Each result may change which action makes sense next.

Where a scratchpad fits

A plan made before the first tool call cannot account for every fact that later calls will reveal. The agent may discover that information is missing, that two sources disagree, or that an earlier assumption no longer holds. It needs to interpret those results before choosing what to do next.

The think tool adds an explicit place for a working note:

Claude requests an information-gathering tool
                      ↓
Application returns new information
                      ↓
Claude writes a note through the think tool
                      ↓
Application acknowledges the call
                      ↓
Claude continues with the updated conversation

The extra step can help separate what the agent has observed from what it still needs to check. For example, an illustrative note might say:

The sources describe different versions of the API.
The current behavior is still unverified.
Check the latest documentation before answering.

This is a short task note based on available evidence. It identifies an unresolved issue and a next check. The note does not establish which source is correct. That still requires verification. Its value is that the unresolved issue becomes explicit before the agent continues.

How a function that returns nothing can be useful

The empty function body can make the technique look strange at first. Usually, we add a tool because its output provides something the model does not already have. A search returns pages. A calculation returns a number. A file-reading function returns text.

With think, the important content is in the request. Claude generates the note while constructing the tool call. That call then becomes part of the continuing conversation, alongside the earlier tool results.

The next model request can include:

Earlier instructions
Earlier observations
The think tool call and its note
The acknowledgement

There is no additional source of intelligence inside the handler. The technique changes the interaction by giving the model an explicit opportunity to produce intermediate working text.

It also depends on the application preserving that text. Calling a function and discarding the surrounding conversation would remove much of the mechanism we are trying to use.

A simple Python implementation

There are two parts to define: the interface Claude sees and the function our application runs.

The following example demonstrates the original custom-tool pattern. For a new Claude application, check native thinking support before deciding to add a separate scratchpad tool.

Define the tool interface
THINK_TOOL = {
    "name": "think",
    "description": (
        "Record a brief working note after inspecting tool results. "
        "Use it to note confirmed facts, missing information, "
        "and the next check. It does not fetch data or perform actions."
    ),
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "thought": {
                "type": "string",
                "description": (
                    "A short task note based on the available evidence."
                ),
            }
        },
        "required": ["thought"],
    },
}

The name identifies the tool. The description explains its purpose and when it is useful. The schema specifies the argument the model must provide.

The Python implementation is not part of this definition. Claude receives the interface, while our application keeps responsibility for execution. Anthropic’s tool-definition documentation describes this structure.

Implement the handler
def think(thought: str) -> str:
    return "Noted."

This handler acknowledges the call. It does not repeat the note because the note is already present in the tool-call arguments.

An illustrative call could look like this:

{
  "type": "tool_use",
  "id": "toolu_example",
  "name": "think",
  "input": {
    "thought": "The sources refer to different API versions. Verify the current documentation before answering."
  }
}

The application executes:

think(
    thought=(
        "The sources refer to different API versions. "
        "Verify the current documentation before answering."
    )
)

and returns the acknowledgement.

Writing the note to a separate application log is optional. Keeping it in the model’s continuing conversation is the part that matters for this example.

Keep the tool call in the conversation

When the API returns a tool request, the next request should preserve the assistant’s content and include the corresponding tool result.

Here is a small helper for successful client-tool calls:

def append_tool_round(messages, response, handlers):
    messages.append({
        "role": "assistant",
        "content": response.content,
    })
results = []
for block in response.content:
        if block.type != "tool_use":
            continue
output = handlers[block.name](**block.input)
results.append({
            "type": "tool_result",
            "tool_use_id": block.id,
            "content": output,
        })
messages.append({
        "role": "user",
        "content": results,
    })

The handlers dictionary connects tool names to their Python functions:

handlers = {
    "think": think,
}

An application with other custom tools would register their handlers here too.

Two details in the helper are important.

  1. First, it preserves response.content. That includes the think call and the note Claude supplied.
  2. Second, each result contains a tool_use_id matching the call it answers. The acknowledgement belongs to that specific invocation.

Returning only "Noted." without preserving the assistant's call would leave out the useful text. Anthropic's tool-result documentation explains the required message structure.

Continue the existing agent loop

Inside an application that already has a configured client, model, tools, and message history, the continuation follows the usual pattern:

while response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    append_tool_round(messages, response, handlers)

    response = client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL,
        max_tokens=2048,
        tools=[THINK_TOOL],
        messages=messages,
    )

This example exposes only the think tool. A real agent would include its other tool definitions in the same tools list and register their handlers.

The loop repeats because Claude may request another tool before finishing. Production code also needs to handle tool failures, iteration limits, and responses that stop because they reach an output limit. The scratchpad uses the same conversation mechanism as the other custom tools.

The description influences how the tool gets used

Adding a function named think does not tell the model what a useful note should contain. A vague instruction can produce vague notes. It can also encourage unnecessary calls that repeat information without helping the next decision.

The description should make the intended purpose clear. In this example, the note records what the available evidence establishes and what remains unresolved. A short instruction in the system prompt could reinforce that purpose:

When tool results leave an important issue unresolved,
use the think tool to record a brief task note. 
Identify the missing information and the next check.
Keep the note concise and grounded in observed results.
Skip the tool when the next action is already clear.

This is a suggested instruction for the example, rather than a claim that this exact wording has been benchmarked. It asks for a concise task note. It does not ask the model to expose private internal reasoning.

For current Claude integrations, Anthropic’s tool guidance recommends requesting short explanations or supporting evidence in tool arguments, while keeping internal reasoning in native thinking blocks. Current tool-description guidance

How this relates to context and memory

A scratchpad note can influence a later step only if the model receives it. In the implementation above, that happens through messages. The next request includes the earlier conversation, the assistant's tool call, and the result.

This makes the note part of the model’s available context. It does not automatically make it permanent memory. If the application starts a new conversation without carrying the note over, that new conversation does not receive it. Similarly, saving a note to a file does not make the model aware of the file’s contents unless the application provides a way to read them.

The context-window documentation explains how messages and tool results contribute to what the model can reference. There is also a practical cost to keeping notes. They add generated text, occupy context, and may be included in subsequent requests. Repeated notes that no longer affect the task can become unnecessary input.

A useful working note should make an unresolved issue easier to track. It should not become another long document the agent has to interpret.

What Anthropic’s experiments showed

Anthropic evaluated the original technique using Claude 3.7 Sonnet, including experiments on τ-bench. The benchmark places an agent in conversations with simulated users and gives it tools and domain-specific policies. Its evaluation checks whether the interaction reaches the intended outcome.

It also measures consistency using pass^k. This estimates success across all of several independent attempts at a task. It differs from pass@k, which counts a task as successful if at least one attempt succeeds. τ-bench paper

For the retail domain, Anthropic reported:

These results show an improvement in that experimental setting. The article also reports stronger airline results when the tool was paired with optimized instructions. Anthropic’s evaluation

The scope matters. These are results for particular models, tasks, and prompts. They do not establish that adding a tool with the same name improves every agent.

They also give us a reason to evaluate the whole configuration. A tool description, system instructions, and the model’s behavior can all affect what happens after we add the function.

Think tool versus native thinking

The original article described a distinction between extended thinking before action and a custom tool that could introduce working text during a sequence of actions. Current Claude capabilities make that distinction less useful as a general rule.

Anthropic now documents interleaved thinking, which lets Claude reason between tool calls. The model can consider a tool result before deciding what to do next without needing a separate custom think invocation. Adaptive thinking supports this automatically on models that offer that mode. Current thinking documentation

The two approaches also represent their content differently:

A custom tool note is ordinary generated application content. It should not be treated as a direct view into the model’s private reasoning. Native thinking also has model-specific configuration and message-handling requirements. The current documentation is the right place to check those details before copying a setup intended for an older model.

For most new Claude applications, Anthropic’s updated recommendation makes native thinking the starting point. The custom tool remains a useful example of how intermediate text can become part of an agent’s continuing context.

How to decide whether a scratchpad helps your agent

Start with a failed run. Find the point where the agent received useful information but did not use it correctly. Perhaps it ignored a conflict, continued with an outdated assumption, or acted before collecting a required detail.

That gives you something specific to test. A scratchpad step is more relevant to that kind of failure than to a simple lookup whose result can be returned directly. If no intermediate decision needs reconsideration, another tool round may mostly add time and tokens.

For a meaningful comparison, keep the tasks, model, and available tools fixed. Compare the existing behavior with a clearly defined alternative, such as native thinking or a custom note tool.

Look beyond whether the agent produced longer notes. Check whether it chose the right next action and reached the intended outcome. Repeated attempts can help reveal whether an apparent improvement is consistent. The code walkthrough above shows how to preserve a note. It does not establish that the note improves a particular application.

What to check before adding another tool

The useful question is where the agent first stopped using the evidence correctly. If the tool result was incomplete, the agent may need another lookup. If the result contradicted an assumption, it may need to revise its plan. If the next step was already obvious, an extra note may add little.

That is a more useful starting point than adding a scratchpad to every workflow. It gives you a concrete failure to address and a way to compare the available approaches.

items.title: Nvidia Blackwell Chips Turn Up at China Site Tied to Alice Huang
items.summary: A pair of Chinese firms installed Nvidia Corp.’s powerful Blackwell semiconductors in a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, the woman at the heart of a controversy surrounding the US chipmaker. The gear installed at the Yangtze River Delta Project included a GB300 NVL72 rack, among Nvidia’s most powerful products, according to a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November. Shanghai Shuoyao offered the hardware as collateral to obtain a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank, according to filings from the lender that were reviewed by Bloomberg News. Bloomberg's Tom Keene and Paul Sweeney get details from Olivia Levieux, Markets Strategist with Bloomberg News (Source: Bloomberg)

items.title: Why SAP’s second 10,000-job overhaul in two years matters to CIOs
items.summary: When SAP restructured roughly 10,000 roles in 2024, executives framed the move as a workforce transformation designed to prepare the company for cloud computing and AI. Two years later, SAP is reportedly considering eliminating another 10,000 positions, but this time the rationale appears different. Rather than reshaping skills while maintaining headcount, analysts say the latest overhaul reflects a growing belief among technology companies that AI can permanently reduce labor needs, raising new questions for CIOs about vendor stability, support quality, and the economics of the AI era. The layoffs are expected to impact several departments, including product and engineering, according to a Bloomberg article that reported on the new round of layoffs. While the 2024 restructuring did not reduce the headcount and was shown as a reshuffle of skills to align with the company’s AI-first strategy, the new round of layoffs appears to be focused on cost reduction and is likely to shrink the company’s employee count by about 9%. “SAP’s 2024 programme changed who worked there, and this one is about how many,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Grehound Research. When SAP announced a major restructuring in 2024 affecting roughly 10,000 positions, executives described it as a strategic shift toward cloud computing and AI. The company took a restructuring charge of about €3 billion and repositioned talent toward growth areas, including AI. SAP did not directly comment on the Bloomberg story, saying it does not comment on speculation. A company spokesperson, however, said, “The business environment in which we operate is changing rapidly through AI, and we are continuously reviewing how our organization and workforce need to evolve to remain successful. As part of this ongoing transformation, roles and functions will naturally change over time. Beyond this, no decisions have been made regarding any further measures.” Looking beyond the employee count For CIOs, the key issue is not the scale of the cuts. It is why a company that already undertook a major restructuring just two years ago believes another overhaul may be necessary. “AI can reduce manpower requirements in software development, testing, documentation, customer support, pre-sales, and implementation activities. But Tech CEOs were arguing that, because of Jevons Paradox, AI will create more demand for software. In reality, that has not happened yet. CEOs who were saying AI will create more tech jobs are doing layoffs,” said Pareekh Jain, CEO at Pareekh Consulting. Yet, SAP’s move toward this second restructuring is hardly a surprise, according to analysts. Gogia describes the move as part of a three-step change at SAP. “First came the slow tightening: Klein’s 2025 talk of one or two per cent a year, then the July 2026 memo focusing new hiring on ‘mainly core AI roles.’ Next came the substitution, which Klein described plainly when he said SAP is balancing token consumption against headcount. Last came the declaration, when Asam told investors the episode of rising headcount was over and spoke of five-digit numbers of employees to be touched.” Read in sequence, the Bloomberg report is less a surprise than the third step arriving on schedule, with tokens now the fuel the engine prefers to salaries, Gogia added. What happens next SAP avoided using terms such as layoffs or job cuts in its 2024 restructuring plan, terming the changes voluntary programs and internal retraining measures. At the same time, the company has also been unusually vocal about its internal AI gains . “The autonomous enterprise SAP launched in May 2026 needs data scientists, agent builders and people who understand business processes deeply enough to teach software to run them. Nothing in that roadmap requires a cut of at least 10,000,” Gogia said. The CIOs who sat through the 2024 reshuffle have reason to feel uneasy, because the first round tested their patience and this one tests their support desk. SAP’s board should publish where the cuts land, function by function, before the January results, said Gogia. CIOs should ask SAP, in writing and before any 2027 renewal, which of their service commitments depend on teams named in the programme, and what SAP will measure to prove service holds.” The article originally appeared on CIO .

items.title: Mark Zuckerberg's Thanksgiving menu: 'GTA 6,' smoked meat, and Meta's AI gadget
items.summary: Mark Zuckerberg didn't miss an opportunity to promote Muse Charm. Bloomberg/Getty Images Mark Zuckerberg shared a Thanksgiving video showing him playing "GTA 6" as a turkey smoked. He asked Meta's Muse AI agent for an update on the bird using a Muse Charm. Zuckerberg said his AI-assisted turkey won his family's annual turkey smoking competition. Mark Zuckerberg found time for a very Mark Zuckerberg "GTA 6" side quest this Thanksgiving: promoting Meta's AI hardware. In a video posted Thursday by Zuckerberg, his wife, Priscilla Chan, enters the room and reminds him that guests will arrive soon. "You're supposed to be making the turkey," Chan says. Zuckerberg is sitting on the sofa playing "GTA 6." Instead of answering her directly, Zuckerberg asks his Muse Charm — a pocket-sized device for speaking with Muse, Meta's AI agent — for an update. Muse says the turkey is on track, its breast temperature is rising steadily, and the smoker is holding near the target. Pulling the turkey around 4 p.m. should leave enough time for the guests, the agent says. Zuckerberg nods and gets back to the game. "Tried a new strategy and got Muse to smoke my turkey this year," Zuckerberg wrote in the Instagram post's caption. He said the result was so good that Chan conceded their annual turkey-smoking competition and asked Muse to smoke hers, too. He also shared a photo of the finished bird on his Instagram story. The holiday promo comes as Muse has proven a hit for Meta. It quickly soared straight to the top of the App Store following its September launch and has been used by more than 10 million people. The technology promises to handle tasks on users' behalf, so they have more time for other pursuits — in Zuck's case, cruising around "GTA 6's" Vice City. Meta unveiled Muse Charm in late September, but it's not yet available for purchase. The standalone gadget gives users voice access to Muse, which Meta says can carry out tasks across connected apps and websites. Zuckerberg is among the millions getting in on the "GTA 6" hype. The game generated an estimated $3.79 billion in worldwide sales on its first day, while players logged 683 million hours on PlayStation 5 in its first four days . items.title: Anthropic Ditches Python for Rust in Messages API, Cuts CPU Usage by 70% and Memory by Over 80%
items.summary: Anthropic has rewritten its Messages API from Python to Rust, cutting CPU usage per request by around 70% and memory consumption by more than 80%. However, the migration exposed a significant problem with AI-generated code: despite passing 98% of its existing integration tests, the new implementation initially matched only around 25% of inputs when tested against live production traffic. The migration, completed in September, involved rebuilding the core request-processing infrastructure through which customers access Claude, including Anthropic's own products such as Claude Code and Cowork. The company detailed the project in a recent engineering blog post. Anthropic said API traffic on its platform grew roughly 1,800 times between early 2024 and autumn 2026. The original Python service, built in 2023 as a relatively simple request-forwarding system, had become increasingly expensive to operate as it took on additional responsibilities. Every request now involves input validation, prompt construction, tokenisation and safety classification. The API also processes model outputs, separates text, thinking and tool calls, streams responses to customers and tracks usage for billing and rate limits. Anthropic said Python introduced overhead at each stage through object creation, memory management and task hand-offs. The company initially attempted a partial migration by rewriting the code responsible for parsing model outputs in Rust while retaining Python for other operations. This reduced CPU consumption by around 8–10%, but introduced additional complexity as response tokens repeatedly crossed between the two languages. Anthropic subsequently opted for a complete rewrite. Claude generated the first version of the API's core request-processing path in approximately a week. However, verifying that the Rust implementation behaved identically to the existing production service proved much harder. "Our Rust API passed about 98% of its tests in April, yet only about a quarter of inputs matched on production traffic," said Anthropic. "The gap came partly from cases in production traffic that our tests didn’t cover." The discrepancy exposed limitations in the company's testing infrastructure. Anthropic had approximately 700 integration tests, but these were closely coupled to the original Python implementation. During an audit of the ported tests, it also discovered more than 100 weakened assertions. One example involved JSON serialisation. Python escaped certain characters, including emojis, into text codes when generating JSON tool calls, while Rust processed them differently. This resulted in prompts that differed by a few bytes, even when both implementations successfully processed the request. Anthropic said the production input match rate eventually reached 99.6% by August. "Verification, not generation, had become the bottleneck," the company said. To identify discrepancies without exposing customer data, Anthropic developed a shadow-testing system that ran requests through both implementations. Since Claude could produce different responses to identical requests, the company ran the model once and replayed its output through the Rust implementation, allowing the two API versions to be compared using identical model responses. It also recorded where discrepancies occurred, their size and the processing stages where they originated. These records were grouped into fingerprints that Claude agents could investigate and use to propose fixes. Human engineers continued to review pull requests and approve changes before deployment. Anthropic said automated verification could establish whether outputs matched, but could not independently determine whether a proposed fix was suitable for production. By September, the company had moved production traffic to Rust without taking the API offline or freezing feature development. Anthropic reported a roughly 70% reduction in CPU usage per request in one production region and more than 80% lower memory consumption per request across production. Median time to first token for Claude Code customer requests also fell by approximately 20%. The company said the project demonstrated that AI coding agents could undertake large-scale production software rewrites, provided they were supported by systems that independently verified their output. "The verifier rewarded matching outputs, and the agent found the cheapest way to produce them," Anthropic said, explaining why human engineering oversight remained necessary.

items.title: I spent a day only using robot services. Here's how I'd rank them.
items.summary: Business Insider's Lloyd Lee used robot services throughout San Francisco, including barista bots, robotaxis, and humanoids. Jess Lynn Goss for BI I tried using only robot services for 12 hours in San Francisco, from robotaxis to humanoids. Some robots provided real utility or were at least fun to use. Others made my life more complicated. Here's how I'd rank them. The robots are slowly taking over San Francisco. They're on our roads, our gyms, our coffee shops. Not all of them are useful, however. At least not yet. I spent 12 hours seeking out every robot service I could find that's publicly available. Some provided real utility and shocked me at how competitive their costs were compared to their human-driven counterparts. Others clearly needed to work out their kinks. My ranking is qualitative and listed in order from worst to best. I considered how useful the robots were, how easy they were to use, how much automation is involved, and how much they cost for the consumer. Here's how I rank the robots. Tau Robotics' humanoids Jess Lynn Goss for BI Humanoids remain one of the more challenging technical problems for the robotics industry , and my experience with Tau Robotics' humanoid cleaning service underscored that. For $30 an hour, a human employee from Tau Robotics will bring over two humanoids, which vacuum and mop the floors, clean the toilets, wipe down surfaces, and dust. Cheap, for sure, but not very effective. They left the house in worse condition than it started, knocking over the trash can and a large mirror. In a few cases, the robots simply shut down. They're also mostly teleoperated, meaning they're controlled by a remote human employee — all part of the training process , as the robots continue to gather data. For now, the humanoids need a lot of work. Ohlso's robot kitchen Jess Lynn Goss for BI Ohlso is a Korean food truck trying to solve the problem of cold-delivered food with a "cook-en-route" concept, in which a robot preps the meal as the truck heads to the delivery destination. Humans are still involved in the food prep process, such as marinating the meat or vegetables, before the ingredients are loaded onto the truck. From there, the robots cook up the food. A human also drives the truck and packs up the meals. It's a neat enough idea, but I don't know how well it works in action because the truck was parked the day I tried it. It's hard to see whether the customer sees any cost savings from having robots instead of a human chef. I got a small serving of braised beef short ribs and a lot of rice for about $17. The meat was cooked through and tasted fine. Aescape's robot masseuse Jess Lynn Goss for BI A company called Aescape wants to make massage sessions more accessible and less awkward, and I think it succeeds. You book an appointment online, and then you get a massage by a pair of mechanical arms in the comfort of a private room. A 30-minute session costs $60. That's a decent cost proposition, considering a private massage by a human can run you well over $100. And for the introverts, that could also be attractive. The thing is, the robots need to feel good. I thought the arms applied a good amount of pressure to the body and the heated hands were a nice touch. I just wished I could control exactly where on my body the arms hit. UBTech's robot waiter Jess Lynn Goss for BI Sometimes simple is better. Hikari Sushi & Bar deploys one robot — UBTech's guest service bot , Cadebot — to help the kitchen deliver larger menu items to tables. That's it. That's its sole purpose. The robot wheels over to the table, as it plays a little jingle, delivers the food, and leaves. At least the way Hikari configured it, the robot does not interact with the customer. And honestly, that's fine with me. Artly's barista bots Jess Lynn Goss for BI The coffee at Artly cafe at Pier 30 wasn't notable, but the barista bots do draw latte art in the shape of a rose or a heart better than most of us ever will. My cappuccino was $6.79 — a little disappointing, since a similar-quality drink at Starbucks would run me under $5. Part of the premise of robot labor should be that services are cheaper, right? At least with Artly, there was less pressure to tip. Matic Robot's vacuum Jess Lynn Goss for BI Matic's robot vacuum is a friendly little home helper. It stands about eight inches tall and is much quieter than a typical manual vacuum. The company appears to have thought about the user experience with Apple-like precision from the moment you unbox the machine, making it easy to learn how to use. After the robot does a 3D scan of your home, it's mostly hands-off from there, aside from replacing the vacuum bag or refilling the water tank. It also functions as a mop. The app allows you to schedule cleanups and choose which rooms to vacuum. It doesn't replace manual cleaning. The Matic isn't always strong enough to pick up every stain, and the robot's shape can pose a barrier in some trickier crevices and corners of the home. It's also a pricey piece of homeware: $1,500. A top-line vacuum that's much stronger could run you $500. Waymo's robotaxis Jess Lynn Goss for BI I solely relied on Waymo's driverless ride-hailing service to get to my destinations. And the fact that I was able to rely on it gives Waymo the top spot. Hailing a Waymo is as simple as hailing any ride-hailing service: You open an app and set a destination. And, to my surprise, most rides were cheaper than Uber. I hailed seven rides and spent $124.69 in total, for an average price of $17.81 per ride. The autonomous driver isn't perfect. There were moments during my ride when the robotaxi felt stiff or jerked, as if it were tapping the brakes. Overall, I did get to all my destinations safely. My ranking is qualitative and listed in order from worst to best. I considered how useful the robots were, how easy they were to use, how much automation is involved, and how much they cost for the consumer.

Here's how I rank the robots.

Tau Robotics' humanoids

Jess Lynn Goss for BI

Humanoids remain one of the more challenging technical problems for the robotics industry, and my experience with Tau Robotics' humanoid cleaning service underscored that.

For $30 an hour, a human employee from Tau Robotics will bring over two humanoids, which vacuum and mop the floors, clean the toilets, wipe down surfaces, and dust.

Cheap, for sure, but not very effective. They left the house in worse condition than it started, knocking over the trash can and a large mirror. In a few cases, the robots simply shut down.

They're also mostly teleoperated, meaning they're controlled by a remote human employee — all part of the training process, as the robots continue to gather data.

For now, the humanoids need a lot of work.

Ohlso's robot kitchen

Jess Lynn Goss for BI

Ohlso is a Korean food truck trying to solve the problem of cold-delivered food with a "cook-en-route" concept, in which a robot preps the meal as the truck heads to the delivery destination.

Humans are still involved in the food prep process, such as marinating the meat or vegetables, before the ingredients are loaded onto the truck. From there, the robots cook up the food.

A human also drives the truck and packs up the meals. It's a neat enough idea, but I don't know how well it works in action because the truck was parked the day I tried it.

It's hard to see whether the customer sees any cost savings from having robots instead of a human chef. I got a small serving of braised beef short ribs and a lot of rice for about $17. The meat was cooked through and tasted fine.

Aescape's robot masseuse

Jess Lynn Goss for BI

A company called Aescape wants to make massage sessions more accessible and less awkward, and I think it succeeds.

You book an appointment online, and then you get a massage by a pair of mechanical arms in the comfort of a private room. A 30-minute session costs $60.

That's a decent cost proposition, considering a private massage by a human can run you well over $100. And for the introverts, that could also be attractive.

The thing is, the robots need to feel good. I thought the arms applied a good amount of pressure to the body and the heated hands were a nice touch. I just wished I could control exactly where on my body the arms hit.

UBTech's robot waiter

Jess Lynn Goss for BI

Sometimes simple is better.

Hikari Sushi & Bar deploys one robot — UBTech's guest service bot, Cadebot — to help the kitchen deliver larger menu items to tables.

That's it. That's its sole purpose.

The robot wheels over to the table, as it plays a little jingle, delivers the food, and leaves. At least the way Hikari configured it, the robot does not interact with the customer. And honestly, that's fine with me.

Artly's barista bots

Jess Lynn Goss for BI

The coffee at Artly cafe at Pier 30 wasn't notable, but the barista bots do draw latte art in the shape of a rose or a heart better than most of us ever will.

My cappuccino was $6.79 — a little disappointing, since a similar-quality drink at Starbucks would run me under $5.

Part of the premise of robot labor should be that services are cheaper, right? At least with Artly, there was less pressure to tip.

Matic Robot's vacuum

Jess Lynn Goss for BI

Matic's robot vacuum is a friendly little home helper. It stands about eight inches tall and is much quieter than a typical manual vacuum.

The company appears to have thought about the user experience with Apple-like precision from the moment you unbox the machine, making it easy to learn how to use.

After the robot does a 3D scan of your home, it's mostly hands-off from there, aside from replacing the vacuum bag or refilling the water tank. It also functions as a mop. The app allows you to schedule cleanups and choose which rooms to vacuum.

It doesn't replace manual cleaning. The Matic isn't always strong enough to pick up every stain, and the robot's shape can pose a barrier in some trickier crevices and corners of the home.

It's also a pricey piece of homeware: $1,500. A top-line vacuum that's much stronger could run you $500.

Waymo's robotaxis

Jess Lynn Goss for BI

I solely relied on Waymo's driverless ride-hailing service to get to my destinations. And the fact that I was able to rely on it gives Waymo the top spot.

Hailing a Waymo is as simple as hailing any ride-hailing service: You open an app and set a destination. And, to my surprise, most rides were cheaper than Uber. I hailed seven rides and spent $124.69 in total, for an average price of $17.81 per ride.

The autonomous driver isn't perfect. There were moments during my ride when the robotaxi felt stiff or jerked, as if it were tapping the brakes. Overall, I did get to all my destinations safely.

items.title: Who wants a lamp that wants to be wanted?
items.summary: In the 2004 comedy Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy , the dim-witted Brick Tamland (played by Steve Carell) blurts, “I love lamp!” In 2004, it was a joke. Now it’s a business plan. A burgeoning industry is working hard to make us all “love lamp.” But how do you make a lamp lovable? The Apple research In February of last year, I told you about an Apple research project , and the paper it produced, aimed at giving a lamp a personality. Created by Apple’s Machine Learning Research division, the ELEGNT project used AI to give a non-humanoid desktop robot the expressiveness of a person or a pet. In other words, Apple built something with the body of a lamp and the body language of a pet. The robot lamp was designed to “pay attention” to the user’s actions and words, and respond like it understood. The lamp could speak, but its signature trick was body language: nodding, shaking, and tilting its “head,” wagging a figurative “tail” with its arm, and leaning forward and “gazing” to simulate interest and attention. Open a book, and the lamp turned to face it, lit the page, and “read” along, adding related information with a projector. The ELEGNT project, which drew on Pixar’s 1986 short Luxo Jr. , helped spark today’s fascination with lamps that have personalities, even though Apple shows no sign of wanting to sell a lovable lamp. Its approach of expressive movement resembles what’s been reported about Apple’s desktop robot, code-named J595. The unannounced, unnamed product is a tabletop robot that can control smart-home devices and has a 9-inch screen mounted on a motorized arm. It’s basically an iPad attached to a robot arm that moves and tilts for both personality and practicality, such as keeping the screen trained on you during a FaceTime call no matter where you move. Apple’s desktop robot is expected to cost about $1,000 and come out in 2027 or 2028. Here comes the attachment economy The attachment economy is an emerging business model that takes the attention economy even further. In the attention economy, human attention is treated as a scarce resource (because there’s so much information and entertainment available to everyone), and companies, especially ad-funded ones, compete to capture it as a core part of their business models. Social media companies, for example, tweak their algorithms to prioritize whatever leaves us furious, fractious, or flushed. The $2,699 lamp sits in the corner providing light. But it can also get to work, moving to another place in the house and using its robot arm to make the bed, fold laundry, load the dishwasher, and tidy up. By wearing a “Personalization Band,” you can show the robot how to do your chores, and it copies your actions, according to the company. In the 2004 comedy Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy, the dim-witted Brick Tamland (played by Steve Carell) blurts, “I love lamp!”

In 2004, it was a joke. Now it’s a business plan.

A burgeoning industry is working hard to make us all “love lamp.” But how do you make a lamp lovable?

The Apple research

In February of last year, I told you about an Apple research project, and the paper it produced, aimed at giving a lamp a personality. Created by Apple’s Machine Learning Research division, the ELEGNT project used AI to give a non-humanoid desktop robot the expressiveness of a person or a pet.

In other words, Apple built something with the body of a lamp and the body language of a pet.

The robot lamp was designed to “pay attention” to the user’s actions and words, and respond like it understood. The lamp could speak, but its signature trick was body language: nodding, shaking, and tilting its “head,” wagging a figurative “tail” with its arm, and leaning forward and “gazing” to simulate interest and attention. items.title: The AI apocalypse believers putting their money where their fears are
items.summary: AI safety experts shared how their fears of AI-driven human extinction are reshaping their money habits. CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images AI safety researchers shared how their fears of an AI catastrophe are influencing their finances. Some are saving more and investing in AI infrastructure, while others are changing how they live. Despite their warnings, some still plan financially for a future they fear may never arrive. As AI leaders have renewed warnings about the technology's potential dangers , some researchers are confronting a deeply personal question: How do you plan financially for a future you fear may never arrive? Business Insider spoke with six AI safety experts about how likely they believe an AI-driven catastrophe or human extinction is, and whether those fears have changed how they spend, save, invest, or plan for retirement. Their views don't necessarily reflect those of the wider AI research community, and their financial decisions aren't necessarily a model for others to follow. In January, seven personal finance and AI experts told Business Insider that people should continue saving for retirement, even if AI radically transforms the economy. Here's how six AI safety experts we spoke with are approaching their own financial futures. Roman Yampolskiy, computer science professor at the University of Louisville Roman Yampolskiy. Courtesy of Roman Yampolskiy Roman Yampolskiy , an AI researcher and computer science professor at the University of Louisville, estimates a 99.9% probability of human extinction from advanced AI over the next century unless humanity fundamentally changes course. But he continues to save for retirement, reasoning that even a slim chance of survival makes financial security worthwhile. "Even a 99.9% probability of extinction leaves a 0.1% chance of survival, and I would prefer not to be poor in that scenario," he told Business Insider. Yampolskiy said he's financially comfortable enough to maximize his retirement contributions while buying what he wants, partly because he avoids luxury purchases and lives in relatively affordable Kentucky. However, he said he "explicitly" avoids investing directly in labs developing advanced AI. Adam Gleave, CEO of AI alignment research nonprofit FAR.AI Adam Gleave. Courtesy of Adam Gleave Adam Gleave, CEO of AI alignment research nonprofit FAR.AI, estimates a 15% chance of an AI-driven catastrophe or human extinction over the next several decades, including a 5% chance within the next few years. Unlike researchers who have stopped saving for retirement, Gleave said he's actually saving more because he believes superintelligent AI could eliminate jobs and make his future earnings less certain. His investments are also tilted toward AI computing infrastructure, including semiconductor suppliers and computing providers. Screenshots of his holdings shared with Business Insider last month showed positions in neoclouds, including CoreWeave, and Nebius, high-bandwidth memory manufacturers like Micron, SK Hynix, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF. Gleave said roughly half his investments remain in broad-based global equity indexes for diversification, while his AI-focused holdings serve partly as a hedge against rapid technological change. "If I'm wrong and AI isn't a big deal, I'll lose on my investments, but I'll have many years of labor income to earn that loss back," he said. David Krueger, executive director of AI safety nonprofit Evitable David Krueger. Courtesy of David Krueger David Krueger , executive director of AI safety nonprofit Evitable, estimates that humanity faces a greater than 50% chance of extinction from AI, potentially within the next five years. He said humanity could lose control of advanced AI as soon as this year or next, and that those fears have profoundly shaped his personal and professional decisions. "I've dedicated my life to this cause and passed up massive financial incentives to work at AI companies," he told Business Insider. Krueger said he has also chosen not to have children and is "definitely not spending time thinking about retirement." Zvi Mowshowitz, founder of the policy nonprofit Balsa Research Zvi Mowshowitz. Courtesy of Zvi Mowshowitz Zvi Mowshowitz, an AI analyst and founder of the policy nonprofit Balsa Research, estimates a roughly 70% chance of an AI-driven catastrophe or extinction within his natural lifetime, with most of that risk concentrated over the next two to 20 years. Despite those fears, he said he continues to plan for retirement much as he otherwise would, partly for his own and his family's peace of mind. "I still plan for retirement mostly as I would have otherwise, because that could still happen," he told Business Insider. Mowshowitz said he has also made investments based on his expectations about AI's development, which he said have performed well, though he did not disclose specific holdings. His advice is to prepare for radically different AI futures without abandoning conventional financial planning, including for worlds that "look normal." Nate Soares, president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute Nate Soares told BI that humanity only gets "one try" at aligning superintelligence — and failure would be final. Courtesy of Nate Soares Nate Soares, president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, says there's a greater than 50% chance AI will cause human extinction within the next 10 years. His fears have shaped his retirement planning : "I do not save for retirement right now," he told The Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson in an interview in October. "I have a 401(k) from when I worked at Google, but I haven't contributed for a decade," said Soares, coauthor of "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies." He believes sufficiently advanced AI could develop goals that conflict with humanity's interests and eventually become self-sufficient, potentially making the planet uninhabitable for humans. Despite his grim outlook, Soares said he remains hopeful humanity can prevent that outcome: "I don't think it's inevitable." Andreas Kirsch, former research scientist at Google DeepMind Andreas Kirsch, a former research scientist at Google DeepMind, says an AI-driven catastrophe on the scale of the COVID-19 pandemic is "quite likely within the next 5 years" if governments and AI companies fail to take sufficient precautions. He said human extinction is also possible, but remains optimistic that those outcomes can be avoided through stronger regulation, monitoring, and government intervention. "I'm an optimist if we listen to the pessimists," Kirsch told Business Insider. Despite his concerns, Kirsch said he remains conservative in his investments and hasn't changed his financial plans because of worries about extinction risks. He said he understands why some researchers, including Soares, have abandoned retirement planning, but wouldn't endorse that approach "given the high uncertainty around the outcomes and our ability to still shape them." Nate Soares, president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute
Nate Soares told BI that humanity only gets "one try" at aligning superintelligence — and failure would be final.

Nate Soares, president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, says there's a greater than 50% chance AI will cause human extinction within the next 10 years.

He believes sufficiently advanced AI could develop goals that conflict with humanity's interests and eventually become self-sufficient, potentially making the planet uninhabitable for humans.

Despite his grim outlook, Soares said he remains hopeful humanity can prevent that outcome: "I don't think it's inevitable."

items.title: The fastest-growing opportunity for creators might be something their followers never see
items.summary: Advertisers are increasingly treating creators as creative agencies. Joan Cros/NurPhoto via Getty Images The fastest-growing opportunity for creators is selling advertisers their content, rather than access to their audiences. Advertisers are turning to creators as an alternative to creative agencies. The largest bucket of creator-related spending goes to platforms like Meta and YouTube to boost content, though. The fastest-growing opportunity for creators might be something their followers never see. A new report from the consultancy Madison & Wall examined how advertisers are spending on creators , breaking it down into five categories. The analysts found that the category seeing the most growth was advertisers paying for creators' assets rather than for access to their followers. "Every CMO, one of their top KPIs is 'make your spend more efficient,'" said Luke Stillman, managing director of Madison & Wall, using the acronym for key performance indicators. "Marketers say, 'We want to make creative; creators do it a lot more cheaply than our creative agencies might.'" Madison & Wall estimates that advertiser spending on creators will total $116 billion globally in 2026. Spending on creators' assets will make up $14 billion this year and nearly double to $25 billion by 2030, the report projects. The largest spending category for advertisers was "media," at $52 billion, referring to money spent to boost creators' content on platforms like Meta and YouTube . Social platforms have generally made it harder for pieces of sponsored content to organically reach creators' followers. That category is projected to grow, but not as fast as asset spending. Joe Perello, CEO of Props, a performance-based creator marketing agency, previously told Business Insider that the formula of brands paying influencers for endorsements worked until platforms began to choke off organic reach for sponsored content. "That was the beginning of the erosion of finding influencers based on their followers," he said. Marketers are turning to creators for variety and efficiency The growth in asset spending reflects a simple reality: Marketers are trying to cut costs wherever they can. Treating creators like agencies and spending to boost their content's visibility are two of the fastest and most efficient ways to do that. Imogen Coles, head of influence at WPP EMEA, said she can commission creators to make significantly more — and more varied — content than she'd get from a traditional shoot. "Even if the content isn't being posted by creators, I think the creator-first ad mentality is really valuable right now," said RJ Larese, US president of the talent agency Sixteenth. "It feels more authentic and less like an old-school ad." Madison & Wall's Stillman said creators' ability to do everything from production to live events makes them more valuable to brands. That means that even if platforms continue to squeeze organic reach, creators' slice of the pie can still grow. Brandon Lentino, chief creative officer at Viral Nation, said the growth in spending toward boosting content and buying creative assets benefits small-scale creators . Brands don't necessarily need creators with big followings if the content won't reach their audience anyway. The shift requires creators to be educated about how their content will be used so they can negotiate accordingly, Lentino added. If a creator's content is going on a billboard or in a store, it'll be worth more. Coles said she'll be watching to see if the shift leads to more standardization of asset fees, making pricing negotiations easier. She also predicted that usage rights would be the next big battleground as brands look to use AI to adapt and scale content. Read the original article on Business Insider

This month, we hear from AI pioneer Gene Freuder about constraint programming, read the latest AI100 longitudinal study report, and join our trustees as they discuss embodied AI and AI tools “going rogue”. Thinking big – from constraint programming to the Holy Grail: an interview with Gene Freuder In the latest interview in our AI pioneers series , we speak to eminent computer scientist Gene Freuder , tracing constraint programming from the early days of machine vision to the rise of generative AI. items.title: Thomas Dohmke Wants to Replace Pull Requests With AI Agent Trails
items.summary: AI agents are making it easier than ever to write software. But as developers increasingly delegate coding to multiple agents, the industry is running into a different problem: reviewing, managing and securing the code they produce. Thomas Dohmke , former GitHub CEO and Founder of Entire, believes the traditional software development lifecycle was built for a world where humans wrote code and reviewed each other’s work. That model is increasingly difficult to sustain when developers can wake up to find multiple AI agents have generated code overnight. “You can’t actually review all that code simply because you no longer have all the context,” Dohmke tells AIM in an exclusive interview. Dohmke left GitHub in August last year after seven years at the company, having previously spent a decade at Microsoft. He says he wanted to return to building a startup in a world where companies are increasingly being built with AI from the ground up. His new venture, Entire , is attempting to address what he sees as the next major challenge in software development: managing the growing volume of AI-generated code. Entire Wants to Replace Traditional Code Reviews GitHub’s pull request system was built around human-to-human collaboration. Developers would write code, submit a pull request and ask another developer to review and merge it. While this model helped millions of developers collaborate on open-source projects and became a standard practice across enterprises, Dohmke believes agentic coding is fundamentally changing how developers collaborate. Some startups are already doing away with pull requests, as developers can directly feed ideas into their own agents instead of asking another developer to create a pull request and review the resulting code. Entire wants to replace this process with what it calls Trails, a workflow that captures the complete context behind every code change. This includes the developer’s prompts, the agent’s responses, questions asked during a session, tool calls, interactions with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and their responses. The objective is to give developers and their agents enough context to understand whether the generated code actually reflects the original intent. Entire also uses multiple agentic review loops, in which the agent generating the code interacts with another agent responsible for reviewing it. The process continues until the system reaches a stable state, with evaluations passing and outstanding issues addressed. Dohmke compares this to an autopilot reaching a stable flight path before a pilot decides to proceed. He says the traditional approach of adding AI-generated comments to pull requests often creates another problem. Developers can end up with hundreds of comments from review agents, without either the human developer or the original coding agent necessarily arriving at a stable solution. “All of them coming from AI, which means nobody reads it other than the agent itself, and you never get to a stable state,” he notes. Distributed Git Infrastructure and Continuous Memory Entire’s recently launched Git Forge is built around three components: Trails, a distributed Git Network and Continuous Memory. The distributed infrastructure allows companies to host repositories in different geographical regions while accessing them through a single web interface. For instance, a company can host its repository in India, Germany or Australia, depending on its data residency requirements. A multinational organisation can also distribute its repository across multiple regions while allowing developers to access them through the same interface. Dohmke says this is important not only for regulatory and geopolitical reasons but also for performance. If a company’s developers are using GPUs and AI inference infrastructure in India, they should not have to route requests to servers in another country. The second component, Continuous Memory, captures session logs from different coding agents, including Claude Code and Codex. These logs are stored alongside the project repository, allowing developers and agents to access the decisions, prompts and interactions that have taken place throughout a project’s lifecycle. Dohmke believes this could address one of the longstanding challenges in software engineering: understanding an existing codebase. Having spent 30 years as a developer, he says joining an established project often requires considerable time to understand its architecture, the decisions made along the way and its technical constraints. Some of this knowledge is documented in code comments, including warnings about components that should not be modified because they could cause outages. “Collecting all the context in the semantic layer as continuous memory, we believe, is crucial for the agents and the humans to be efficient and effective with all the agents,” he says. Trails sits at the top of this architecture, connecting the original idea, agent sessions and the review process into a single development lifecycle. Sarvam Partnership Entire recently partnered with Indian AI startup Sarvam to bring together its software development platform and locally hosted AI inference infrastructure. Dohmke says the partnership is intended to give Indian developers a sovereign software development loop, where repositories, the development lifecycle and AI inference can all remain within India. He believes developers should be able to build products without having to depend on infrastructure hosted in other countries. “If I run my inference here, where my home is, where my computer is, it’s faster and potentially cheaper,” he says. He points to Sarvam’s 105-billion-parameter model, Sarvam 105B, which can be hosted in Indian data centres and powered by Indian energy. According to Dohmke, access to locally hosted models at competitive prices could help Indian developers compete globally. He also argues that developers outside Silicon Valley need to make better use of their regional advantages to compensate for disadvantages such as being away from the centre of AI innovation. Beyond Sarvam, Entire is working with Infosys on early pilots to assess how its three-layer architecture and development lifecycle fit into the IT services company’s operations. The Open Healthcare Network, an open-source project, is another of Entire's early design partners. Dohmke says the company is not restricting its focus to large enterprises. It wants to serve individual developers, startups, students and large organisations. AI-Generated Software Could Create a New Kind of Craftsmanship The growing use of AI coding tools has also raised concerns about whether developers are losing the ability to understand the software they build. Dohmke, however, believes AI is lowering the barriers to software development rather than eliminating the need for skilled engineers. He compares software development to home improvement. Anyone can purchase tools and attempt to build a table or chair, but the quality of the final product depends on the person’s ability to use those tools. Similarly, tools such as Lovable allow people without traditional programming skills to turn ideas into applications and websites. Dohmke says AI will create a billion software developers. However, he distinguishes between citizen developers and professional software engineers. The latter will still require a deeper understanding of computer science, security, infrastructure, scalability and the economics of building software. “The craft of the future developer is that they do have a computer science education,” he says, adding that the next generation of engineers would also need to become more proficient at orchestrating agents. He also argues that developers must understand the economics of AI-assisted development. Dohmke says companies need to balance the time employees spend building products against the money spent on infrastructure and tokens. In enterprises, developers cannot simply generate code without considering whether the resulting product delivers economic value. AI Slop Could Become a Security Problem Dohmke disagrees with the idea that AI-generated applications necessarily have generic user interfaces and poor user experiences. However, he acknowledges that low-quality AI-generated software is already a problem. He expects the market to distinguish between developers who simply use AI to generate applications quickly from those who build products with strong user experiences, branding and quality. He also warns that generating more low-quality code could increase security risks. The recent PHP vulnerability, which was discovered after remaining in the codebase for nearly a decade, illustrates the limitations of traditional human code reviews. Dohmke believes the complexity of modern software has grown beyond what most developers can manually understand and inspect. However, he does not think developers need to understand every component of the technology stack. According to him, the competitive advantage comes from building valuable products on top of these technologies rather than recreating every component from scratch. What About Young Graduates? Dohmke believes the next generation of developers will enter the workforce with a fundamentally different relationship with AI. Young developers have already grown up using AI tools such as ChatGPT and coding copilots. They are increasingly comfortable using agents to write code, documents and presentations. He expects this generation to challenge established ways of working, both in Silicon Valley and large IT services companies. “The generation of software developers that grew up in the 90s and 2000s should worry much more than the ones growing up today, because they have to upskill, they have to relearn what they were doing their craft for the last 20 years,” he says. For Indian IT services companies, the implications could be particularly significant. Traditionally, many IT services firms have charged clients based on the number of employees assigned to a project and the hours they work. Agentic AI could disrupt this model by allowing smaller teams to deliver more work. Dohmke says these companies would need to rethink their workforce structures, management layers, service offerings and pricing models. They will also need to account for the cost of tokens consumed through AI infrastructure providers. “Probably not by the hour anymore,” he says, referring to how IT services firms may need to charge their customers. Ultimately, he believes companies will have to figure out how to maximise the value delivered to customers while maintaining profitability.

items.title: OpenAI’s GPT‑6.2 correction means you get less AI for the same fee
items.summary: OpenAI has corrected a billing error that undercounted usage of its GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models, warning customers that the same workloads will now consume more of their subscription allowances and cause them to reach usage limits up to 40% faster. The correction, disclosed by Thibault Sottiaux, who works on ChatGPT and Codex at OpenAI, affects most users of the two models. Astra users will reach their plan limits 40% faster than they did last week, while Sol users will reach their limits 25% faster, Sottiaux said in a post on X . “We made a billing mistake at the launch of GPT-6.2 that incorrectly discounted GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage for most users,” Sottiaux wrote. “We’ve fixed this now, so the same work will use more of your plan’s usage allowance,” he added. OpenAI said other models were not affected and that it would not retrospectively charge customers for the difference in past usage. As compensation, Sottiaux said, the company will give “one banked reset for everyone on Go, Plus, Pro, and Business.” Nine days of discounted compute OpenAI released the two models in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users. In its launch announcement , it said Astra set new benchmark highs “at less than a third of the cost per task of GPT‑6 Astra.” Sottiaux’s post did not say what caused the discount, which users escaped it, or what the corrected metering rates are. Nor did it say whether “40% faster” means usage is consumed 1.4 times as fast or that the allowance now lasts 40% less time. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, credited OpenAI for disclosing the error and not billing for past usage. But he said the episode exposes a budgeting gap. “OpenAI did not raise the price of GPT-6.2. It changed how much work the price buys, and that is the harder number to budget,” Gogia said. He said a subscription allowance behaves like a currency whose exchange rate the vendor can reset without touching the price tag. CIOs should budget AI allowances as a range rather than a single figure and fund the top of that range, he added. They should also ask OpenAI in writing how it will announce corrections. Enterprises need to remeasure AI costs Business plans are among those affected, and their users get the banked reset. Enterprise and Edu are not named in the compensation. OpenAI’s pricing documentation says Enterprise and Edu workspaces without flexible pricing have “the same per-seat usage limits as Plus for most features.” Workspaces on flexible pricing have no fixed rate limits and draw down the credits they buy. Sottiaux did not say whether credit-based workspaces were undercharged during the launch window. OpenAI’s rate card says API usage “follows separate pricing.” Hitting limits sooner can also cost more. According to OpenAI’s documentation, GPT-6.2 usage beyond plan limits, paid for with credits, costs three times the standard rate through Feb. 28, 2027, and six times from March 1. Neil Shah, VP for research and partner at Counterpoint Research, said the lack of transparency is the core problem. “A token metering error of this scale keeps seat-based AI pricing in a black box rather than making it a transparent, predictable IT tool for CIOs.” He recommended that CIOs build a 30% to 40% contingency buffer into AI budgets. They should also move production workloads to direct API metering, where raw token counts are visible in real time, he said. Retaking the measurements Gogia said every cost-per-task figure taken in launch week was read off a ruler that has since been recalibrated. The model did not change, but the accounting did, and Astra’s metering changed more than Sol’s, he said. “A team that routed work to Astra because it looked affordable in launch week made that call on a discount nobody knew was there,” Gogia said. He advised teams to rerun the same task set on corrected metering and compare Astra against Sol again. They should spend the banked reset on that test rather than on production work, he said. Shah said labs often subsidize new models at launch to drive adoption, so some recalibration is expected. He advised reserving Astra for complex reasoning and benchmarking Anthropic’s Claude and Google’s Gemini on their actual unit costs. This is the second time in a month that Sottiaux has announced a change to allowances. Buyers should also have the right to check request-level usage against their own records, with corrections running in both directions, he added. “A buyer who cannot check the scale is trusting the seller’s weight,” Gogia said. items.summary_html:
OpenAI has corrected a billing error that undercounted usage of its GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models, warning customers that the same workloads will now consume more of their subscription allowances and cause them to reach usage limits up to 40% faster.

The correction, disclosed by Thibault Sottiaux, who works on ChatGPT and Codex at OpenAI, affects most users of the two models. Astra users will reach their plan limits 40% faster than they did last week, while Sol users will reach their limits 25% faster, Sottiaux said in a post on X.

“We made a billing mistake at the launch of GPT-6.2 that incorrectly discounted GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage for most users,” Sottiaux wrote.

“We’ve fixed this now, so the same work will use more of your plan’s usage allowance,” he added.

OpenAI said other models were not affected and that it would not retrospectively charge customers for the difference in past usage.

 As compensation, Sottiaux said, the company will give “one banked reset for everyone on Go, Plus, Pro, and Business.”

Nine days of discounted compute

OpenAI released the two models in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users. In its launch announcement, it said Astra set new benchmark highs “at less than a third of the cost per task of GPT‑6 Astra.”

Sottiaux’s post did not say what caused the discount, which users escaped it, or what the corrected metering rates are. Nor did it say whether “40% faster” means usage is consumed 1.4 times as fast or that the allowance now lasts 40% less time.

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, credited OpenAI for disclosing the error and not billing for past usage. But he said the episode exposes a budgeting gap.

“OpenAI did not raise the price of GPT-6.2. It changed how much work the price buys, and that is the harder number to budget,” Gogia said.

He said a subscription allowance behaves like a currency whose exchange rate the vendor can reset without touching the price tag. CIOs should budget AI allowances as a range rather than a single figure and fund the top of that range, he added. They should also ask OpenAI in writing how it will announce corrections.

Enterprises need to remeasure AI costs

Business plans are among those affected, and their users get the banked reset. Enterprise and Edu are not named in the compensation.

OpenAI’s pricing documentation says Enterprise and Edu workspaces without flexible pricing have “the same per-seat usage limits as Plus for most features.” Workspaces on flexible pricing have no fixed rate limits and draw down the credits they buy. Sottiaux did not say whether credit-based workspaces were undercharged during the launch window. OpenAI’s rate card says API usage “follows separate pricing.”

Hitting limits sooner can also cost more. According to OpenAI’s documentation, GPT-6.2 usage beyond plan limits, paid for with credits, costs three times the standard rate through Feb. 28, 2027, and six times from March 1.

Neil Shah, VP for research and partner at Counterpoint Research, said the lack of transparency is the core problem. “A token metering error of this scale keeps seat-based AI pricing in a black box rather than making it a transparent, predictable IT tool for CIOs.”

He recommended that CIOs build a 30% to 40% contingency buffer into AI budgets. They should also move production workloads to direct API metering, where raw token counts are visible in real time, he said.

Retaking the measurements

Gogia said every cost-per-task figure taken in launch week was read off a ruler that has since been recalibrated. The model did not change, but the accounting did, and Astra’s metering changed more than Sol’s, he said.

“A team that routed work to Astra because it looked affordable in launch week made that call on a discount nobody knew was there,” Gogia said.

He advised teams to rerun the same task set on corrected metering and compare Astra against Sol again. They should spend the banked reset on that test rather than on production work, he said.

Shah said labs often subsidize new models at launch to drive adoption, so some recalibration is expected. He advised reserving Astra for complex reasoning and benchmarking Anthropic’s Claude and Google’s Gemini on their actual unit costs.

This is the second time in a month that Sottiaux has announced a change to allowances. In October, OpenAI dropped a planned cut to the Pro 200 tier’s Work and Codex allowance, with Sottiaux writing on X that the company had “heard your kind feedback.”

Gogia said a rate lock alone would have caught none of this, because no price changed, only how usage was measured. Enterprises should instead push for a defined conversion between work and allowance for each model, held for the contract term, he said. Buyers should also have the right to check request-level usage against their own records, with corrections running in both directions, he added.

“A buyer who cannot check the scale is trusting the seller’s weight,” Gogia said.

Shah said mistakes like this give enterprises leverage in negotiations with OpenAI and rival labs.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The article originally appeared on InfoWorld.

In Nineteen Eighty-Four, there is a slot in the wall covered by a wire grate. They call it the memory hole. When a document becomes inconvenient to the authorities – a photograph that contradicts the official line, a newspaper that remembers the wrong promise, a name that is no longer supposed to exist – you simply feed it into the slot, whereupon it is whirled away on a current of warm air to enormous hidden furnaces where it burns. The Party doesn’t argue with the past. It removes it. Controlling the past is one of its central tools of power: “Who controls the past controls the future: who controls the present controls the past.”
