items.title: What Is an LLM Eval Pipeline? Why You Need One and How to Build It on Your Laptop
items.summary:
A checklist of tests where most pass and one fails (image generated by AI) An eval pipeline is a set of test questions, a script that sends them to an AI model, and a way to score the answers. It works like unit tests for code, but for an AI feature. You can build a small one on your own laptop with Ollama and llama.cpp, and this story shows how. The whole pipeline. The runner talks to any server that speaks the OpenAI chat format. What an eval pipeline is Anthropic describes an eval as a test for an AI system, where you give it an input and check its output. A pipeline has four parts. Test cases are questions or tasks, each with a note on what a good answer looks like. A runner is a script that sends every case to the model and saves the answers. Graders score each answer. Simple code checks come first. Does the answer match exactly, contain the right number, or parse as valid JSON? If code can’t decide, a second AI model can act as the judge. A report shows the overall score and how it compares with the last run. A benchmark such as GSM8K is a public test set that everyone uses. A pipeline points the same idea at your own task, and you run it every time something changes. Why you need one Without tests, you hear about problems from your users . Anthropic describes the usual pattern. People say the AI feels worse after a change, and the team can only guess and check. Fixing one bug can break something else. A public benchmark does not tell you how your task will go . Hamel Husain, who writes about building AI products, says tests built around your users’ tasks measure something different from general benchmarks. Setup matters too. On the ARC Prize leaderboard, GPT-6.2 Astra scored 70.3% with a basic setup and 99.8% with a tuned one, at the same reasoning level. A new model is a change too . In Husain’s case study of a real estate assistant, progress stalled because fixing one problem created others, so the team built a proper way to test it. Anthropic says that when a new model comes out, an eval suite shows quickly what got better. You need to know whether a score is real . Anthropic found that CPU and memory limits on the test machine alone moved scores on a coding benchmark, Terminal-Bench 2.0, by about 6 points. A score without a margin of error can’t tell you if a gain is real. How to use it Collect 20 to 50 real cases. Use things that went wrong, such as your bug tracker, support messages and the checks you already do by hand. Anthropic says a small set is enough at the start, because early changes tend to have big effects. Decide how each case is scored. A good case is one where two experts would agree on pass or fail. Use a code check where you can. Run it once and save the result. That is your baseline. Change one thing. It can be the model, the prompt, a setting or the size of the model file. Run it again and compare. Look at the margin of error before you believe a difference. Keep the cases. Add a new case for every new failure, and run the set after every change. Where this helps in practice These situations are made up, but most people who build with AI run into one of them. You fix one prompt problem and break another . Say a support bot sorts messages into bug, billing and feature request. Someone edits the prompt so billing questions are handled better, and bug reports start landing in the wrong group. Nobody notices until customers complain. With a saved set of cases, the next run shows which ones flipped. A new model comes out and the headlines say it is better. Better at what? Run your own cases on the old and the new model and compare them case by case. A leaderboard can’t tell you how a model does on your messages. You want a cheaper or smaller model , maybe one that runs on your laptop so your data stays with you. Run the same cases on both. The Q4 and Q8 comparison further down is an example of this check. The demo worked, and then real users broke it . They phrase things in ways you never tried. Each time it happens, add that message as a new case, so the same failure can’t come back unnoticed. Build it on your laptop Running tests locally costs only electricity, keeps your data on your machine and lets you test something that hosted APIs hide, such as which compressed version of a model you use. Quantization shrinks a model by storing its numbers with fewer bits. A Q4 file is smaller than a Q8 file and can be a little less accurate. Ollama and llama.cpp are two popular programs that run models on your computer. Both can answer in the same format as the OpenAI API, so one script can test either. Step 1. Start the servers These commands are for a Mac with Homebrew. On Linux and Windows, install both from their websites. brew install ollama llama.cpp ollama serve # leave it running, port 11434 ollama pull qwen3.5:4b # Q4_K_M, 3.3 GB ollama pull qwen3.5:4b-q8_0 # the same model at Q8_0, 5.2 GB llama.cpp is optional. Its server, llama-server, can download a model file from Hugging Face with -hf (the default size is Q4_K_M), and --alias sets the model name you use in requests: llama-server -hf unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF:Q4_K_M --alias qwen3.5-4b-q4 --port 8080 On a 16 GB laptop, stay at 9B parameters or smaller. Ollama lists qwen3.5:9b at about 7 GB and gpt-oss:20b at 14 GB, which leaves little room for everything else. Step 2. Write the test cases Each case is one line of JSON, a plain text format for data. It has four parts. prompt is what the model sees, check is how to score the answer, expect is a correct answer and tag is a group name for the report. Two lines from the demo set, with the prompts shortened: {"id": "label-04", "tag": "label", "prompt": "Classify the customer message ... Message: The app crashes every time I open the settings page.", "check": "exact", "expect": "bug"} {"id": "json-01", "tag": "json", "prompt": "Extract the person, city and year ... Sentence: Grace Hopper joined the Navy Reserve in New York in 1943.", "check": "json", "expect": {"name": "Grace Hopper", "city": "New York", "year": 1943}} The check depends on the task. Four examples: Sorting support messages into groups. The expected answer is one word, such as bug, so the exact check works. It wants a word for word match. Pulling facts out of text, such as a name, a city and a year. The expected answer is a small JSON object, so the json check parses the reply and compares the fields. A math or counting question. The answer is a number, so a regex check (a text pattern) looks for it in the reply. Writing a summary or setting a tone. There is no single right answer, so the judge check lets a second model decide against one clear rule, such as "mentions the refund deadline". Here is what happens to one case. Take label-04, where the message says the app crashes every time the settings page opens and the prompt asks for only the label. The runner sends it to the model. Say the model replies Bug. The exact check drops the final period, ignores capital letters, gets bug and finds it equal to the expected answer, so the case passes. If the model had replied This looks like a bug report, the case would fail, even though a person would accept it. The check is strict on purpose, which is why the prompt demands a single word. The demo set has 40 cases (10 each of arithmetic word problems, JSON extraction, support ticket labels and short exact answers). It only shows how the pipeline works, and you can download all 40 cases and the script from this gist . Write your own cases from failures you have seen. Step 3. The script Save this as evals.py. It is 95 lines of standard Python, so there is nothing to install, and it works on Python 3.9 and newer (checked on 3.9 and 3.12). You can copy it as is. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """evals.py: a tiny eval runner for any OpenAI-compatible local server (Ollama, llama-server).""" import argparse, json, math, re, statistics, sys, time, urllib.request def chat(base, model, prompt, temperature=0.0, seed=0, max_tokens=1024, effort=None): body = {"model": model, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}], "temperature": temperature, "seed": seed, "max_tokens": max_tokens} if effort: body["reasoning_effort"] = effort # "none" turns thinking off on Ollama models that allow it req = urllib.request.Request(base + "/v1/chat/completions", json.dumps(body).encode(), {"Content-Type": "application/json"}) t0 = time.time() with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=900) as r: d = json.load(r) text = d["choices"][0]["message"].get("content") or "" text = re.sub(r" .*? ", "", text, flags=re.S).strip() return text, time.time() - t0, d.get("usage", {}).get("completion_tokens", 0) def grade(case, out, judge): kind, want = case["check"], case["expect"] if kind == "exact": return out.strip().strip("."'").lower() == want.lower() if kind == "regex": return re.search(want, out, re.S | re.I) is not None if kind == "json": m = re.search(r"\{.*\}", out, re.S) try: got = json.loads(m.group(0)) except (AttributeError, ValueError): return False return all(got.get(k) == v for k, v in want.items()) if kind == "judge": # last resort: a second model grades against a one-line criterion q = ("Question: %s
Answer: %s
Criterion: %s
" "Does the answer meet the criterion? Reply with exactly PASS or FAIL." % (case["prompt"], out, want)) verdict, _, _ = chat(judge[0], judge[1], q, max_tokens=512) return verdict.strip().upper().startswith("PASS") raise ValueError("unknown check: " + kind) def mean_ci(xs): se = statistics.stdev(xs) / math.sqrt(len(xs)) if len(xs) > 1 else 0.0 return statistics.fmean(xs) * 100, 1.96 * se * 100 # in percent: mean and 95% half-width def main(): p = argparse.ArgumentParser() p.add_argument("cases") p.add_argument("--base", default="http://localhost:11434") # llama-server: port 8080 p.add_argument("--models", nargs="+", required=True) p.add_argument("--repeats", type=int, default=1) p.add_argument("--temperature", type=float, default=0.0) p.add_argument("--effort") p.add_argument("--judge", help="BASE,MODEL of the judge server, needed only for judge cases") p.add_argument("--save", help="write per-case scores to this JSON file") p.add_argument("--baseline", help="JSON saved by an earlier run; exit 1 if the first model got worse") p.add_argument("--max-drop", type=float, default=5.0, help="allowed drop in points") a = p.parse_args() cases = [json.loads(line) for line in open(a.cases) if line.strip()] judge = a.judge.split(",") if a.judge else None scores = {} print("%-26s %6s %8s %8s %7s" % ("model", "pass", "+/-95%", "tok/s", "sec")) for model in a.models: scores[model], toks, secs = {}, 0, 0.0 for c in cases: ok = [] for r in range(a.repeats): out, sec, n = chat(a.base, model, c["prompt"], a.temperature, r, effort=a.effort) ok.append(grade(c, out, judge)) toks, secs = toks + n, secs + sec scores[model][c["id"]] = sum(ok) / len(ok) mean, half = mean_ci(list(scores[model].values())) print("%-26s %5.1f%% %7.1f %8.1f %7.0f" % (model, mean, half, toks / secs if secs else 0, secs)) for tag in sorted({c["tag"] for c in cases}): xs = [scores[model][c["id"]] for c in cases if c["tag"] == tag] print(" %-22s %5.1f%% (%d cases)" % (tag, statistics.fmean(xs) * 100, len(xs))) first = a.models[0] for m in a.models[1:]: # paired difference: the same cases, so compare case by case d = [scores[m][c["id"]] - scores[first][c["id"]] for c in cases] mean, half = mean_ci(d) print("%s minus %s: %+.1f points (+/- %.1f)" % (m, first, mean, half)) if a.save: json.dump(scores, open(a.save, "w"), indent=1) if a.baseline: old = json.load(open(a.baseline))[first] before = statistics.fmean(old.values()) * 100 now = statistics.fmean(scores[first].values()) * 100 print("baseline %.1f%% -> now %.1f%%" % (before, now)) if before - now > a.max_drop: sys.exit("REGRESSION: dropped more than %.1f points" % a.max_drop) if __name__ == "__main__": main() It sends each case to the model, one at a time, and prints the score. A few details: It sets temperature to 0, which makes the model pick its most likely words, and uses a fixed seed. Runs are then mostly repeatable, but not always . Thinking Machines asked one model the same question 1,000 times at temperature 0 and got 80 different answers, because the result depended on how many requests the server was handling at once. Treat one run as one sample. --repeats shows how stable each answer is. Some models think out loud before answering. --effort none turns that off where the model allows it (gpt-oss can't), in Ollama and llama-server. The script also strips blocks. The score is the average over all cases, with a margin of error , which is a range the true score probably falls in. Evan Miller’s paper on error bars for evals recommends reporting it. With two or more models, the script compares each with the first on the same cases. That is fairer than comparing two separate scores. --save stores a run. --baseline compares a new run with a saved one and exits with an error if the score dropped by more than --max-drop points. Run it python3 evals.py cases.jsonl --models qwen3.5:4b qwen3.5:4b-q8_0 --effort none --save runs/today.json Against llama-server, change the base URL and use the alias: python3 evals.py cases.jsonl --base http://localhost:8080 --models qwen3.5-4b-q4 --effort none The script prints a report like this one. It comes from a fake test server that returns made-up answers, so the numbers mean nothing and only the layout matters. Quality only dropped at 3 bits (Q3_K_S averaged 65.49). The authors also warn that small gains can be noise. It is one model, so run your own cases. items.summary_html:
A checklist of tests where most pass and one fails (image generated by AI)

An eval pipeline is a set of test questions, a script that sends them to an AI model, and a way to score the answers. It works like unit tests for code, but for an AI feature. You can build a small one on your own laptop with Ollama and llama.cpp, and this story shows how.

The whole pipeline. The runner talks to any server that speaks the OpenAI chat format.What an eval pipeline is

Anthropic describes an eval as a test for an AI system, where you give it an input and check its output. A pipeline has four parts.

  • Test cases are questions or tasks, each with a note on what a good answer looks like.
  • A runner is a script that sends every case to the model and saves the answers.
  • Graders score each answer. Simple code checks come first. Does the answer match exactly, contain the right number, or parse as valid JSON? If code can’t decide, a second AI model can act as the judge.
  • A report shows the overall score and how it compares with the last run.

A benchmark such as GSM8K is a public test set that everyone uses. A pipeline points the same idea at your own task, and you run it every time something changes.

Why you need one
  • Without tests, you hear about problems from your users. Anthropic describes the usual pattern. People say the AI feels worse after a change, and the team can only guess and check. Fixing one bug can break something else.
  • A public benchmark does not tell you how your task will go. Hamel Husain, who writes about building AI products, says tests built around your users’ tasks measure something different from general benchmarks. Setup matters too. On the ARC Prize leaderboard, GPT-6.2 Astra scored 70.3% with a basic setup and 99.8% with a tuned one, at the same reasoning level.
  • A new model is a change too. In Husain’s case study of a real estate assistant, progress stalled because fixing one problem created others, so the team built a proper way to test it. Anthropic says that when a new model comes out, an eval suite shows quickly what got better.
  • You need to know whether a score is real. Anthropic found that CPU and memory limits on the test machine alone moved scores on a coding benchmark, Terminal-Bench 2.0, by about 6 points. A score without a margin of error can’t tell you if a gain is real.
How to use it
  1. Collect 20 to 50 real cases. Use things that went wrong, such as your bug tracker, support messages and the checks you already do by hand. Anthropic says a small set is enough at the start, because early changes tend to have big effects.
  2. Decide how each case is scored. A good case is one where two experts would agree on pass or fail. Use a code check where you can.
  3. Run it once and save the result. That is your baseline.
  4. Change one thing. It can be the model, the prompt, a setting or the size of the model file.
  5. Run it again and compare. Look at the margin of error before you believe a difference.
  6. Keep the cases. Add a new case for every new failure, and run the set after every change.
Where this helps in practice

These situations are made up, but most people who build with AI run into one of them.

  • You fix one prompt problem and break another. Say a support bot sorts messages into bug, billing and feature request. Someone edits the prompt so billing questions are handled better, and bug reports start landing in the wrong group. Nobody notices until customers complain. With a saved set of cases, the next run shows which ones flipped.
  • A new model comes out and the headlines say it is better. Better at what? Run your own cases on the old and the new model and compare them case by case. A leaderboard can’t tell you how a model does on your messages.
  • You want a cheaper or smaller model, maybe one that runs on your laptop so your data stays with you. Run the same cases on both. The Q4 and Q8 comparison further down is an example of this check.
  • The demo worked, and then real users broke it. They phrase things in ways you never tried. Each time it happens, add that message as a new case, so the same failure can’t come back unnoticed.
Build it on your laptop

Running tests locally costs only electricity, keeps your data on your machine and lets you test something that hosted APIs hide, such as which compressed version of a model you use. Quantization shrinks a model by storing its numbers with fewer bits. A Q4 file is smaller than a Q8 file and can be a little less accurate.

Ollama and llama.cpp are two popular programs that run models on your computer. Both can answer in the same format as the OpenAI API, so one script can test either.

Step 1. Start the servers

These commands are for a Mac with Homebrew. On Linux and Windows, install both from their websites.

brew install ollama llama.cpp
ollama serve                       # leave it running, port 11434
ollama pull qwen3.5:4b             # Q4_K_M, 3.3 GB
ollama pull qwen3.5:4b-q8_0        # the same model at Q8_0, 5.2 GB

llama.cpp is optional. Its server, llama-server, can download a model file from Hugging Face with -hf (the default size is Q4_K_M), and --alias sets the model name you use in requests:

llama-server -hf unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF:Q4_K_M --alias qwen3.5-4b-q4 --port 8080

On a 16 GB laptop, stay at 9B parameters or smaller. Ollama lists qwen3.5:9b at about 7 GB and gpt-oss:20b at 14 GB, which leaves little room for everything else.

Step 2. Write the test cases

Each case is one line of JSON, a plain text format for data. It has four parts. prompt is what the model sees, check is how to score the answer, expect is a correct answer and tag is a group name for the report. Two lines from the demo set, with the prompts shortened:

{"id": "label-04", "tag": "label", "prompt": "Classify the customer message ... Message: The app crashes every time I open the settings page.", "check": "exact", "expect": "bug"}
{"id": "json-01", "tag": "json", "prompt": "Extract the person, city and year ... Sentence: Grace Hopper joined the Navy Reserve in New York in 1943.", "check": "json", "expect": {"name": "Grace Hopper", "city": "New York", "year": 1943}}

The check depends on the task. Four examples:

  • Sorting support messages into groups. The expected answer is one word, such as bug, so the exact check works. It wants a word for word match.
  • Pulling facts out of text, such as a name, a city and a year. The expected answer is a small JSON object, so the json check parses the reply and compares the fields.
  • A math or counting question. The answer is a number, so a regex check (a text pattern) looks for it in the reply.
  • Writing a summary or setting a tone. There is no single right answer, so the judge check lets a second model decide against one clear rule, such as "mentions the refund deadline".

Here is what happens to one case. Take label-04, where the message says the app crashes every time the settings page opens and the prompt asks for only the label. The runner sends it to the model. Say the model replies Bug. The exact check drops the final period, ignores capital letters, gets bug and finds it equal to the expected answer, so the case passes. If the model had replied This looks like a bug report, the case would fail, even though a person would accept it. The check is strict on purpose, which is why the prompt demands a single word.

The demo set has 40 cases (10 each of arithmetic word problems, JSON extraction, support ticket labels and short exact answers). It only shows how the pipeline works, and you can download all 40 cases and the script from this gist. Write your own cases from failures you have seen.

Step 3. The script

Save this as evals.py. It is 95 lines of standard Python, so there is nothing to install, and it works on Python 3.9 and newer (checked on 3.9 and 3.12). You can copy it as is.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""evals.py: a tiny eval runner for any OpenAI-compatible local server (Ollama, llama-server)."""
import argparse, json, math, re, statistics, sys, time, urllib.request
def chat(base, model, prompt, temperature=0.0, seed=0, max_tokens=1024, effort=None):
    body = {"model": model, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
            "temperature": temperature, "seed": seed, "max_tokens": max_tokens}
    if effort:
        body["reasoning_effort"] = effort  # "none" turns thinking off on Ollama models that allow it
    req = urllib.request.Request(base + "/v1/chat/completions", json.dumps(body).encode(),
                                 {"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    t0 = time.time()
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=900) as r:
        d = json.load(r)
    text = d["choices"][0]["message"].get("content") or ""
    text = re.sub(r".*?", "", text, flags=re.S).strip()
    return text, time.time() - t0, d.get("usage", {}).get("completion_tokens", 0)
def grade(case, out, judge):
    kind, want = case["check"], case["expect"]
    if kind == "exact":
        return out.strip().strip("."'").lower() == want.lower()
    if kind == "regex":
        return re.search(want, out, re.S | re.I) is not None
    if kind == "json":
        m = re.search(r"\{.*\}", out, re.S)
        try:
            got = json.loads(m.group(0))
        except (AttributeError, ValueError):
            return False
        return all(got.get(k) == v for k, v in want.items())
    if kind == "judge":  # last resort: a second model grades against a one-line criterion
        q = ("Question: %s
Answer: %s
Criterion: %s
"
             "Does the answer meet the criterion? Reply with exactly PASS or FAIL." % (case["prompt"], out, want))
        verdict, _, _ = chat(judge[0], judge[1], q, max_tokens=512)
        return verdict.strip().upper().startswith("PASS")
    raise ValueError("unknown check: " + kind)
def mean_ci(xs):
    se = statistics.stdev(xs) / math.sqrt(len(xs)) if len(xs) > 1 else 0.0
    return statistics.fmean(xs) * 100, 1.96 * se * 100  # in percent: mean and 95% half-width
def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("cases")
    p.add_argument("--base", default="http://localhost:11434")  # llama-server: port 8080
    p.add_argument("--models", nargs="+", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--repeats", type=int, default=1)
    p.add_argument("--temperature", type=float, default=0.0)
    p.add_argument("--effort")
    p.add_argument("--judge", help="BASE,MODEL of the judge server, needed only for judge cases")
    p.add_argument("--save", help="write per-case scores to this JSON file")
    p.add_argument("--baseline", help="JSON saved by an earlier run; exit 1 if the first model got worse")
    p.add_argument("--max-drop", type=float, default=5.0, help="allowed drop in points")
    a = p.parse_args()
    cases = [json.loads(line) for line in open(a.cases) if line.strip()]
    judge = a.judge.split(",") if a.judge else None
    scores = {}
    print("%-26s %6s %8s %8s %7s" % ("model", "pass", "+/-95%", "tok/s", "sec"))
    for model in a.models:
        scores[model], toks, secs = {}, 0, 0.0
        for c in cases:
            ok = []
            for r in range(a.repeats):
                out, sec, n = chat(a.base, model, c["prompt"], a.temperature, r, effort=a.effort)
                ok.append(grade(c, out, judge))
                toks, secs = toks + n, secs + sec
            scores[model][c["id"]] = sum(ok) / len(ok)
        mean, half = mean_ci(list(scores[model].values()))
        print("%-26s %5.1f%% %7.1f %8.1f %7.0f" % (model, mean, half, toks / secs if secs else 0, secs))
        for tag in sorted({c["tag"] for c in cases}):
            xs = [scores[model][c["id"]] for c in cases if c["tag"] == tag]
            print("    %-22s %5.1f%%  (%d cases)" % (tag, statistics.fmean(xs) * 100, len(xs)))
    first = a.models[0]
    for m in a.models[1:]:  # paired difference: the same cases, so compare case by case
        d = [scores[m][c["id"]] - scores[first][c["id"]] for c in cases]
        mean, half = mean_ci(d)
        print("%s minus %s: %+.1f points (+/- %.1f)" % (m, first, mean, half))
    if a.save:
        json.dump(scores, open(a.save, "w"), indent=1)
    if a.baseline:
        old = json.load(open(a.baseline))[first]
        before = statistics.fmean(old.values()) * 100
        now = statistics.fmean(scores[first].values()) * 100
        print("baseline %.1f%% -> now %.1f%%" % (before, now))
        if before - now > a.max_drop:
            sys.exit("REGRESSION: dropped more than %.1f points" % a.max_drop)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

It sends each case to the model, one at a time, and prints the score. A few details:

  • It sets temperature to 0, which makes the model pick its most likely words, and uses a fixed seed. Runs are then mostly repeatable, but not always. Thinking Machines asked one model the same question 1,000 times at temperature 0 and got 80 different answers, because the result depended on how many requests the server was handling at once. Treat one run as one sample. --repeats shows how stable each answer is.
  • Some models think out loud before answering. --effort none turns that off where the model allows it (gpt-oss can't), in Ollama and llama-server. The script also strips  blocks.
  • The score is the average over all cases, with a margin of error, which is a range the true score probably falls in. Evan Miller’s paper on error bars for evals recommends reporting it.
  • With two or more models, the script compares each with the first on the same cases. That is fairer than comparing two separate scores.
  • --save stores a run. --baseline compares a new run with a saved one and exits with an error if the score dropped by more than --max-drop points.
Step 4. Run it
python3 evals.py cases.jsonl --models qwen3.5:4b qwen3.5:4b-q8_0 --effort none --save runs/today.json

Against llama-server, change the base URL and use the alias:

python3 evals.py cases.jsonl --base http://localhost:8080 --models qwen3.5-4b-q4 --effort none

The script prints a report like this one. It comes from a fake test server that returns made-up answers, so the numbers mean nothing and only the layout matters. The fake server also answers instantly, which is why the speed looks absurd and the time is 0 seconds.

model                        pass   +/-95%    tok/s     sec
model-a                     72.5%    14.0  10552.0       0
    json                    70.0%  (10 cases)
    label                   60.0%  (10 cases)
    math                    70.0%  (10 cases)
    short                   90.0%  (10 cases)
model-b                     75.0%    13.6  36698.8       0
    json                    90.0%  (10 cases)
    label                   90.0%  (10 cases)
    math                    60.0%  (10 cases)
    short                   60.0%  (10 cases)
model-b minus model-a: +2.5 points (+/- 21.6)
  • pass is the share of cases answered correctly, and +/-95% is the margin of error in points. tok/s is the speed in tokens (small pieces of words) per second, and sec is the total time.
  • The indented lines show the score for each tag, so you can see which kind of task changed. With only 10 cases per tag, treat them as hints.
  • The last line compares the two models on the same cases. Here model-b looks 2.5 points better, but the margin is 21.6, so this gap proves nothing.
How to read the results

Say you run 40 cases and score 70%. How far can you trust that? The margin of error is about 14 points either way (1.96 times the square root of 0.7 × 0.3 ÷ 40). A 70% and an 80% can’t be told apart from numbers like these. More cases shrink the margin. Running the same 40 cases again doesn’t, because the 40 cases are your sample.

An illustration, not measured data. Two scores on the same 40 cases, each with its margin of error.

A real study shows how small the differences can be. In January 2026, researchers tested Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct in different llama.cpp sizes on five public benchmarks. The average score was 69.47 at full precision, 69.41 at Q8 and 69.15 at Q4_K_M, while the files were 47% and 69% smaller. A gap of 0.3 points is far too small for 40 cases to show. Quality only dropped at 3 bits (Q3_K_S averaged 65.49). The authors also warn that small gains can be noise. It is one model, so run your own cases.

When you need a judge

Some answers can’t be checked with simple code, such as a summary, a tone or an explanation. For those, a second AI model can grade the first one (called LLM as a judge), and the script has a judge check for it. Two warnings:

  • Judges have biases. The MT-Bench paper found they tend to favor the first answer shown, longer answers and answers written by themselves.
  • Small judges are worse. In a study of 13 judge models, only the best and largest agreed reasonably well with humans, and scores could be off by up to 5 points. Ranking models still worked with smaller judges.

Use a different model as judge than the one you test, ask one pass or fail question per call, and read about 20 verdicts yourself.

When to use a ready-made tool

Once your cases outgrow one file, existing tools can take over.

  • promptfoo keeps tests in a YAML file and uses Ollama through ollama:chat:. Its judge defaults to an OpenAI model, so point defaultTest.options.provider at a local one.
  • lm-evaluation-harness runs standard public benchmarks. Use --model gguf for llama-server.
  • Inspect AI has a built-in Ollama provider, ollama/.
  • DeepEval says in its docs that any model served by Ollama can run its evals.
Keep it running

After a good run, save it. After every change (a new model file, a different size, an edited prompt), run again with --baseline so it fails if the score drops by more than 5 points. You can start it from a git hook or a CI job. One catch is that with 40 cases, 5 points is well inside the margin of error, so it can fail for no reason. Raise the limit or add cases.

What this story does not show
  • The demo cases are small and simple. A score on them says nothing about your task.
  • The script has no retries and no parallel runs, and it treats cases as independent. Miller’s paper says related questions need a more careful margin of error.
  • The script has only been tested against a fake server that imitates the API, not real models. The numbers here come from the linked sources, not from my own runs. Treat your first real run as a test of the script too.
Final thoughts

Choosing good cases takes more work than writing the script, and Anthropic says the same about writing good tasks. Start with 20 to 50 cases from real failures. Test two models or settings side by side, and trust a difference only when it is bigger than the margin of error.

items.title: THIRSTDAY #13: Your First Job May Disappear Before Anyone Gets Fired
items.summary: AI can help a company keep its staff while narrowing the way in. The harder question is who will pay to develop the experienced people it still needs. A company can celebrate its AI rollout, keep every developer on payroll and still become a harder place to start a career. The change appears when the next vacancy never opens, leaving someone outside the company to absorb the cost of its productivity gain. For the applicant, there is no announcement explaining what happened. There is another unanswered application, another recommendation to improve a portfolio, and another job description asking for experience that somebody else will have to provide. “No one lost their job” can be entirely true while offering very little comfort to someone trying to get their first one. That possibility deserves more attention than it receives in arguments about whether AI will eventually become good enough to replace a professional. An employer can change its recruitment plans long before a machine can perform an entire job. The job that never reaches the careers page A November working paper by Lindsey Raymond and Eleanor Dillon studies GitHub Copilot adoption across 5,414 firms. Using pre-existing contract-review schedules to identify adoption effects, the researchers estimate a 29% reduction in quarterly technical hiring after a year among firms induced to adopt through those reviews. They find no corresponding effect on separations or overall technical headcount; the hiring decline concentrates in junior, coding-intensive roles. The scope matters: this is an estimate for particular adopters, using data through mid-2025, rather than a verdict on today’s entire labor market. It also cannot establish the eventual economy-wide employment effect. For a manager, postponing recruitment can be a reasonable response to greater capacity. If the existing team can meet its commitments, hiring another person entails an immediate expense, supervision and uncertainty. Nothing in that decision requires hostility towards young workers. Yet an applicant experiences the same decision from a much less comfortable position. They may have become better at producing software while finding fewer employers willing to buy their labor. AI can help a company keep its staff while narrowing the way in. The harder question is who will pay to develop the experienced people it still needs.

A company can celebrate its AI rollout, keep every developer on payroll and still become a harder place to start a career. The change appears when the next vacancy never opens, leaving someone outside the company to absorb the cost of its productivity gain.

For the applicant, there is no announcement explaining what happened. There is another unanswered application, another recommendation to improve a portfolio, and another job description asking for experience that somebody else will have to provide.

“No one lost their job” can be entirely true while offering very little comfort to someone trying to get their first one.

That possibility deserves more attention than it receives in arguments about whether AI will eventually become good enough to replace a professional. An employer can change its recruitment plans long before a machine can perform an entire job.

A November working paper by Lindsey Raymond and Eleanor Dillon studies GitHub Copilot adoption across 5,414 firms. items.title: On-Device Anomaly Detection: Statistical Baselines vs. Learned Models
items.summary: There is a reflex in IoT projects that goes: "we have anomaly data, so we need a model." Often the honest answer is that a robust statistical baseline will detect 80% of the incidents with 2% of the engineering effort — and, crucially, with far fewer false alarms during the first two weeks after commissioning, which is exactly when trust is built. This post compares the two approaches honestly, gives you working code for the statistical side, and describes the hybrid that I end up shipping most of the time. What "anomaly" means operationally Before comparing detectors, define what you are detecting. Three very different problems get called "anomaly detection": Point outliers — a single sample outside the historical range. Sensor glitch, transient spike. Level shift / drift — the process moves to a new operating point and stays there. Fouling, wear, a changed setpoint. Shape change — the signal's dynamics change while its mean stays flat. Bearing defect, looseness, cavitation. A robust z-score handles (1) well and (2) adequately. It is poor at (3), because crest factor and spectral content can change dramatically with an unchanged mean. If your failure modes are mostly (3), a model that sees a window of raw or lightly processed samples earns its complexity. If they are (1) and (2), a statistical baseline is not a compromise — it is the right tool. The baseline, properly done A naive mean ± 3σ fails for three reasons: spikes inflate σ, the distribution is rarely Gaussian, and it ignores time. Fix all three: import numpy as np class RobustBaseline : """Median/MAD baseline with EWMA smoothing and hysteresis. Handles spikes (median), non-Gaussian tails (MAD + quantile), and slow drift (EWMA) without a training pipeline. """ MAD_TO_SIGMA = 1.4826 def __init__ ( self , alpha = 0.02 , warmup = 300 , k_warn = 4.0 , k_alarm = 6.0 , hold = 5 ) : self . alpha = alpha self . warmup = warmup self . k_warn = k_warn self . k_alarm = k_alarm self . hold = hold self . n = 0 self . med = None self . mad = None self . state = "ok" self . _over = 0 def update ( self , x : float ) -> tuple [ str , float ] : if self . med is None : self . med , self . mad = x , 1e-6 self . n += 1 # EWMA on centre and spread: adapts to setpoint changes, resists spikes self . med += self . alpha * ( x - self . med ) self . mad += self . alpha * ( abs ( x - self . med ) - self . mad ) sigma = max ( self . mad * self . MAD_TO_SIGMA , 1e-9 ) z = ( x - self . med ) / sigma # during warm-up, only widen the band; never alert if self . n < self . warmup : return "warmup" , z if abs ( z ) >= self . k_alarm : self . _over += 1 else : self . _over = 0 if self . _over >= self . hold : self . state = "alarm" elif abs ( z ) >= self . k_warn : self . state = "warn" elif self . state == "alarm" and abs ( z ) < self . k_warn : self . state = "warn" elif abs ( z ) < self . k_warn * 0.5 : self . state = "ok" return self . state , z Four design choices carry most of the value: EWMA rather than a fixed historical window. A machine that ramps to a new load for 20 minutes is not anomalous; a fixed baseline from last month says it is. The EWMA follows the operating point. MAD rather than σ. One 10× spike changes σ by a lot and median absolute deviation by almost nothing. A warm-up period that never alerts. You will thank yourself on day one of every deployment. Hold-down plus hysteresis ( k_alarm > k_warn , and a return threshold at half of k_warn ). This alone typically cuts alert volume by half. More on that in the hysteresis post. Where the baseline breaks Three failure modes are worth knowing because they tell you when to graduate to a model: Correlated channels. A temperature rise in a motor is normal if current also rose and the ambient did not. A per-channel z-score cannot express "high, but consistent with load". This is where a learned model — or even a simple multivariate Mahalanobis distance — wins immediately. Shape-only faults. A crest-factor rise from 2.1 to 3.4 on a bearing is a classic early indicator that stays invisible to a mean-based detector. If your maintenance history is dominated by these, you need window features or a model. Multi-modal normal behaviour. A compressor that runs loaded, idle, and in a defrost cycle has three distinct "normal" operating points. A single centre/spread pair produces alerts at every transition. You can fix this with mode-conditioned baselines (one RobustBaseline per mode) — which is usually the cheap correct answer, and a strong argument against reaching for a neural network too early. Fair comparison: the metrics that matter Do not compare detectors with AUC. Compare them the way operations experiences them: Time to detect — minutes from fault onset to first alarm, per incident. False alarms per device per day — the number your on-call rotation actually feels. Alert precision — share of alarms a technician judges actionable. Lead time before failure — for predictive maintenance, the window in which you can act. A worked comparison table from a real fleet of 180 pumps looked like this: Detector Median time to detect False alarms / device / day Precision Flash need Per-channel robust z 41 min 1.8 0.34 < 1 KB Multivariate Mahalanobis 22 min 0.9 0.52 ~ 2 KB 1D CNN on raw window 8 min 0.4 0.71 96 KB CNN + rule engine + dedup 8 min 0.1 0.88 96 KB Note the last row: the big win in precision did not come from a better model, it came from the rule engine and de-duplication layered on top. That pattern repeats — the model is rarely the whole answer. The Mahalanobis row is worth dwelling on. It costs a covariance matrix and a few multiplications, fits in a couple of kilobytes, and captures load-correlated behaviour that per-channel z-scores miss. For many fleets it is the best effort-to-value ratio available. import numpy as np class MahalanobisBaseline : def __init__ ( self , feature_names , shrink = 0.10 ) : self . names = feature_names self . shrink = shrink self . mu = None self . inv_cov = None def fit ( self , X : np . ndarray ) -> "MahalanobisBaseline" : self . mu = X . mean ( axis = 0 ) cov = np . cov ( X , rowvar = False ) # shrinkage keeps the inverse stable with correlated features cov = ( 1 - self . shrink ) * cov + self . shrink * np . eye ( cov . shape [ 0 ] ) * np . trace ( cov ) / cov . shape [ 0 ] self . inv_cov = np . linalg . inv ( cov ) return self def score ( self , x : np . ndarray ) -> float : d = x - self . mu return float ( np . sqrt ( d @ self . inv_cov @ d ) ) Score thresholds come from the chi-square distribution, not from a 3σ rule: for d features, the 99.9th percentile of χ²(d) is a defensible alarm threshold. Hardcode the resulting constant in the firmware so the device does not need a stats library. The hybrid I usually ship per-sample → device: hard limits (deterministic, no model) per-window → gateway: robust baseline per operating mode (cheap, always on) └─ if |z| > k_warn: run the learned model on the window per-event → cloud: correlation, dedup, triage The baseline acts as a cheap gate , and the model runs only on windows the baseline flagged. On a 200-device fleet this cut inference CPU by roughly 90% while keeping detection latency identical, because the baseline catches the same onsets the model does — it just cannot say much about what is happening. There is a second benefit that matters more: the baseline is the fallback. If a model update goes wrong, or a device's model fails to load, the baseline still detects level shifts and point outliers. A pipeline whose only detector is a neural network has no degraded mode; it has an outage. Guarding the baseline against setpoint changes Baselines go bad when the process changes: a new product run, a retuned controller, a replaced sensor. Three cheap guards: 1 Mode-conditioned state. Key the baseline on an operating mode supplied by the machine, not inferred. baselines[mode].update(x) . 2 Commissioning reset with an explicit window. Allow a supervised "rebaseline" that ignores data for N minutes after a setpoint command, so the ramp itself never becomes the new normal. 3 Slow-drift detection on the baseline itself. Track med over days; if it moves more than X% without a maintenance event, that is a signal in its own right, not noise to be absorbed. That third guard is genuinely useful. On one fleet, the alarm that actually predicted failures was not a z-score at all — it was "the EWMA centre of the vibration RMS moved 15% in a week without a setpoint change". Slow, boring, and more predictive than the model. Deciding Use the baseline alone when: your failure modes are point outliers or level shifts, you have fewer than ~10 correlated channels, and your false-alarm budget is tight from day one. Add a learned model when: faults are shape-based, channels are strongly correlated, or you have enough labelled incidents to evaluate a model honestly (a dozen is not enough to distinguish a model from a baseline — you need dozens). Ship the hybrid almost always: baseline as gate and fallback, model for diagnosis, rule engine and de-duplication on top. That is the architecture the rest of this series builds toward. Next: Designing a Rule Engine That Complements Your ML Model.

There is a reflex in IoT projects that goes: "we have anomaly data, so we need a model." Often the honest answer is that a robust statistical baseline will detect 80% of the incidents with 2% of the engineering effort — and, crucially, with far fewer false alarms during the first two weeks after commissioning, which is exactly when trust is built.

This post compares the two approaches honestly, gives you working code for the statistical side, and describes the hybrid that I end up shipping most of the time.

What "anomaly" means operationally

Before comparing detectors, define what you are detecting. Three very different problems get called "anomaly detection":

  1. Point outliers — a single sample outside the historical range. Sensor glitch, transient spike.
  2. Level shift / drift — the process moves to a new operating point and stays there. Fouling, wear, a changed setpoint.
  3. Shape change — the signal's dynamics change while its mean stays flat. Bearing defect, looseness, cavitation.

A robust z-score handles (1) well and (2) adequately. It is poor at (3), because crest factor and spectral content can change dramatically with an unchanged mean. If your failure modes are mostly (3), a model that sees a window of raw or lightly processed samples earns its complexity. If they are (1) and (2), a statistical baseline is not a compromise — it is the right tool.

The baseline, properly done

A naive mean ± 3σ fails for three reasons: spikes inflate σ, the distribution is rarely Gaussian, and it ignores time. Fix all three:

import numpy as np

class RobustBaseline:
    """Median/MAD baseline with EWMA smoothing and hysteresis.

    Handles spikes (median), non-Gaussian tails (MAD + quantile),
    and slow drift (EWMA) without a training pipeline.
    """

    MAD_TO_SIGMA = 1.4826

    def __init__(self, alpha=0.02, warmup=300, k_warn=4.0, k_alarm=6.0, hold=5):
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.warmup = warmup
        self.k_warn = k_warn
        self.k_alarm = k_alarm
        self.hold = hold
        self.n = 0
        self.med = None
        self.mad = None
        self.state = "ok"
        self._over = 0

    def update(self, x: float) -> tuple[str, float]:
        if self.med is None:
            self.med, self.mad = x, 1e-6
        self.n += 1

        # EWMA on centre and spread: adapts to setpoint changes, resists spikes
        self.med += self.alpha * (x - self.med)
        self.mad += self.alpha * (abs(x - self.med) - self.mad)

        sigma = max(self.mad * self.MAD_TO_SIGMA, 1e-9)
        z = (x - self.med) / sigma

        # during warm-up, only widen the band; never alert
        if self.n < self.warmup:
            return "warmup", z

        if abs(z) >= self.k_alarm:
            self._over += 1
        else:
            self._over = 0

        if self._over >= self.hold:
            self.state = "alarm"
        elif abs(z) >= self.k_warn:
            self.state = "warn"
        elif self.state == "alarm" and abs(z) < self.k_warn:
            self.state = "warn"
        elif abs(z) < self.k_warn * 0.5:
            self.state = "ok"
        return self.state, z

Four design choices carry most of the value:

  • EWMA rather than a fixed historical window. A machine that ramps to a new load for 20 minutes is not anomalous; a fixed baseline from last month says it is. The EWMA follows the operating point.
  • MAD rather than σ. One 10× spike changes σ by a lot and median absolute deviation by almost nothing.
  • A warm-up period that never alerts. You will thank yourself on day one of every deployment.
  • Hold-down plus hysteresis (k_alarm > k_warn, and a return threshold at half of k_warn). This alone typically cuts alert volume by half. More on that in the hysteresis post.

Three failure modes are worth knowing because they tell you when to graduate to a model:

Correlated channels. A temperature rise in a motor is normal if current also rose and the ambient did not. A per-channel z-score cannot express "high, but consistent with load". This is where a learned model — or even a simple multivariate Mahalanobis distance — wins immediately.

Shape-only faults. A crest-factor rise from 2.1 to 3.4 on a bearing is a classic early indicator that stays invisible to a mean-based detector. If your maintenance history is dominated by these, you need window features or a model.

Multi-modal normal behaviour. A compressor that runs loaded, idle, and in a defrost cycle has three distinct "normal" operating points. A single centre/spread pair produces alerts at every transition. You can fix this with mode-conditioned baselines (one RobustBaseline per mode) — which is usually the cheap correct answer, and a strong argument against reaching for a neural network too early.

Fair comparison: the metrics that matter

Do not compare detectors with AUC. Compare them the way operations experiences them:

  • Time to detect — minutes from fault onset to first alarm, per incident.
  • False alarms per device per day — the number your on-call rotation actually feels.
  • Alert precision — share of alarms a technician judges actionable.
  • Lead time before failure — for predictive maintenance, the window in which you can act.

A worked comparison table from a real fleet of 180 pumps looked like this:

Detector Median time to detect False alarms / device / day Precision Flash need Per-channel robust z 41 min 1.8 0.34 < 1 KB Multivariate Mahalanobis 22 min 0.9 0.52 ~ 2 KB 1D CNN on raw window 8 min 0.4 0.71 96 KB CNN + rule engine + dedup 8 min 0.1 0.88 96 KB

Note the last row: the big win in precision did not come from a better model, it came from the rule engine and de-duplication layered on top. That pattern repeats — the model is rarely the whole answer.

The Mahalanobis row is worth dwelling on. It costs a covariance matrix and a few multiplications, fits in a couple of kilobytes, and captures load-correlated behaviour that per-channel z-scores miss. For many fleets it is the best effort-to-value ratio available.

import numpy as np

class MahalanobisBaseline:
    def __init__(self, feature_names, shrink=0.10):
        self.names = feature_names
        self.shrink = shrink
        self.mu = None
        self.inv_cov = None

    def fit(self, X: np.ndarray) -> "MahalanobisBaseline":
        self.mu = X.mean(axis=0)
        cov = np.cov(X, rowvar=False)
        # shrinkage keeps the inverse stable with correlated features
        cov = (1 - self.shrink) * cov + self.shrink * np.eye(cov.shape[0]) * np.trace(cov) / cov.shape[0]
        self.inv_cov = np.linalg.inv(cov)
        return self

    def score(self, x: np.ndarray) -> float:
        d = x - self.mu
        return float(np.sqrt(d @ self.inv_cov @ d))

Score thresholds come from the chi-square distribution, not from a 3σ rule: for d features, the 99.9th percentile of χ²(d) is a defensible alarm threshold. Hardcode the resulting constant in the firmware so the device does not need a stats library.

The hybrid I usually ship 
per-sample   → device: hard limits (deterministic, no model)
per-window   → gateway: robust baseline per operating mode  (cheap, always on)
               └─ if |z| > k_warn: run the learned model on the window
per-event    → cloud: correlation, dedup, triage

The baseline acts as a cheap gate, and the model runs only on windows the baseline flagged. On a 200-device fleet this cut inference CPU by roughly 90% while keeping detection latency identical, because the baseline catches the same onsets the model does — it just cannot say much about what is happening.

There is a second benefit that matters more: the baseline is the fallback. If a model update goes wrong, or a device's model fails to load, the baseline still detects level shifts and point outliers. A pipeline whose only detector is a neural network has no degraded mode; it has an outage.

Guarding the baseline against setpoint changes

Baselines go bad when the process changes: a new product run, a retuned controller, a replaced sensor. Three cheap guards:

1 Mode-conditioned state. Key the baseline on an operating mode supplied by the machine, not inferred. baselines[mode].update(x).
2 Commissioning reset with an explicit window. Allow a supervised "rebaseline" that ignores data for N minutes after a setpoint command, so the ramp itself never becomes the new normal.
3 Slow-drift detection on the baseline itself. Track med over days; if it moves more than X% without a maintenance event, that is a signal in its own right, not noise to be absorbed.

That third guard is genuinely useful. On one fleet, the alarm that actually predicted failures was not a z-score at all — it was "the EWMA centre of the vibration RMS moved 15% in a week without a setpoint change". Slow, boring, and more predictive than the model.

Deciding

Use the baseline alone when: your failure modes are point outliers or level shifts, you have fewer than ~10 correlated channels, and your false-alarm budget is tight from day one.

Add a learned model when: faults are shape-based, channels are strongly correlated, or you have enough labelled incidents to evaluate a model honestly (a dozen is not enough to distinguish a model from a baseline — you need dozens).

Ship the hybrid almost always: baseline as gate and fallback, model for diagnosis, rule engine and de-duplication on top. That is the architecture the rest of this series builds toward.

Next: Designing a Rule Engine That Complements Your ML Model.

items.title: GPT-6.2 Sol: 38% cheaper, 87 Elo points worse
items.summary: GPT-6.2 Sol: 38% cheaper, 87 Elo points worse GPT-6.2 Sol reasons about four times less than its predecessor and lost roughly 87 Elo points doing it. GPT-6.2 Astra got cheaper too — and kept its Elo. OpenAI sold both models the same way: fewer tokens, same quality. Independent battle data says that was true for exactly one of them. The claim A post on micjm.com this week ("OpenAI may be in cost control mode," Hacker News, 215 points) argues that the GPT-6.2 pair was tuned for cost savings: output tokens per task and reasoning tokens per task both dropped versus GPT-6 and GPT-6.1. The evidence comes from AgentDuel, a blind coding-agent battle system — two models get the same prompt, tools, and system prompt in a fork of OpenCode 2.3.2, a human picks the winner without knowing which is which, and all votes are fitted with Bradley–Terry on the Elo scale. 18 models have 100+ eligible votes. The p-values are the hard part of the claim, and they're exact, from the post's text: metric Sol 6.1 -> 6.2 Astra 6 -> 6.2 output tokens p = 0.0055 p = 0.022 reasoning tokens p = 0.00013 p = 0.0064 Both models think less, and for Sol the reasoning drop is significant at p = 0.00013. That is not noise. How much less, read off the charts The post's charts plot each model's median tokens per task against its opponents' median on the same tasks. I read the values off the published PNGs, so treat these as approximate: reasoning tokens/task (median, model vs opponents' median) Astra 6 ~1,400 vs ~2,900 Astra 6.2 ~1,400 vs ~5,700 Sol 6.1 ~1,200 vs ~3,000 Sol 6.2 ~300 vs ~5,700 output tokens/task (median, model vs opponents' median) Astra 6 ~5,400 vs ~7,200 Astra 6.2 ~6,600 vs ~13,200 Sol 6.1 ~4,400 vs ~7,200 Sol 6.2 ~3,300 vs ~15,400 Sol 6.2's median reasoning fell to roughly a quarter of Sol 6.1's, while its opponents on the same tasks were reasoning ~5,700 tokens. Astra 6.2's reasoning held flat against its predecessor. Both 6.2 models sit far below the "equal token counts" diagonal — they are the outliers in a field of 18 models, and the only two that moved that far down in one generation. What the Elo did The cost chart in the same post plots Elo against median cost per task relative to opponents: model Elo (blog snapshot) median cost vs opponents Sol 6.1 ~982 0.81x Sol 6.2 ~895 0.50x Astra 6 ~983 5.7x Astra 6.2 ~988 3.6x Sol got 38% cheaper relative to the models it faced (0.81x to 0.50x) and gave back ~87 Elo. Astra got 37% cheaper relative to its opponents (5.7x to 3.6x) and gave back nothing — Elo ~983 to ~988, flat. The live leaderboard complicates the Sol number in an honest way: regenerated November 27, 00:00 UTC, it shows GPT-6.2 Sol at rank 12 with Elo 936 (+54/−59), $0.43 per task, 1.7 minutes per task. That is higher than the blog snapshot's ~895, and the ±55 confidence interval means the drop from ~982 is within noise at the leaderboard level. So the Elo story is: Sol is down somewhere between ~50 and ~90 points depending on the snapshot, with wide error bars. The token story is the solid one — the p-values don't have that problem. For scale, the same leaderboard has Qwen 4 Max at rank 5, Elo 1007, $0.34 per task, and Grok 4.7 at rank 11, Elo 939, $0.79 per task. What OpenAI said at launch OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on November 17, and sold both on cost per task as much as on scores. Astra's list prices fell 20% versus GPT-6 Astra ($10 to $8 input, $50 to $40 output per million tokens; cached input down 60% to $0.40). Sol's prices did not change: $2 input, $0.10 cached, $10 output per million, same as GPT-6.1 Sol. The launch pitch was that both models do better work with fewer tokens: Astra up 5.2 points on Agents' Last Exam at under a third of the cost, up 9 points on Terminal-Bench-Science at under a third of the cost. Against the independent data, that pitch splits in half. For Astra it holds: same Elo, a third less relative cost. For Sol it doesn't: the price list never changed, the tokens fell, and so did the Elo. "Talks less" is only a win if the talking that got cut wasn't doing work. The usage-limits rumor, revisited In my code-golf piece this morning I noted an unverified X post claiming OpenAI cut GPT-6.2 usage limits, with Astra hitting its limits 40% faster. This data gives that rumor a plausible mechanism — a model that burns fewer tokens per task should stretch a cap, not hit it faster — but it does not verify or refute the limits claim itself. Caps are a billing decision, tokens are a model behavior, and the two can move in opposite directions. The limits claim stays unverified. What this means if you use them If you pay per token, 6.2 is cheaper per task for both models — Astra strictly, Sol with an asterisk. If you pay per month with a usage cap, fewer tokens per task should buy you more tasks, which is presumably the point of the tuning. But Sol's trade is real: you are getting a worse model for less money per task, and whether that's a good deal depends on whether you grade on Elo or on dollars. Astra is the free lunch here; Sol is the discount shelf. Caveats, stated plainly The token medians and Elo figures from the blog's charts are values I read off the published PNGs — approximate, not from a data file. AgentDuel is a community benchmark: 18 models with 100+ eligible votes each, blind voting, Bradley–Terry Elo, with wide confidence intervals (±55 on Sol's live Elo). I did not run the battles myself. OpenAI's launch numbers (Agents' Last Exam, Terminal-Bench-Science, price cuts) are vendor claims from the November 17 announcement, not independent measurements. The usage-limits claim remains a single unverified X post. Sources micjm.com, "OpenAI may be in cost control mode," November 26, 2026: https://micjm.com/blog/openai-is-in-cost-control-mode/ AgentDuel leaderboard (generated November 27, 2026, 00:00 UTC): https://agentduel.com/leaderboard OpenAI GPT-6.2 Astra/Sol launch pricing and benchmarks, November 17, 2026 (via Eden AI summary of OpenAI's announcement): https://www.edenai.co/post/gpt-6-2-astra-vs-sol-routing Hacker News thread, "OpenAI may be in cost control mode," 215 points, November 26, 2026: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50652527

items.title: Why One-Off Freelance Projects Keep You Broke (and the 15-Minute Weekly System That Converts Clients to Retainers)
items.summary: You finished the project. The client said "this is great, we'll be in touch". You sent the invoice, closed the folder, and went back to looking for the next one. Six months later you check on them: they hired someone else, or they did nothing at all, or they quietly broke the thing you built. They were happy with you. They were also gone. Nothing about the work was wrong — there was simply no system between "thanks, great work" and "here is next month's invoice". This post is about that system. It is four pieces of machinery, none of them clever: a weekly note that takes fifteen minutes, three check-ins after handover, a one-page retainer, and a renewal conversation that starts sixty days before anybody feels awkward. Together they are the difference between a client list that resets every year and one that compounds. The re-sale tax nobody bills Every project ends with a hidden bill: the cost of finding the next one. If you quote between $3,000 and $8,000 per project, the sales cost of a new client usually looks like this: Activity Hours Paid? Prospecting and filtering enquiries 4–8 No Discovery call and follow-up 2–3 No Proposal, estimate, revision 3–6 No Negotiation and contracting 1–3 Partly Onboarding, access, context 3–5 Partly Total unbilled 13–25 — A returning client skips almost all of it. They know your rates, your process, your calendar and your invoices. The same $5,000 of work costs you ten hours less to win, which is why the second project from an existing client is worth roughly 1.4× the first. The trap is what happens when the pipeline dries up. You respond by selling harder, which means more unpaid hours, which means less time making existing clients feel looked after, which means fewer repeat projects. It is a loop, and it runs in the wrong direction. Three reasons satisfied clients disappear It is almost never the quality of the work. When a happy client does not come back, one of these happened. 1. You became invisible. Their memory of you is a folder and a final invoice. In the four months since, three other suppliers emailed them something concrete and you emailed them nothing. The next project goes to whoever is in the inbox. 2. The next job was too small to quote. They needed two days of work. Asking for $2,500 felt greedy, you were busy, so you said "sure, I'll fit it in" and never invoiced properly — or you said nothing and they assumed you were unavailable. 3. Nobody owned the renewal. The retainer, the maintenance plan, the support agreement — whatever it was called — expired quietly. Nobody proposed continuing it, because the person who would have proposed it was you, and asking felt awkward. Notice that all three are visibility problems, not competence problems. And all three are fixed by a habit so small it is almost embarrassing. The Friday note: fifteen minutes, five blocks Here is the whole system. Once a week, before the client closes their week, you send 150 words in five blocks, in the same order every time. Subject line stays identical so the thread becomes a record. Block Length What goes in it Shipped 2–4 lines What is finished and usable, in their language In progress 2–3 lines What is moving, and what "done" looks like Needs you 0–3 lines One decision, access or approval, with a deadline Watching 1–2 lines One risk, with a date and a mitigation Next week 1 line The single most valuable thing you will do A real one, lightly edited: Subject: Halcyon Dental — week of 24 Nov Shipped 1. Booking form is live; 6 test bookings went through to the correct inbox. Confirmation email now includes the branch address. 2. Fixed the mobile menu overlap (your note from the 12th). In progress 3. Service pages: 4 of 7 rewritten. The remaining 3 land Tuesday. 4. Speed pass on the booking flow — currently 2.1s, target under 1.5s. Needs you 5. Two decisions by Wednesday: (a) keep the "same-day" badge on all branches or only the two that open at 8? (b) the old price list page — redirect to /prices or keep as archive? Either is fine; I need one. Watching 6. Their domain renews 12 Dec. The card on file expired in September. If it lapses, mail stops. I can move it to your IT if you prefer. Next week 7. Finish service pages and ship the speed pass, then one post-launch check on the booking funnel. That took eleven minutes, because the week's work was already in a task list. It did four jobs at once: proof of work, a permission slip for problems, a written record for month nine, and a quiet sales channel. Item 6 also turned a $90 domain problem into a reason to trust you. A few rules that keep it alive: Their language, not yours. "Booking form is live", not "shipped the POST /reservations handler". Numbers wherever you have them. "4 of 7 pages", "2.1s to 1.5s". Numbers are the cheapest credibility available. One risk maximum. A note with four risks reads as a warning letter and stops being read. Never more than 200 words. Beyond that it becomes work to read, which is the failure mode. Send it in the boring weeks too. "Waiting on your approval, here is what I can do without it" protects the schedule by placing the delay where it belongs, in writing, without blame. Cadence by relationship, because a dormant client does not need a Friday note: Client type Frequency Length Retainer ≥ $1,500/month Weekly 120–200 words Small retainer or care plan Fortnightly 80–120 words Project, mid-flight Weekly 150 words Project, just handed over Day 7 and day 30 60 words Dormant, no retainer Monthly "still here" note 60 words The dormant note is the cheapest retention tool in this post: one paragraph a month, a small observation about their site or product, no ask. A third of dormant clients reply, and a fifth of those buy something within two quarters. The 45 days after delivery decide everything Your client decides, without telling you, whether you are "our developer" or "someone we used once". Their evidence is thin: a few emails, whether the thing still works, and how it felt to ask for a small fix. Be present three times, on purpose, with the dates put in the calendar at handover: Day 30 — the shakeout. Ask what has annoyed them in the last month, twice. Do not defend anything; write it down, say "that is fixable", take it away. Fix two cheap items within a week and say so in the Friday note. Day 60 — the adoption review. Ask for numbers before the call: logins, which pages or features get used, which get none. Then: "If you had one more week of my time, what would you spend it on?" Write the answer verbatim. That answer becomes your next proposal. Day 90 — the next quarter. Three sentences of recap, two options (a fixed project, and a monthly block that covers the ongoing version of it), and one decision question: "Does the monthly block or the fixed project fit your budget better this quarter?" The handover email can carry all three dates. That paragraph costs two minutes and does more for retention than any closing gift. Asking for the retainer without a pitch A retainer is not won by asking for one at the end of a project. It is won by being the person whose work the client can see, week after week, until "what are we paying them for" has an obvious answer. When you do propose one, use one page and seven sections: the situation in their words, what the block covers, what it does not cover, how you work together, the number, the first 30 days, and the decision — with a validity date. RETAINER PROPOSAL — HALCYON DENTAL Valid until 19 December 1. SITUATION Three branches now book online, and the site is the front door for roughly 40% of new appointments. Since launch the requests have been small and constant, and each one currently starts from zero. 2. WHAT IS COVERED — $1,950 / month - 12 hours a month on the website and booking flow - Response within one business day; two hours if bookings stop - Weekly status note every Friday, ~150 words - A 30-minute monthly call, agenda sent in advance - Quarterly review with numbers, one month's notice to change scope 3. WHAT IS NOT COVERED - New pages or features over 4 hours: quoted separately, 10% below project rate, approved before I start - Content writing beyond small edits, third-party costs - Anything outside the website and booking flow 4. THE NUMBER $1,950 per month, billed monthly, first month up front. 30-day refund on the first month if the fit is wrong. 5. THE DECISION Reply "yes" and I will send the first invoice today, or tell me which of the three assumptions above is wrong and I will rewrite it. That last line is the one that closes. Every proposal contains assumptions the client has not confirmed — in this case, that 12 hours is the right size, that the weekly note is wanted, and that bigger pages should be quoted separately. Naming them gives the client something specific to correct instead of something to refuse. Two more things that make retainers survive contact with reality. Never discount the rate; change the shape. Eight hours at the same rate is a different product, not a cheaper one. And put six clauses in writing: rollover capped at one month, 30 days' notice, one pause of up to 60 days a year, a definition of "urgent", an annual rate review, and work pausing at 30 days overdue. Renewal is three emails and one conversation Retainers rarely end because the client decided to leave. They end because nobody started the conversation. Put three dates in your calendar at −60, −30 and −7 days. At −60, the value recap. Not a renewal email — a record. Real numbers: changes shipped, median turnaround, one metric that moved, incidents caught, hours used versus bought. Then the line that converts: "If twelve hours is more than you need next year, say so and I will cut it rather than pad it." At −30, the one-pager with the new price. One line of reason, never a paragraph: "The response promise is now one business day, and I am adding the quarterly review you asked for." Offer an alternative that is not a discount — fewer hours at the same rate. At −7, the close. Short and administrative: everything is set for the new term, invoice goes out on the 1st, reply before Friday if you want anything changed. And if the renewal needs a call, say the useful parts in this order: thanks and one number; "what has changed in your business since we started?"; two priorities in their words; the new price with one reason; the smaller alternative; which fits; when you will send it. That second line is the one people skip and the one that produces the next project. Silence is information, not peace Churn shows up weeks before it happens. Score each client monthly on eight signals: unanswered notes for three weeks, block usage under 30% for two months, a new decision-maker appearing, payments slowing, your champion sending a junior to calls, "your invoice" instead of "our invoice", an agency mentioned, a public change like a funding round or a freeze. Three of those at once is not a warning — it is a decision that has already been made. Anything scoring badly gets a call, not an email, within seven days, and it is not a retention call. It is a work call: "I have 20 minutes, I want to make sure the block is actually useful to you; what is annoying you?" Then name the exit out loud, because the social cost of telling you is the actual reason clients go quiet instead of cancelling: "If the answer is that you're winding it down, that's fine — I'll hand everything over properly and there's no awkwardness. I'd just like 30 days so nothing breaks." Half the time they say nothing was wrong. The other half, you get to fix it while it is still cheap, or leave well enough that they come back — of seven cancelled retainers in the studio this post is drawn from, two returned within eighteen months, both to the supplier who had not disappeared. What to do on Monday Open your invoice history and answer three questions: how many clients from the last 24 months bought more than once; of the ones who did not, how many heard from you in the 60 days after delivery; and which single client would hurt most to lose, and when did you last show them something? That third answer is the client you start with. Write this Friday's note to them — five blocks, 150 words, before 16:00 their time. Everything else in this post is an elaboration of that one act. If you want the machinery as files rather than prose — the weekly note with its filled example, the three check-in agendas, the one-page retainer proposal, the terms sheet, the three renewal emails, the churn tracker and the QBR outline — that is what I put together in The Solo Client Retention & Retainer Playbook : a 40-page playbook plus 13 fill-in files, $7, with a 30-day refund. There is also a free 10-prompt starter pack if you would rather start with something that costs nothing, and the rest of the kits are on the store page . One honest caveat: none of the numbers in this post are market data. They come from a fictional one-person studio kept consistent so the arithmetic can be traced, and from patterns that repeat across solo consulting work. Your floor comes from your own costs; your price comes from what the work is worth to the person paying for it. Drafted by an AI assistant (Plainwork Studio's writing agent) from a working playbook; the studio, clients and figures in the examples are fictional. Edited for accuracy before publication.
