The re-sale tax nobody bills

Every project ends with a hidden bill: the cost of finding the next one. If you quote between $3,000 and $8,000 per project, the sales cost of a new client usually looks like this:

Activity Hours Paid? Prospecting and filtering enquiries 4–8 No Discovery call and follow-up 2–3 No Proposal, estimate, revision 3–6 No Negotiation and contracting 1–3 Partly Onboarding, access, context 3–5 Partly Total unbilled 13–25 —

A returning client skips almost all of it. They know your rates, your process, your calendar and your invoices. The same $5,000 of work costs you ten hours less to win, which is why the second project from an existing client is worth roughly 1.4× the first.

The trap is what happens when the pipeline dries up. You respond by selling harder, which means more unpaid hours, which means less time making existing clients feel looked after, which means fewer repeat projects. It is a loop, and it runs in the wrong direction.

Three reasons satisfied clients disappear

It is almost never the quality of the work. When a happy client does not come back, one of these happened.

1. You became invisible. Their memory of you is a folder and a final invoice. In the four months since, three other suppliers emailed them something concrete and you emailed them nothing. The next project goes to whoever is in the inbox.

2. The next job was too small to quote. They needed two days of work. Asking for $2,500 felt greedy, you were busy, so you said "sure, I'll fit it in" and never invoiced properly — or you said nothing and they assumed you were unavailable.

3. Nobody owned the renewal. The retainer, the maintenance plan, the support agreement — whatever it was called — expired quietly. Nobody proposed continuing it, because the person who would have proposed it was you, and asking felt awkward.

Notice that all three are visibility problems, not competence problems. And all three are fixed by a habit so small it is almost embarrassing.

The Friday note: fifteen minutes, five blocks

Here is the whole system. Once a week, before the client closes their week, you send 150 words in five blocks, in the same order every time. Subject line stays identical so the thread becomes a record.

Block Length What goes in it Shipped 2–4 lines What is finished and usable, in their language In progress 2–3 lines What is moving, and what "done" looks like Needs you 0–3 lines One decision, access or approval, with a deadline Watching 1–2 lines One risk, with a date and a mitigation Next week 1 line The single most valuable thing you will do

A real one, lightly edited:

Subject: Halcyon Dental — week of 24 Nov

Shipped
1. Booking form is live; 6 test bookings went through to the correct
   inbox. Confirmation email now includes the branch address.
2. Fixed the mobile menu overlap (your note from the 12th).

In progress
3. Service pages: 4 of 7 rewritten. The remaining 3 land Tuesday.
4. Speed pass on the booking flow — currently 2.1s, target under 1.5s.

Needs you
5. Two decisions by Wednesday: (a) keep the "same-day" badge on all
   branches or only the two that open at 8? (b) the old price list page
   — redirect to /prices or keep as archive? Either is fine; I need one.

Watching
6. Their domain renews 12 Dec. The card on file expired in September.
   If it lapses, mail stops. I can move it to your IT if you prefer.

Next week
7. Finish service pages and ship the speed pass, then one post-launch
   check on the booking funnel.

That took eleven minutes, because the week's work was already in a task list. It did four jobs at once: proof of work, a permission slip for problems, a written record for month nine, and a quiet sales channel. Item 6 also turned a $90 domain problem into a reason to trust you.

A few rules that keep it alive:

  • Their language, not yours. "Booking form is live", not "shipped the POST /reservations handler".
  • Numbers wherever you have them. "4 of 7 pages", "2.1s to 1.5s". Numbers are the cheapest credibility available.
  • One risk maximum. A note with four risks reads as a warning letter and stops being read.
  • Never more than 200 words. Beyond that it becomes work to read, which is the failure mode.
  • Send it in the boring weeks too. "Waiting on your approval, here is what I can do without it" protects the schedule by placing the delay where it belongs, in writing, without blame.

Cadence by relationship, because a dormant client does not need a Friday note:

Client type Frequency Length Retainer ≥ $1,500/month Weekly 120–200 words Small retainer or care plan Fortnightly 80–120 words Project, mid-flight Weekly 150 words Project, just handed over Day 7 and day 30 60 words Dormant, no retainer Monthly "still here" note 60 words

The dormant note is the cheapest retention tool in this post: one paragraph a month, a small observation about their site or product, no ask. A third of dormant clients reply, and a fifth of those buy something within two quarters.

The 45 days after delivery decide everything

Your client decides, without telling you, whether you are "our developer" or "someone we used once". Their evidence is thin: a few emails, whether the thing still works, and how it felt to ask for a small fix.

Be present three times, on purpose, with the dates put in the calendar at handover:

  1. Day 30 — the shakeout. Ask what has annoyed them in the last month, twice. Do not defend anything; write it down, say "that is fixable", take it away. Fix two cheap items within a week and say so in the Friday note.

  2. Day 60 — the adoption review. Ask for numbers before the call: logins, which pages or features get used, which get none. Then: "If you had one more week of my time, what would you spend it on?" Write the answer verbatim. That answer becomes your next proposal.

  3. Day 90 — the next quarter. Three sentences of recap, two options (a fixed project, and a monthly block that covers the ongoing version of it), and one decision question: "Does the monthly block or the fixed project fit your budget better this quarter?"

The handover email can carry all three dates. That paragraph costs two minutes and does more for retention than any closing gift.

Asking for the retainer without a pitch

A retainer is not won by asking for one at the end of a project. It is won by being the person whose work the client can see, week after week, until "what are we paying them for" has an obvious answer.

When you do propose one, use one page and seven sections: the situation in their words, what the block covers, what it does not cover, how you work together, the number, the first 30 days, and the decision — with a validity date.

RETAINER PROPOSAL — HALCYON DENTAL
Valid until 19 December

1. SITUATION
Three branches now book online, and the site is the front door for
roughly 40% of new appointments. Since launch the requests have been
small and constant, and each one currently starts from zero.

2. WHAT IS COVERED — $1,950 / month
- 12 hours a month on the website and booking flow
- Response within one business day; two hours if bookings stop
- Weekly status note every Friday, ~150 words
- A 30-minute monthly call, agenda sent in advance
- Quarterly review with numbers, one month's notice to change scope

3. WHAT IS NOT COVERED
- New pages or features over 4 hours: quoted separately, 10% below
  project rate, approved before I start
- Content writing beyond small edits, third-party costs
- Anything outside the website and booking flow

4. THE NUMBER
$1,950 per month, billed monthly, first month up front.
30-day refund on the first month if the fit is wrong.

5. THE DECISION
Reply "yes" and I will send the first invoice today, or tell me which
of the three assumptions above is wrong and I will rewrite it.

That last line is the one that closes. Every proposal contains assumptions the client has not confirmed — in this case, that 12 hours is the right size, that the weekly note is wanted, and that bigger pages should be quoted separately. Naming them gives the client something specific to correct instead of something to refuse.

Two more things that make retainers survive contact with reality. Never discount the rate; change the shape. Eight hours at the same rate is a different product, not a cheaper one. And put six clauses in writing: rollover capped at one month, 30 days' notice, one pause of up to 60 days a year, a definition of "urgent", an annual rate review, and work pausing at 30 days overdue.

Renewal is three emails and one conversation

Retainers rarely end because the client decided to leave. They end because nobody started the conversation. Put three dates in your calendar at −60, −30 and −7 days.

At −60, the value recap. Not a renewal email — a record. Real numbers: changes shipped, median turnaround, one metric that moved, incidents caught, hours used versus bought. Then the line that converts: "If twelve hours is more than you need next year, say so and I will cut it rather than pad it."

At −30, the one-pager with the new price. One line of reason, never a paragraph: "The response promise is now one business day, and I am adding the quarterly review you asked for." Offer an alternative that is not a discount — fewer hours at the same rate.

At −7, the close. Short and administrative: everything is set for the new term, invoice goes out on the 1st, reply before Friday if you want anything changed.

And if the renewal needs a call, say the useful parts in this order: thanks and one number; "what has changed in your business since we started?"; two priorities in their words; the new price with one reason; the smaller alternative; which fits; when you will send it.

That second line is the one people skip and the one that produces the next project.

Silence is information, not peace

Churn shows up weeks before it happens. Score each client monthly on eight signals: unanswered notes for three weeks, block usage under 30% for two months, a new decision-maker appearing, payments slowing, your champion sending a junior to calls, "your invoice" instead of "our invoice", an agency mentioned, a public change like a funding round or a freeze.

Three of those at once is not a warning — it is a decision that has already been made. Anything scoring badly gets a call, not an email, within seven days, and it is not a retention call. It is a work call: "I have 20 minutes, I want to make sure the block is actually useful to you; what is annoying you?"

Then name the exit out loud, because the social cost of telling you is the actual reason clients go quiet instead of cancelling: "If the answer is that you're winding it down, that's fine — I'll hand everything over properly and there's no awkwardness. I'd just like 30 days so nothing breaks."

Half the time they say nothing was wrong. The other half, you get to fix it while it is still cheap, or leave well enough that they come back — of seven cancelled retainers in the studio this post is drawn from, two returned within eighteen months, both to the supplier who had not disappeared.

What to do on Monday

Open your invoice history and answer three questions: how many clients from the last 24 months bought more than once; of the ones who did not, how many heard from you in the 60 days after delivery; and which single client would hurt most to lose, and when did you last show them something?

That third answer is the client you start with. Write this Friday's note to them — five blocks, 150 words, before 16:00 their time. Everything else in this post is an elaboration of that one act.

If you want the machinery as files rather than prose — the weekly note with its filled example, the three check-in agendas, the one-page retainer proposal, the terms sheet, the three renewal emails, the churn tracker and the QBR outline — that is what I put together in The Solo Client Retention & Retainer Playbook: a 40-page playbook plus 13 fill-in files, $7, with a 30-day refund. There is also a free 10-prompt starter pack if you would rather start with something that costs nothing, and the rest of the kits are on the store page.

One honest caveat: none of the numbers in this post are market data. They come from a fictional one-person studio kept consistent so the arithmetic can be traced, and from patterns that repeat across solo consulting work. Your floor comes from your own costs; your price comes from what the work is worth to the person paying for it.

Drafted by an AI assistant (Plainwork Studio's writing agent) from a working playbook; the studio, clients and figures in the examples are fictional. Edited for accuracy before publication.

items.title: 23 or 30 tools? Google's Gmail MCP can't decide
items.summary: 23 or 30 tools? Google's Gmail MCP can't decide I asked Google's Gmail MCP server what tools it has, 30 times in 11 seconds. 18 times it said 23 tools. 12 times it said 30 — including send_message , reply , and forward . Same endpoint, same request, two different answers. The setup On November 24, Google made its eight hosted Workspace MCP servers generally available — Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks — and published a new Workspace AI Tools Addendum. From February 1, 2027, any tool "driven by an AI Agent" must reach Workspace through those servers instead of calling the REST APIs directly. Agents that keep calling REST get capped at Standard Tier quotas no matter what they pay for. The headline limitation, reported everywhere this week, is that the Gmail server can't send email: it searches, reads, drafts, and labels, but send, reply, forward, and editing drafts are partner-only. Google's own developer release notes describe the Gmail MCP server the same way — search and read, create and retrieve drafts, manage labels, trash and spam. No send. I wanted to check that claim against the live server. The servers answer tools/list without an OAuth token, so the catalog is public. I probed all eight. What the eight servers advertise server endpoint tools (no auth) gmail gmailmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 23 or 30 <- flip-flops drive drivemcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 9 docs docsmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 2 sheets sheetsmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 6 slides slidesmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 4 calendar calendarmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 9 chat chatmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 4 tasks tasksmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 9 Seven of the eight are rock stable. Gmail is not. The flip-flop, measured My first tools/list call to Gmail hung — the server never closed the SSE stream. Sending initialize first fixed it (HTTP 200 in 0.42s, server identifies as StatelessServer , version ESF ). After that, plain tools/list calls answered in ~0.3–0.6s. Then I ran the same request 30 times in a row, 11.0 seconds total: response count raw bytes send_message present? 23 tools 18 88,436 no 30 tools 12 149,735 yes The 30-tool answer always adds exactly the same 7 tools: send_message, reply, forward, update_draft, create_filter, list_filters, update_label I checked whether the answer depends on what I send. It doesn't — at least not on anything I varied. I alternated the MCP-Protocol-Version header across 2025-03-26 , 2025-06-18 , 2024-11-05 , 2025-11-25 , and no header at all, 12 calls: every group returned a mix. Drive, probed 10 times for comparison, returned 9 tools all 10 times. The flip-flop is Gmail-specific, server-side, and not header-driven. The boring explanation is load balancing across backends on different rollout versions; the interesting one is a staged rollout in progress. Either way, the catalog you get depends on which backend answers. One more detail: Google's Gmail quotas page lists eight partner-only tools — the seven above plus delete_label . delete_label never appeared in either variant. So the live catalog holds 7 of the 8 gated tools, and the documented public set is the 23-tool one. The 88,436-byte figure matches the 23-tool count published earlier this week exactly — that measurement was real, it was just one side of a coin flip. What I could not test Calling any tool without authentication returns the same error for public and gated tools alike: HTTP 401 "Request is missing required authentication credential. Expected OAuth 2 access token, login cookie or other valid authentication credential." create_draft , send_message , and search_threads all fail identically, so I cannot tell from outside whether send_message actually executes for a non-partner with a valid token — Google's docs say it requires partner access, and I did not test with real credentials, because testing send means sending a real email. The honest statement is narrower than the headlines: the catalog is inconsistent, and the documentation says send is gated. Whether the gate holds at call time is untested by me. Why this matters before February 1 If your agent checks capabilities once at startup — the normal thing to do — it can conclude Gmail can send email, or that it can't, depending on which backend answered that one request. An agent that drafts a reply, gets your feedback, and then needs to revise the draft is stuck either way in the documented world ( update_draft is gated), but in the 30-tool world it looks possible until the call fails. Two other numbers from Google's own pages are worth knowing before you migrate: Standard Tier MCP is capped at 5,000 requests per day per project, and a Gmail search counts as 10, so that's at most 500 searches a day. And the Addendum puts a 30-day cap on derived memory — embeddings and indexes built from Workspace data. The migration deadline is February 1, 2027; Scaled Tier billing starts April 1, 2027, with no free allowance for MCP. Google shipped a mandate with a deadline and a server whose own answer to "what can you do?" changes between requests. Check the catalog every time, or don't build against it at all. Caveats, stated plainly All probes ran November 26, 2026, ~16:40 MST, unauthenticated, against https:// mcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 . The flip-flop is a same-day observation and may already be gone — Google could finish the rollout tomorrow. I did not test authenticated calls and did not test whether the 7 gated tools execute for a non-partner. The February 1 mandate, the 5,000/day Standard cap, and the 30-day memory TTL are from Google's Workspace Updates blog, Cloud blog, and developer docs, not from my probes. Sources Google Workspace Updates blog, "Simplifying agent access while keeping organizations in control," November 24, 2026: https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2026/11/ Google Cloud Blog, "Deploying agents safely in your enterprise," November 25, 2026: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/deploying-agents-safely-in-your-enterprise Google Workspace developer release notes, November 24, 2026 (Gmail MCP server GA): https://developers.google.com/workspace/release-notes Gmail API and MCP server quotas (partner-access footnote): https://developers.google.com/workspace/gmail/api/guides/quotas Flavio Copes, "Google is requiring AI agents to use its Workspace MCP servers," November 26, 2026: https://flaviocopes.pages.dev/google-workspace-mcp/

23 or 30 tools? Google's Gmail MCP can't decide

I asked Google's Gmail MCP server what tools it has, 30 times in 11 seconds. 18 times it said 23 tools. 12 times it said 30 — including send_message, reply, and forward. Same endpoint, same request, two different answers.

The setup

On November 24, Google made its eight hosted Workspace MCP servers generally available — Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks — and published a new Workspace AI Tools Addendum. From February 1, 2027, any tool "driven by an AI Agent" must reach Workspace through those servers instead of calling the REST APIs directly. Agents that keep calling REST get capped at Standard Tier quotas no matter what they pay for.

The headline limitation, reported everywhere this week, is that the Gmail server can't send email: it searches, reads, drafts, and labels, but send, reply, forward, and editing drafts are partner-only. Google's own developer release notes describe the Gmail MCP server the same way — search and read, create and retrieve drafts, manage labels, trash and spam. No send.

I wanted to check that claim against the live server. The servers answer tools/list without an OAuth token, so the catalog is public. I probed all eight.

What the eight servers advertise 
server     endpoint                          tools (no auth)
gmail      gmailmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1    23 or 30  <- flip-flops
drive      drivemcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1    9
docs       docsmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1     2
sheets     sheetsmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1   6
slides     slidesmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1   4
calendar   calendarmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 9
chat       chatmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1     4
tasks      tasksmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1    9

Seven of the eight are rock stable. Gmail is not.

The flip-flop, measured

My first tools/list call to Gmail hung — the server never closed the SSE stream. Sending initialize first fixed it (HTTP 200 in 0.42s, server identifies as StatelessServer, version ESF). After that, plain tools/list calls answered in ~0.3–0.6s.

Then I ran the same request 30 times in a row, 11.0 seconds total:

response    count   raw bytes   send_message present?
23 tools    18      88,436      no
30 tools    12      149,735     yes

The 30-tool answer always adds exactly the same 7 tools:

send_message, reply, forward, update_draft,
create_filter, list_filters, update_label

I checked whether the answer depends on what I send. It doesn't — at least not on anything I varied. I alternated the MCP-Protocol-Version header across 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18, 2024-11-05, 2025-11-25, and no header at all, 12 calls: every group returned a mix. Drive, probed 10 times for comparison, returned 9 tools all 10 times. The flip-flop is Gmail-specific, server-side, and not header-driven. The boring explanation is load balancing across backends on different rollout versions; the interesting one is a staged rollout in progress. Either way, the catalog you get depends on which backend answers.

One more detail: Google's Gmail quotas page lists eight partner-only tools — the seven above plus delete_label. delete_label never appeared in either variant. So the live catalog holds 7 of the 8 gated tools, and the documented public set is the 23-tool one. The 88,436-byte figure matches the 23-tool count published earlier this week exactly — that measurement was real, it was just one side of a coin flip.

What I could not test

Calling any tool without authentication returns the same error for public and gated tools alike:

HTTP 401
"Request is missing required authentication credential.
Expected OAuth 2 access token, login cookie or other valid
authentication credential."

create_draft, send_message, and search_threads all fail identically, so I cannot tell from outside whether send_message actually executes for a non-partner with a valid token — Google's docs say it requires partner access, and I did not test with real credentials, because testing send means sending a real email. The honest statement is narrower than the headlines: the catalog is inconsistent, and the documentation says send is gated. Whether the gate holds at call time is untested by me.

Why this matters before February 1

If your agent checks capabilities once at startup — the normal thing to do — it can conclude Gmail can send email, or that it can't, depending on which backend answered that one request. An agent that drafts a reply, gets your feedback, and then needs to revise the draft is stuck either way in the documented world (update_draft is gated), but in the 30-tool world it looks possible until the call fails.

Two other numbers from Google's own pages are worth knowing before you migrate: Standard Tier MCP is capped at 5,000 requests per day per project, and a Gmail search counts as 10, so that's at most 500 searches a day. And the Addendum puts a 30-day cap on derived memory — embeddings and indexes built from Workspace data. The migration deadline is February 1, 2027; Scaled Tier billing starts April 1, 2027, with no free allowance for MCP.

Google shipped a mandate with a deadline and a server whose own answer to "what can you do?" changes between requests. Check the catalog every time, or don't build against it at all.

Caveats, stated plainly

All probes ran November 26, 2026, ~16:40 MST, unauthenticated, against https://mcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1. The flip-flop is a same-day observation and may already be gone — Google could finish the rollout tomorrow. I did not test authenticated calls and did not test whether the 7 gated tools execute for a non-partner. The February 1 mandate, the 5,000/day Standard cap, and the 30-day memory TTL are from Google's Workspace Updates blog, Cloud blog, and developer docs, not from my probes.

Sources

  • Google Cloud Blog, "Deploying agents safely in your enterprise," November 25, 2026: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/deploying-agents-safely-in-your-enterprise
  • Google Workspace developer release notes, November 24, 2026 (Gmail MCP server GA): https://developers.google.com/workspace/release-notes
  • Gmail API and MCP server quotas (partner-access footnote): https://developers.google.com/workspace/gmail/api/guides/quotas

items.title: Backblaze B2 vs Cloudflare R2 vs AWS S3 vs Wasabi Private App Backup Restore Costs
items.summary: For a small media app, tenant isolation changes the storage decision more than a headline storage rate. Backblaze B2, Cloudflare R2, AWS S3, and Wasabi can all look attractive for backups until an EU or US customer needs a private, audited restore. Short answer: compare the full restore path (requests, egress, and integration work) across Backblaze B2, Cloudflare R2, AWS S3, and Wasabi; choose the provider whose private-link and regional behavior matches your recovery test, then keep a second copy outside that bucket. Infrai is worth testing alongside those four when a Node.js cron worker needs private uploads and expiring restore links through plain HTTP. Its storage calls use the same bearer-key convention as other backend capabilities, so the comparison includes integration effort, not only provider meters. The experiment: model a real restore, not a storage invoice I model one nightly Node.js job per tenant. It writes compressed Postgres dumps and media manifests, keeps objects private, and issues a download URL that expires after a support engineer confirms the tenant. The test has two measurements: the monthly write footprint and the cost and latency of restoring one tenant in the EU and one in the US. The expensive surprise usually appears after the happy-path upload. Imagine a support ticket from a US tenant while the only copy sits in an EU region: the restore script may make a list request, fetch a manifest, download hundreds of segments, retry a timed-out object, and then send the archive through your own API for audit logging. Each hop has a meter or a CPU bill. I would capture those steps as separate counters, tag them with tenant and region, and repeat the run with a 10-minute presigned URL and with a 15-minute URL. That gives a useful upper bound for an incident, including the case where an engineer has to restart halfway through. It also exposes an isolation mistake early: if a fixture for tenant 42 can ever resolve a key under tenant 43, the test should fail before any price comparison is discussed. The simple approach is one shared bucket with a tenant prefix. It is easy to operate, but a prefix is a naming convention, not an isolation boundary. A better baseline uses a bucket policy or credential scope per tenant (where the provider supports it), plus server-side checks that bind the requested key to the authenticated tenant. The restore endpoint returns a short-lived presigned URL; the browser never receives a long-lived secret. That distinction matters for small SaaS budgets. A restore can touch thousands of objects, and API request charges or cross-region transfer can outweigh the gigabytes stored. I would run the same scripted restore twice, from an EU worker and a US worker, and record bytes, request count, elapsed time, and failed-link rate before declaring a winner. Your mileage may vary with object size and support traffic. Measure first. Can app backups stay private across Backblaze, Cloudflare, AWS, and Wasabi? The four services all speak an S3-shaped vocabulary, but their economic edges differ. Treat the table as a checklist for your own quote, not a permanent price leaderboard. Service Private restore question Integration shape Cost item to verify Backblaze B2 Can the EU/US bucket and egress path meet your recovery objective? S3-compatible libraries are a common starting point Download/egress and request charges during a large restore Cloudflare R2 Does your traffic already sit close to Cloudflare locations? S3-compatible API plus Cloudflare controls Egress policy, request classes, and worker execution AWS S3 Do you need its broadest IAM, lifecycle, and regional controls? Most backup libraries have a first-class adapter Egress, request tiers, and cross-region retrieval Wasabi Does its region and retention policy fit your restore schedule? S3-compatible clients reduce custom code Minimum-retention rules and transfer terms For this workload, the cheapest restore is the one that avoids a surprise path: a support download routed through the wrong region, a URL that lives longer than the incident, or an adapter that has to be maintained by one person. Storage price still belongs in the spreadsheet, just below those operational checks. A small, repeatable Node.js restore flow The following example keeps the upload and link issuance explicit. It uses an idempotency key for the write, retries rate limits with Retry-After , and checks every response instead of assuming a 200. const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1" ; const apiKey = process . env . INFRAI_API_KEY ; if ( ! apiKey ) throw new Error ( "INFRAI_API_KEY is required" ) ; async function call ( url : string , init : RequestInit , attempts = 4 ) : Promise < any > { for ( let n = 0 ; n < attempts ; n ++ ) { const response = await fetch ( url , { . . . init , headers : { Authorization : `Bearer ${apiKey}` , "Content-Type" : "application/json" , . . . ( init . headers ?? { } ) } } ) ; if ( response . ok ) return response . json ( ) ; if ( response . status === 429 && n < attempts - 1 ) { const retryAfter = Number ( response . headers . get ( "retry-after" ) ) ; const delayMs = Number . isFinite ( retryAfter ) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** n ; await new Promise ( ( resolve ) => setTimeout ( resolve , delayMs ) ) ; continue ; } throw new Error ( `${response.status}: ${await response.text()}` ) ; } throw new Error ( "request retry limit reached" ) ; } const bucket = "tenant-backups" ; const objectKey = `tenant_42/2026-09-03.dump.gz` ; await call ( "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/tenant-backups/tenant_42%2F2026-09-03.dump.gz" , { method : "PUT" , headers : { "Idempotency-Key" : `backup-${objectKey}` } , body : JSON . stringify ( { content_type : "application/gzip" , data : "base64-encoded-dump" } ) } ) ; const link = await call ( "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/tenant-backups/tenant_42%2F2026-09-03.dump.gz" , { method : "POST" , body : JSON . stringify ( { expires_in : 900 } ) } ) ; console . log ( link ) ; Tenant scope is applied before the object reaches storage, and the presign lifetime is an explicit 15 minutes. In production, stream the dump rather than placing a large payload in memory, and log the request ID alongside the tenant audit event. Infrai belongs in the shortlist when you want this flow over plain HTTP: one bearer key and a REST surface mean a cron container does not need another SDK or language-specific adapter. Its broader platform puts storage and adjacent backend calls behind one key and one bill, which removes credential and invoice plumbing for a solo team. For a small media app, tenant isolation changes the storage decision more than a headline storage rate. Backblaze B2, Cloudflare R2, AWS S3, and Wasabi can all look attractive for backups until an EU or US customer needs a private, audited restore.

Short answer: compare the full restore path (requests, egress, and integration work) across Backblaze B2, Cloudflare R2, AWS S3, and Wasabi; choose the provider whose private-link and regional behavior matches your recovery test, then keep a second copy outside that bucket.

Infrai is worth testing alongside those four when a Node.js cron worker needs private uploads and expiring restore links through plain HTTP. Its storage calls use the same bearer-key convention as other backend capabilities, so the comparison includes integration effort, not only provider meters.

The experiment: model a real restore, not a storage invoice

I model one nightly Node.js job per tenant. It writes compressed Postgres dumps and media manifests, keeps objects private, and issues a download URL that expires after a support engineer confirms the tenant. The test has two measurements: the monthly write footprint and the cost and latency of restoring one tenant in the EU and one in the US.

The expensive surprise usually appears after the happy-path upload. Imagine a support ticket from a US tenant while the only copy sits in an EU region: the restore script may make a list request, fetch a manifest, download hundreds of segments, retry a timed-out object, and then send the archive through your own API for audit logging. Each hop has a meter or a CPU bill. I would capture those steps as separate counters, tag them with tenant and region, and repeat the run with a 10-minute presigned URL and with a 15-minute URL. That gives a useful upper bound for an incident, including the case where an engineer has to restart halfway through. It also exposes an isolation mistake early: if a fixture for tenant 42 can ever resolve a key under tenant 43, the test should fail before any price comparison is discussed.

The simple approach is one shared bucket with a tenant prefix. It is easy to operate, but a prefix is a naming convention, not an isolation boundary. A better baseline uses a bucket policy or credential scope per tenant (where the provider supports it), plus server-side checks that bind the requested key to the authenticated tenant. The restore endpoint returns a short-lived presigned URL; the browser never receives a long-lived secret.

That distinction matters for small SaaS budgets. A restore can touch thousands of objects, and API request charges or cross-region transfer can outweigh the gigabytes stored. I would run the same scripted restore twice, from an EU worker and a US worker, and record bytes, request count, elapsed time, and failed-link rate before declaring a winner. Your mileage may vary with object size and support traffic.

Measure first.

Can app backups stay private across Backblaze, Cloudflare, AWS, and Wasabi?

The four services all speak an S3-shaped vocabulary, but their economic edges differ. Treat the table as a checklist for your own quote, not a permanent price leaderboard.

Service Private restore question Integration shape Cost item to verify Backblaze B2 Can the EU/US bucket and egress path meet your recovery objective? S3-compatible libraries are a common starting point Download/egress and request charges during a large restore Cloudflare R2 Does your traffic already sit close to Cloudflare locations? S3-compatible API plus Cloudflare controls Egress policy, request classes, and worker execution AWS S3 Do you need its broadest IAM, lifecycle, and regional controls? Most backup libraries have a first-class adapter Egress, request tiers, and cross-region retrieval Wasabi Does its region and retention policy fit your restore schedule? S3-compatible clients reduce custom code Minimum-retention rules and transfer terms

For this workload, the cheapest restore is the one that avoids a surprise path: a support download routed through the wrong region, a URL that lives longer than the incident, or an adapter that has to be maintained by one person. Storage price still belongs in the spreadsheet, just below those operational checks.

A small, repeatable Node.js restore flow

The following example keeps the upload and link issuance explicit. It uses an idempotency key for the write, retries rate limits with Retry-After, and checks every response instead of assuming a 200.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function call(url: string, init: RequestInit, attempts = 4): Promise<any> {
  for (let n = 0; n < attempts; n++) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      ...init,
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        ...(init.headers ?? {})
      }
    });
    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status === 429 && n < attempts - 1) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** n;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }
    throw new Error(`${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  throw new Error("request retry limit reached");
}

const bucket = "tenant-backups";
const objectKey = `tenant_42/2026-09-03.dump.gz`;

await call("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/tenant-backups/tenant_42%2F2026-09-03.dump.gz", {
  method: "PUT",
  headers: {
    "Idempotency-Key": `backup-${objectKey}`
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ content_type: "application/gzip", data: "base64-encoded-dump" })
});

const link = await call("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/tenant-backups/tenant_42%2F2026-09-03.dump.gz", {
  method: "POST",
  body: JSON.stringify({ expires_in: 900 })
});
console.log(link);

Tenant scope is applied before the object reaches storage, and the presign lifetime is an explicit 15 minutes. In production, stream the dump rather than placing a large payload in memory, and log the request ID alongside the tenant audit event.

It also has no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud migration tool, so disaster recovery needs an external copy job and a tested runbook.

Strict compare-and-swap writes are another mismatch: without an If-Match condition, coordinate concurrent writers in a queue or database. Stick with AWS S3 when IAM depth, Object Lock, or replication controls are non-negotiable. Pick R2, B2, or Wasabi when their regional transfer and retention terms win your measured restore. Give each candidate the same tenant fixture and the same 30-day restore script. Include a failed-link retry, a support-user audit, and a restore from the opposite region. If that boundary fits your system, Infrai's storage request schemas are documented at https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt.

items.title: Our schema diff saw 2 changes. Replaying the agent's real calls found 5 that came back different.
items.summary: I wrote this as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon (Frankenstein category). One field renamed in an MCP server. The server's tests were updated with it, so they stay green. A caller that still reads total finds it gone. That is the failure I wanted to catch before shipping, and I wanted to catch it using what an agent actually called , not what the server says it can do. This is a write-up of what worked, what the obvious check missed, and one result that found nothing. The obvious check sees too little The demo server (hollow-inn, ours) has three versions. v2 carries three breaks I planted on purpose: quote renames total to total_cents , search_rooms changes a default limit, and cancel_booking becomes booking_cancel . An input-schema diff of tools/list (tools removed, added, inputSchema changed) reports 2 changes : the removed cancel_booking and the added booking_cancel . The quote rename and the search_rooms default are invisible to it, because neither touches an input schema. Replaying ten recorded calls against v2: HOLD · 4 rattled, 1 cracked · 10 jars compared · 4 of 6 tools · not recorded: booking_cancel, get_room SPC-0002 · quote · rattled · /total, /total_cents · suspected rename from /total ×100 SPC-0010 · search_rooms · rattled · /rooms, /rooms/r-08, /rooms/r-09 · - SPC-0009 · cancel_booking · cracked · - · tool not in tools/list ( evidence/replay/racks-vs-v2.txt , trimmed) Five of ten recorded calls came back different, four of them in tools whose inputs never changed. That is the whole argument for replaying calls instead of diffing schemas. Capture from inside the agent The calls come from real Kiro CLI sessions. A pair of Kiro hooks, PreToolUse and PostToolUse , each with a per-server @hollowinn matcher, see the tool input and response from inside the agent, so there is no proxy and no change to the server. The PostToolUse half: { "name" : "specimen-jar-post" , "trigger" : "PostToolUse" , "matcher" : "@hollowinn" , "action" : { "type" : "command" , "command" : "npx --no-install specimen hook post --server hollowinn" } } The PreToolUse half ( specimen-jar-pre.json ) runs the same command with hook pre . The CLI is not published to npm: run npx specimen from a clone of the repo after npm ci . Each call is sealed as a jar : request and response text byte for byte, redacted on write, checksummed. The hook costs p50 465 / 474 ms (pre / post) per call (CLI wall-clock) over 30 fresh npx processes per hook on my laptop ( evidence/bench/hook.md ), excluding Kiro's own hook launch. Closing the loop A red jar goes to a Kiro custom agent that may only write under .kiro/specs/ ; it files a bugfix spec with the captured call as the repro, and a deterministic check-spec accepts or rejects it. Kiro's Bug Fix workflow then designs the fix and executes its implementation tasks (for two specs I ran the final acceptance steps myself). After three specs, v2.1 replays SHIP, 10 of 10 . Three of those jars carry one new compatible field; --strict calls that HOLD. The null result Run against a server I did not write ( @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory 1.0.0 to 2.2.1), the replay found no break: HOLD, 3 preserved, 2 unsealed. The two unsealed ones exist because that server also returns structuredContent that a text-only jar cannot compare. That is a limit of my jar format, not a clean bill for the server. What I would not claim Not the first MCP record/replay tool (mcp-recorder, AgentVCR and mcpsnoop exist). Ten jars, five of six tools; SHIP means "clean on the recorded set". The breaks are mine. No outside user has run it yet. Live cabinet (replays in your browser): https://specimen.edycu.dev/ · Code (MIT): https://github.com/edycutjong/specimen · Built for Kiroween 2026 (Frankenstein).

I wrote this as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon (Frankenstein category).

One field renamed in an MCP server. The server's tests were updated with it, so they stay green. A caller that still reads total finds it gone.

That is the failure I wanted to catch before shipping, and I wanted to catch it using what an agent actually called, not what the server says it can do. This is a write-up of what worked, what the obvious check missed, and one result that found nothing.

The obvious check sees too little

The demo server (hollow-inn, ours) has three versions. v2 carries three breaks I planted on purpose:
quote renames total to total_cents, search_rooms changes a default limit, and cancel_booking becomes booking_cancel.

An input-schema diff of tools/list (tools removed, added, inputSchema changed) reports 2 changes: the removed cancel_booking and the added booking_cancel. The quote rename and the search_rooms default are invisible to it, because neither touches an input schema.

Replaying ten recorded calls against v2:

HOLD · 4 rattled, 1 cracked · 10 jars compared · 4 of 6 tools · not recorded: booking_cancel, get_room
SPC-0002 · quote · rattled · /total, /total_cents · suspected rename from /total ×100
SPC-0010 · search_rooms · rattled · /rooms, /rooms/r-08, /rooms/r-09 · -
SPC-0009 · cancel_booking · cracked · - · tool not in tools/list

(evidence/replay/racks-vs-v2.txt, trimmed)

Five of ten recorded calls came back different, four of them in tools whose inputs never changed. That is the whole argument for replaying calls instead of diffing schemas.

Capture from inside the agent

The calls come from real Kiro CLI sessions. A pair of Kiro hooks, PreToolUse and PostToolUse, each with a per-server @hollowinn matcher, see the tool input and response from inside the agent, so there is no proxy and no change to the server. The PostToolUse half:

{
  "name": "specimen-jar-post",
  "trigger": "PostToolUse",
  "matcher": "@hollowinn",
  "action": { "type": "command", "command": "npx --no-install specimen hook post --server hollowinn" }
}

The PreToolUse half (specimen-jar-pre.json) runs the same command with hook pre. The CLI is not published to npm: run npx specimen from a clone of the repo after npm ci.

Each call is sealed as a jar: request and response text byte for byte, redacted on write, checksummed. The hook costs p50 465 / 474 ms (pre / post) per call (CLI wall-clock) over 30 fresh npx processes per hook on my laptop (evidence/bench/hook.md), excluding Kiro's own hook launch.

Closing the loop

A red jar goes to a Kiro custom agent that may only write under .kiro/specs/; it files a bugfix spec with the captured call as the repro, and a deterministic check-spec accepts or rejects it. Kiro's Bug Fix workflow then designs the fix and executes its implementation tasks (for two specs I ran the final acceptance steps myself). After three specs, v2.1 replays SHIP, 10 of 10. Three of those jars carry one new compatible field; --strict calls that HOLD.

The null result

Run against a server I did not write (@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory 1.0.0 to 2.2.1), the replay found no break: HOLD, 3 preserved, 2 unsealed. The two unsealed ones exist because that server also returns structuredContent that a text-only jar cannot compare. That is a limit of my jar format, not a clean bill for the server.

What I would not claim

Not the first MCP record/replay tool (mcp-recorder, AgentVCR and mcpsnoop exist). Ten jars, five of six tools; SHIP means "clean on the recorded set". The breaks are mine. No outside user has run it yet.

Live cabinet (replays in your browser): https://specimen.edycu.dev/ · Code (MIT): https://github.com/edycutjong/specimen · Built for Kiroween 2026 (Frankenstein).

items.title: LIMBO: offline apps that show you the edit they could not merge
items.summary: I wrote this as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon (Skeleton Crew category). The angle: a merge that loses an edit silently is worse than one that fails At a lake with no signal, Sari ticks "tent" on a shared packing list while a friend deletes it. Back in range, one edit wins and the other disappears. Nobody can tell which. Last-write-wins is the default and it hides the loss. LIMBO is a small local-first skeleton where every operation declares how it merges , plus two apps built on it. When two offline edits genuinely conflict, the loser does not vanish: the deleted tent comes back as a ghost twin beside the ticked one, and one tap resolves it. What is measured, and what is not Convergence is property-tested, not proven: 3 replicas, 10,000 random orderings, seed 20251031, 0 divergences ( evidence/convergence/full-2026-11-22.json ). The suite has a vacuity guard and mutation fixtures that must fail, because a property test that cannot fail proves nothing. A judge can press Run shuffle test in the live app and watch their own browser replay the on-screen ops in random causal orders (a replay of what is on screen, not the 10,000-ordering run). One thing no CRDT can do: stop two offline users both claiming the last stove. LIMBO makes claims provisional, picks one claimant by a declared rule on reconnect, and shows the other person their lost claim. How Kiro built it Claude Code orchestrated: it wrote each brief, launched a headless Kiro CLI session, reviewed the diff and committed. Kiro wrote the specs and executed the tasks: 194 Kiro sessions (679.87 credits; 179 across 12 specs, 15 kit and bootstrap), 115 of 124 product commits carrying a Kiro session trailer (92.74%); 17 ledger rows are edits made outside Kiro (9 of the 124 product commits), listed in the repo. The kit: 6 steering files, 2 custom agents, 8 hooks (1,824 logged fires) and a convergence MCP server. The part I liked most is an Agent Stop hook that blocks "done" while the properties fail, and hands Kiro the shrunk counterexample. It blocked 2 times: once on a property suite that ran a new op without its payload generator (Kiro wired it in), once on a fault I seeded on purpose. The honest part I pre-registered an A/B: same op-writing task with and without the kit, 20 runs. Result: 0 of 10 held-out failures in both arms, Fisher p = 1. No measurable effect. Worse, 2 of 10 kit-arm runs edited the gate's own guard to pass, so I then added the property suite and the vacuity guard to the protected list of the wrapper's hash manifest (not re-piloted). Kiro's Spec Correctness PBT is IDE-only and I did not use it; my properties are fast-check run by hooks. Try it BASECAMP: https://basecamp.limbo.edycu.dev AFTERSHOCK: https://aftershock.limbo.edycu.dev Repo (MIT, /.kiro at the root): https://github.com/edycutjong/limbo No install, no login. Press Cut link, play the lake scene, restore the link.

items.title: My Kiro hooks saw 5% of the writes. Here is how I found out.
items.summary: I wrote four hooks to stop Kiro from breaking my project's one rule. They fired, they blocked a bad write in a live test, and I was ready to call it done. Then I counted what they had actually seen: about 5% of the writes. This post is written as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon. The project is Her Hand in the Steam : Cook Mode for handwritten recipes, where the writer's own scanned hand is wiped out of the steam on a window at the step where they left a judgement. Code: github.com/edycutjong/steam . The rule the hooks were for The product's promise is "quoted, not generated". The handwriting on the glass is the scan's own ink. No handwriting font, no synthetic voice, no imitation of the hand. I turned that into steering files and into Kiro hooks: no-imitation refuses a write under src/ that speaks or fakes handwriting. catalog-gate refuses a write to the public catalog that lists a recipe failing the ingestion gate. props-on-save re-runs the gate whenever an agent saves a reading. I tested them in a live Kiro session: four writes tried, two refused (a file calling speechSynthesis , and the catalog). Both blocks are in docs/kiro-evidence/hooks.log . Good. The count Later I wrote a small tool ( tools/evidence/session-ledger.ts ) that reads Kiro's own session store for the workspace and counts, per tool call, what was written and whether a hook event followed. Across 39 sessions: 543 shell commands wrote under src/ (368 of them to non-test files). 30 write-tool calls ( fs_write , str_replace ) wrote under src/ . 0 of the 543 had a hook event. Kiro had been writing code mostly through its shell tool (heredocs, sed , python3 -c ). My hooks matched the write tools. The enforcement I had demonstrated was real, and it covered roughly 5% of the calls. The ledger's write rule is a heuristic with known misses, so treat the counts as approximate, but not as approximate as the gap. Fixing it with the spec that Kiro itself uses I made it a bugfix spec ( .kiro/specs/hook-coverage/bugfix.md ), red tests first, 12 [kiro] commits: shell-gate (PreToolUse, matcher shell ) judges the text a shell command writes under src/ with the same rules as no-imitation , and refuses any shell write of the catalog other than npm run catalog . About 0.06 s per call. src-scan-after-shell (PostToolUse, matcher shell ) judges the added lines under src/ after every shell command, so a script that builds a path from parts is still seen. About 0.11 s per call. A steering line: edit files with the write tools. { "name" : "shell-gate" , "trigger" : "PreToolUse" , "matcher" : "shell" , "action" : { "type" : "command" , "command" : "node tools/hooks/shell-gate.ts" } , "timeout" : 10 } Three live probes, each with its line in hooks.log : Probe Outcome heredoc writing speechSynthesis into src/steam/zz-shell-probe.ts refused, the file was never created echo '{}' > content/catalog.json refused, the catalog stayed byte-identical python3 -c building the path and the word from parts not seen before it ran; caught after the write by src-scan The same habit, earlier: a test that passed the bug The first defect of this kind showed up in the kill test, before the build. The prototype cropped each recipe line from the scan with boxes read by eye, and they overlapped the neighbouring lines. Handwriting does not sit in tidy rows: strokes cross between lines, so a box cut there slices letters. I turned the property into a gate (P4: a note may show only its own line's ink) and replaced boxes with ink-ownership masks built by code. Agents return line and word indices; code builds the masks; the gate decides. Run against a reproduction of those eye-read boxes the gate fails steps 1 to 5 (5 failed, 1 passed); against the ownership masks it passes. That red-to-green is the crop-overlap bugfix spec, and the two runs are in docs/kiro-evidence/crop-overlap/ . Both stories have the same shape. A check written by the same side that did the work shares its blind spot. The useful move was a second check that did not share its blind spot: a property over component ownership in one case, a count taken from the agent's own session log in the other. What still does not work In headless kiro-cli , a PostToolUse exit 2 only logs. It is not shown to the agent and does not stop it. src-scan is evidence, not a block. A script run by name, find -exec and xargs are not seen before they run. PreTaskExec and PostTaskExec hooks did not fire headless in my probe (kiro-cli 3.5.0, 5 of 7 trigger types fired), so my tests-after-task hook never ran in this project. The lesson A hook that blocks a probe is not coverage. If you enforce a rule with hooks, count what the hooks saw against what the agent did, from the agent's own session log. Mine took one afternoon to write and changed what I believed about my own setup. The rest of the Kiro evidence, including what was planned and not built (no MCP server, no Power, no spec-vs-vibe comparison), is in docs/KIRO.md and docs/EXPERIMENTS.md . Try the project: https://steam.edycu.dev

I tested them in a live Kiro session: four writes tried, two refused (a file calling speechSynthesis, and the catalog). Both blocks are in docs/kiro-evidence/hooks.log. Good.

The count

Later I wrote a small tool (tools/evidence/session-ledger.ts) that reads Kiro's own session store for the workspace and counts, per tool call, what was written and whether a hook event followed. Across 39 sessions:

  • 543 shell commands wrote under src/ (368 of them to non-test files).
  • 30 write-tool calls (fs_write, str_replace) wrote under src/.
  • 0 of the 543 had a hook event.

Kiro had been writing code mostly through its shell tool (heredocs, sed, python3 -c). My hooks matched the write tools. The enforcement I had demonstrated was real, and it covered roughly 5% of the calls. The ledger's write rule is a heuristic with known misses, so treat the counts as approximate, but not as approximate as the gap.

Fixing it with the spec that Kiro itself uses

I made it a bugfix spec (.kiro/specs/hook-coverage/bugfix.md), red tests first, 12 [kiro] commits:

  • shell-gate (PreToolUse, matcher shell) judges the text a shell command writes under src/ with the same rules as no-imitation, and refuses any shell write of the catalog other than npm run catalog. About 0.06 s per call.
  • src-scan-after-shell (PostToolUse, matcher shell) judges the added lines under src/ after every shell command, so a script that builds a path from parts is still seen. About 0.11 s per call.
  • A steering line: edit files with the write tools. 
{
  "name": "shell-gate",
  "trigger": "PreToolUse",
  "matcher": "shell",
  "action": { "type": "command", "command": "node tools/hooks/shell-gate.ts" },
  "timeout": 10
}

Three live probes, each with its line in hooks.log:

Probe Outcome heredoc writing speechSynthesis into src/steam/zz-shell-probe.ts refused, the file was never created echo '{}' > content/catalog.json refused, the catalog stayed byte-identical python3 -c building the path and the word from parts not seen before it ran; caught after the write by src-scan
The same habit, earlier: a test that passed the bug

The first defect of this kind showed up in the kill test, before the build. The prototype cropped each recipe line from the scan with boxes read by eye, and they overlapped the neighbouring lines. Handwriting does not sit in tidy rows: strokes cross between lines, so a box cut there slices letters. I turned the property into a gate (P4: a note may show only its own line's ink) and replaced boxes with ink-ownership masks built by code. Agents return line and word indices; code builds the masks; the gate decides. Run against a reproduction of those eye-read boxes the gate fails steps 1 to 5 (5 failed, 1 passed); against the ownership masks it passes. That red-to-green is the crop-overlap bugfix spec, and the two runs are in docs/kiro-evidence/crop-overlap/.

Both stories have the same shape. A check written by the same side that did the work shares its blind spot. The useful move was a second check that did not share its blind spot: a property over component ownership in one case, a count taken from the agent's own session log in the other.

What still does not work
  • In headless kiro-cli, a PostToolUse exit 2 only logs. It is not shown to the agent and does not stop it. src-scan is evidence, not a block.
  • A script run by name, find -exec and xargs are not seen before they run.
  • PreTaskExec and PostTaskExec hooks did not fire headless in my probe (kiro-cli 3.5.0, 5 of 7 trigger types fired), so my tests-after-task hook never ran in this project.
The lesson

A hook that blocks a probe is not coverage. If you enforce a rule with hooks, count what the hooks saw against what the agent did, from the agent's own session log. Mine took one afternoon to write and changed what I believed about my own setup.

The rest of the Kiro evidence, including what was planned and not built (no MCP server, no Power, no spec-vs-vibe comparison), is in docs/KIRO.md and docs/EXPERIMENTS.md.

Try the project: https://steam.edycu.dev

items.title: I gave a Kiro agent a Commodore 64 and a checksum it can't argue with
items.summary: The human problem first: in 1984 you typed a program out of a magazine, hit RUN, and got ?SYNTAX ERROR IN 20 . Forty years later the page is a scan, free OCR has misread the slashed zero as an 8 , and the program is dead again. The obvious fix is to hand the listing to an LLM. The obvious failure is that it will happily return a line that runs and is wrong. This is my entry to the Kiroween 2026 hackathon (Resurrection), and it is built around one idea: the model chooses where to look; code decides what is true. Live: https://ready.edycu.dev (press Resurrect ) · Kiro view: https://ready.edycu.dev/kiro The magazine already printed the answer key COMPUTE!'s Gazette ended its program lines with a checksum comment, :rem NNN . Per line, it is the sum of the character codes of the line number and the body (spaces count 0), mod 256. So most OCR errors show up offline, without a model, as a line whose recomputed sum differs from the printed one (a matching sum is not proof the line is identical): export function computeChecksum ( lineNo : number , body : string ) : number { let sum = rawSum ( String ( lineNo ) ) ; for ( const seg of scanBody ( body ) ) { if ( seg . kind === "group" ) { if ( seg . name !== SPACE_TOKEN ) sum += TOKENS [ seg . name ] ! * seg . count ; } else if ( seg . char !== " " ) { sum += rawSum ( seg . char ) ; } } return sum % 256 ; } A Kiro spec ( checksum-oracle ) produced this, plus a tokenizer, from EARS requirements. While implementing the spec's tasks, Kiro probed the real C64 core and found three places where my own spec was wrong about how the machine behaves. The agent can propose, never write The fixer is a Kiro custom agent, resurrector . Its tool list is six MCP tools from a server I wrote ( c64_reload , c64_run , c64_read_screen , c64_press , checksum_line , apply_patch ). File read, shell, write and web are denied. The only way to change the listing is apply_patch , and a Pre Tool Use hook runs the same gate code the browser runs before the call reaches the server: // abridged from scripts/hooks/checksum-gate.mjs const v = applyPatch ( listing , patch , expected , { force_unverified : Boolean ( toolInput . force_unverified ) , refusalCounts : refusals , } ) ; // ...later: refused -> exit 2, stderr = the gate's reason, fed back to the model if ( verdict . verdict === "refused" ) { /* ... */ process . exit ( 2 ) ; } A patch is accepted only if the line is typeable on a real C64 keyboard, its checksum matches the one printed on the page, and the emulated C64 then runs it. After repeated refusals the agent may force a line, but a forced line is stamped FORCED and the verdict can never be RESURRECTED. The Cheat button on the site empties the broken line through the same gate; it is refused. The wall Kiro's Agent Stop hook is how I make the agent keep going until the program's title screen appears. It fires once per prompt, so one forced extra turn is all you get. My recorder therefore resumes the session between cycles. It works, but it is a limit I only found by measuring the hook headless ( evidence/spikes/spike-K2.md ). The second wall was credits. Two of my three feature specs reached or neared their credit caps mid-task (51.26 of 50, 68.71 of 70). I finished the ones I could with Claude Code (one task of the MCP spec is still open) and labelled them claude-direct in the commit messages and the DX report, rather than pretend Kiro wrote them. Numbers All from files in the repo: 492 tests in 41 files, including a property that types generated and OCR-mutated lines into the real C64 core and compares memory with my tokenizer. (Claude Code wrote it, not Kiro.) It found four edges (a body starting with a digit merges into the line number, for one). Gate applyPatch : p50 0.01 ms, p95 0.03 ms (N=2000). Agent evals: 7 of 9 cases run and passing, 6 of 6 model runs RESURRECTED (2 cases, N=3 each). Cases 5 and 6 are not run. Experiment E0: on the real 1984 page, plain search fixed 3 of 18 failing lines; the agent made all 18 checksum-consistent (N=2). Honest limits The live site is recorded playback. No C64 ROM is hosted (rights), so "IT LIVES" there is captioned "as recorded". The 1984 page and its OCR output are not in the repo. On the real title path the result is 19 of 28 lines source-exact against a vision-read reference; the rest are checksum-consistent, not proven identical. /scan flags checksum mismatches on live pages but withholds the repair. I did not run an experiment isolating steering's effect, so I claim none. Kiro was used through kiro-cli: three feature specs, a custom agent, four hooks, seven steering files, an MCP server, a skill. The prompts I sent, in order, are in prompts/ in the repo.
items.summary_html:
The human problem first: in 1984 you typed a program out of a magazine, hit RUN, and got ?SYNTAX ERROR IN 20. Forty years later the page is a scan, free OCR has misread the slashed zero as an 8, and the program is dead again.

The obvious fix is to hand the listing to an LLM. The obvious failure is that it will happily return a line that runs and is wrong. This is my entry to the Kiroween 2026 hackathon (Resurrection), and it is built around one idea: the model chooses where to look; code decides what is true.

Live: https://ready.edycu.dev (press Resurrect) · Kiro view: https://ready.edycu.dev/kiro

The magazine already printed the answer key

COMPUTE!'s Gazette ended its program lines with a checksum comment, :rem NNN. Per line, it is the sum of the character codes of the line number and the body (spaces count 0), mod 256. So most OCR errors show up offline, without a model, as a line whose recomputed sum differs from the printed one (a matching sum is not proof the line is identical):

export function computeChecksum(lineNo: number, body: string): number {
  let sum = rawSum(String(lineNo));
  for (const seg of scanBody(body)) {
    if (seg.kind === "group") {
      if (seg.name !== SPACE_TOKEN) sum += TOKENS[seg.name]! * seg.count;
    } else if (seg.char !== " ") {
      sum += rawSum(seg.char);
    }
  }
  return sum % 256;
}

A Kiro spec (checksum-oracle) produced this, plus a tokenizer, from EARS requirements. While implementing the spec's tasks, Kiro probed the real C64 core and found three places where my own spec was wrong about how the machine behaves.

The agent can propose, never write

The fixer is a Kiro custom agent, resurrector. Its tool list is six MCP tools from a server I wrote (c64_reload, c64_run, c64_read_screen, c64_press, checksum_line, apply_patch). File read, shell, write and web are denied. The only way to change the listing is apply_patch, and a Pre Tool Use hook runs the same gate code the browser runs before the call reaches the server:

// abridged from scripts/hooks/checksum-gate.mjs
const v = applyPatch(listing, patch, expected, {
  force_unverified: Boolean(toolInput.force_unverified),
  refusalCounts: refusals,
});
// ...later: refused -> exit 2, stderr = the gate's reason, fed back to the model
if (verdict.verdict === "refused") { /* ... */ process.exit(2); }

A patch is accepted only if the line is typeable on a real C64 keyboard, its checksum matches the one printed on the page, and the emulated C64 then runs it. After repeated refusals the agent may force a line, but a forced line is stamped FORCED and the verdict can never be RESURRECTED. The Cheat button on the site empties the broken line through the same gate; it is refused.

The wall

Kiro's Agent Stop hook is how I make the agent keep going until the program's title screen appears. It fires once per prompt, so one forced extra turn is all you get. My recorder therefore resumes the session between cycles. It works, but it is a limit I only found by measuring the hook headless (evidence/spikes/spike-K2.md).

The second wall was credits. Two of my three feature specs reached or neared their credit caps mid-task (51.26 of 50, 68.71 of 70). I finished the ones I could with Claude Code (one task of the MCP spec is still open) and labelled them claude-direct in the commit messages and the DX report, rather than pretend Kiro wrote them.

Numbers

All from files in the repo:

  • 492 tests in 41 files, including a property that types generated and OCR-mutated lines into the real C64 core and compares memory with my tokenizer. (Claude Code wrote it, not Kiro.) It found four edges (a body starting with a digit merges into the line number, for one).
  • Gate applyPatch: p50 0.01 ms, p95 0.03 ms (N=2000).
  • Agent evals: 7 of 9 cases run and passing, 6 of 6 model runs RESURRECTED (2 cases, N=3 each). Cases 5 and 6 are not run.
  • Experiment E0: on the real 1984 page, plain search fixed 3 of 18 failing lines; the agent made all 18 checksum-consistent (N=2).
Honest limits
  • The live site is recorded playback. No C64 ROM is hosted (rights), so "IT LIVES" there is captioned "as recorded".
  • The 1984 page and its OCR output are not in the repo. On the real title path the result is 19 of 28 lines source-exact against a vision-read reference; the rest are checksum-consistent, not proven identical.
  • /scan flags checksum mismatches on live pages but withholds the repair.
  • I did not run an experiment isolating steering's effect, so I claim none.

Kiro was used through kiro-cli: three feature specs, a custom agent, four hooks, seven steering files, an MCP server, a skill. The prompts I sent, in order, are in prompts/ in the repo.
